name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lahn advocates for privatized Medicaid, defends attack ad against Sand
description: BRITT — Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn defended his Medicaid stance Saturday at the Hancock County Fair in Britt, expressing a need to continue Gov. Kim Reynolds’ healthcare policy. Lahn said delivering healthcare through the private sector with government oversight is “bipartisan,” saying 42 states including Iowa use managed care organizations[...]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, left, speaks to voters at the Hancock County Fair in Britt on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kadin Luhmann for Iowa Capital Dispatch)BRITT — Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn defended his Medicaid stance Saturday at the Hancock County Fair in Britt, expressing a need to continue Gov. Kim Reynolds’ healthcare policy.
Lahn said delivering healthcare through the private sector with government oversight is “bipartisan,” saying 42 states including Iowa use managed care organizations, including many Democratic states.
“I don’t think the government would do a good job of delivering healthcare for the people of Iowa,” Lahn said. “I think that the private sector can do a great job delivering this, but the government has to hold them accountable. We have to make sure we’re getting the right care, proper payment, and also I will not allow any of these companies to use AI in denying coverage from people.”
Emma O’Brien, a communications staffer for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, said Lahn wants to continue “failed health care policies.”
“Zach Lahn has spent his career as a political operative trying to kick people off their health insurance,” O’Brien said. “Now, he’s promising to continue Iowa’s failed privatized Medicaid system, spearheaded under Gov. Reynolds, which has led to worse care and higher costs for Iowans.”
Lahn defends ad that Sand called ‘dishonest’
During a town hall in Fort Dodge Monday, Sand railed against an attack ad paid for by the Lahn campaign. The advertisement featured edited clips from KCCI broadcasts, in which anchors say the “auditor’s office took no action” when millions of dollars in state funds went missing.
“The only thing that he ran for six weeks after the general election was an attack on me and my record that was so fundamentally dishonest that the TV station, when they saw their anchor’s words being taken out of context, actually made a news story about the television ad to tell people how dishonest it was,” Sand said.
In 2024, $53 million in court debt payments were misallocated to due a computer error in Iowa’s judicial payment systems. Republican lawmakers criticized Sand, who also serves as state auditor. for failing to alert lawmakers or intervene. Sand 
Sand said in December 2024 the auditor’s office had been in contact with officials from the state judicial branch and Department of Transportation multiple times after being notified of the issue in October 2022, and that the office remained in contact with the judicial branch in conducting internal and independent investigations into the issue. He also said the auditor’s office did not have staff equipped to investigate computer errors.

Lahn argued Saturday the ad is not dishonest, and Sand had the authority to step in and do something.
“They’re not false. He is not doing his job,” Lahn said. “In 2025, his office had the statutory authority to get involved in that, and they didn’t do it. Once they miss their audit, he is statutorily allowed to get involved into that, and at the very least, provide help.”
Lahn calls for expanding ESA program for private schools
Lahn spoke with voters Saturday at the Hancock County Fair, where people told him that some of their biggest concerns involve education in Iowa.
Lahn said he wants to expand the Education Savings Account program, which provides taxpayer funds for private school expenses regardless of family income, while simultaneously improving public schools, saying market-based competition will make both better.
“My job as governor is to make sure we have the number one public schools in the country,” Lahn said. “I just had a superintendent at one of my stops today say to me he wants competition. He welcomes competition. He just needs to be unburdened to compete, and so my job is to find these superintendents who want to compete with innovative models and cut out the red tape, give them innovation waivers and a budget to do it, so they know we’re behind them.
Lahn advocates for local foods in schools
Lahn said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins about wanting to put more locally sourced food in Iowa public schools.
“One of my biggest initiatives is how do we get more food served in public schools that is grown in the state of Iowa,” Lahn said. We need to create a new market for small farmers because a lot of this food that’s being served in public schools is already under a USDA food subsidized program, but only the big guys can get in it.”
Lahn optimistic about potential in blue counties
Lahn was also optimistic about his chances in Democratic Iowa counties, such as Polk and Johnson, where he performed well in the primary election.
“I think if you look at where we overperformed the most in the primary, it was Polk County,” Lahn said. “We had a lot of support, and we also had a lot of young people and a lot of non-primary voters come out to support us because we have a message that’s very different, very Iowa-centric. We want to make Iowa the healthiest place to raise a family, tackle the cancer crisis, clean up our water. These are things that Polk County, Johnson County care about.”

title: 3 dead, 2 injured in Twin Falls In-N-Out shooting
description: This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Aug. 1, 2026. Three people are dead and two are injured after a shooting Saturday afternoon at the Twin Falls In-N-Out, according to a city spokesperson. Joshua Palmer, Twin Falls’ public information officer, confirmed those numbers, though he said in a text message officials […]
text:
Three people are dead and two are injured after a shooting Saturday afternoon at the Twin Falls In-N-Out, according to a city spokesperson. (Photo by Douglas Sacha/Getty Images)This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Aug. 1, 2026.
Three people are dead and two are injured after a shooting Saturday afternoon at the Twin Falls In-N-Out, according to a city spokesperson.
Joshua Palmer, Twin Falls’ public information officer, confirmed those numbers, though he said in a text message officials “expect that number to be higher” as the investigation and response continues.
Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said in a late afternoon press conference that the suspected shooter is dead “nearby on the scene” and that he believes “the threat to the community is over.”
“We are working to try to ascertain his identity and the motivations behind [the shooting] and we’ll be able to figure that out in the next coming days,” Hicks said.
He shared few details, but called it “a very chaotic scene.”

Idahoans, join me in keeping the Twin Falls community in your prayers as law enforcement and first responders respond to an active shooter situation near In-N-Out.
Please avoid the area and follow directions from law enforcement as they work to keep everyone safe.
— Brad Little (@GovernorLittle) August 1, 2026

Hicks urged anyone with information about the shooting to reach out to law enforcement.
“Anyone with information related to this incident who has not already spoken with law enforcement is asked to contact dispatch at 208-735-4357,” a Twin Falls PD press release said.
Several videos posted to social media appear to show a man wearing a black shirt and jeans carrying a large rifle.
One depicts him shooting the front windshield of a parked Tesla, while another shows the man carrying the rifle and walking through the In-N-Out drive-thru.
Twin Falls Police said in a Facebook post that roads in the area, including the Perrine Bridge linking the city with Interstate 84, were closed but have since reopened.
St. Luke’s Health System issued a “critical alert” urging the public to avoid its Magic Valley hospital unless there’s an emergency.
Boise State Public Radio will update this story as more details become available.



Idaho officials responded in statements and social media posts about the shooting:
Idaho Gov. Brad Little, in an X post: “Idahoans, join me in keeping the Twin Falls community in your prayers as law enforcement and first responders respond to an active shooter situation near In-N-Out. Please avoid the area and follow directions from law enforcement as they work to keep everyone safe.”
Idaho Democratic Party chairwoman Lauren Necochea, in an emailed statement: “All of Idaho is grieving after the shooting in Twin Falls. Families are facing losses they never should have had to endure, and a community is struggling to understand how an ordinary day could end in such horror. My heart is with loved ones mourning innocent lives taken, the victims who were injured, and everyone whose sense of safety was shattered. Tragedies like this reveal the worst of what people can do, but also the best of who we can be. I am deeply grateful for the first responders and neighbors who moved toward danger, cared for others, and showed up when they were needed most. In the days ahead, may we carry that same compassion and courage forward and make sure the people of Twin Falls do not face this alone.”
Idaho Republican Party chairwoman Dorothy Moon, in an emailed statement:
“I am grateful that the threat to the community has ended and that there is no longer an ongoing danger to the public. Our hearts go out to the families who have lost loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone who is anxiously awaiting news about family and friends.
Idaho has always been a place where neighbors look out for one another and families can live in peace. Today’s tragedy is a heartbreaking reminder that senseless acts of violence can touch any community.
I want to express my deepest gratitude to the law enforcement officers, EMS personnel, and other first responders who responded with courage and professionalism under unimaginable circumstances.
I ask all Idahoans to join me in praying for the victims, their families, the people of Twin Falls, and everyone involved in the response and recovery. May God bring comfort to those who are grieving, healing to those who were injured, and strength to the entire community in the difficult days ahead.”
U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “I’m monitoring the news out of Twin Falls of an active shooter situation. I urge locals and visitors to obey all directions from law enforcement, avoid the area, and report any suspicious activity immediately. I’m grateful for the swift response of Idaho’s first responders.”
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “Vicki and I are monitoring the shooting in Twin Falls. We pray for the safety of all involved and thank the brave first responders on scene.”
U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “My team and I are closely monitoring the situation in Twin Falls.
I am disheartened to learn of the senseless loss of life. Please join me in praying for the victims’ families, the surrounding community, our brave law enforcement officers and first responders on scene, and all those affected by this tragedy.”
U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “I am aware of the shooting in the area of In-N-Out in Twin Falls. My team is closely monitoring the situation as more information becomes available from the Twin Falls Police Department.
I am praying for everyone affected and for the brave first responders who are on the scene.”



Idaho Capital Sun editor Christina Lords contributed to this report.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Adams ends governor run speculation at Kentucky’s annual Fancy Farm Picnic
description: FANCY FARM — After fueling speculation about a run for governor, Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams said he wouldn’t step into the ring next year and instead was backing U.S. Rep. James Comer.  Ahead of the annual Fancy Farm Picnic, Adams told the Lexington Herald-Leader he was thinking about launching a campaign for governor at […]
text:
Supporters of Republican Andy Barr and Democrat Charles Booker, both running for U.S. Senate, squared off at the annual Fancy Farm political picnic on Aug. 1, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)FANCY FARM — After fueling speculation about a run for governor, Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams said he wouldn’t step into the ring next year and instead was backing U.S. Rep. James Comer. 
Ahead of the annual Fancy Farm Picnic, Adams told the Lexington Herald-Leader he was thinking about launching a campaign for governor at the picnic. However, as the last speaker Saturday, Adams said “the best thing I can do for my team is to call on all Republicans to join me in supporting James Comer to be our next governor.” 
“The Democrats are going to pull out all the stops to claw onto the one office they can still win,” Adams said. “We absolutely have to nominate our strongest ticket. The first thing we must do to strengthen our chances is to avoid some messy primary where we all attack each other.” 
Secretary of State Michael Adams announced he would not be running for governor in 2027 at the annual Fancy Farm picnic on Aug. 1, 2027. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
While a U.S. Senate seat is up for election this November, Kentucky’s 2027 race was the main attraction at the Fancy Farm Picnic this weekend. The picnic, in the tiny West Kentucky town of Fancy Farm, is a barbecue fundraiser for the St. Jerome Catholic Church in Graves County but is better known as a political roast in front of a crowd of passionate Republicans and Democrats. 
Two Democrats have announced their bids to succeed two-term Gov. Andy Beshear in office and addressed the fervent crowd on Saturday — Lieutenant Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former Beshear senior adviser Rocky Adkins. 
Coleman pushed back at some criticism she received when she asked government employees during the COVID pandemic to review unemployment claims for people she knew, including her hairdresser. 
“I do want to apologize for helping her during COVID because it’s actually Allison Ball’s hairdresser that needed all the help she could get,” Coleman said, referring to the Republican auditor who was also a speaker. 
Supporters of Democratic governor candidate Jacqueline Coleman cheered at the Fancy Farm picnic. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
Both Coleman and Adkins were critical of Comer, who has yet to announce a bid for the 2027 race. He’s currently seeking reelection in the 1st Congressional District.
Adkins said that while Comer voted against an infrastructure bill passed during the Biden administration, he has had press conferences celebrating local projects the money funded. 
“He forgot to put in that press conference that, yes, he voted against the funding to pay for the bill,” Adkins said. 
Comer bit back as well. He said he was happy for Coleman that since Adkins is no longer the “top bureaucrat” in the Beshear administration, she can start “taking credit for all the great things these Republican legislators have done.” 
As for Adkins, Comer said: “Since after 49 years you are no longer on the government team, I’m worried you’ll starve to death.” Since “none of the current special interests” will pay for him, Comer then started a collection plate for Adkins. 
Democrat Rocky Adkins, who is running for governor in 2027, sits on stage at the annual Fancy Farm picnic on Aug. 1, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
Speaking to reporters afterwards, Comer said he discussed running for governor with President Donald Trump but he would make a decision soon. He added that he was hopeful at “the prospect of having a pretty united Republican ticket” as Democrats have generally fared well in Kentucky’s governor races in the last few decades. 
“I was very surprised and very happy,” Comer said on Adams’ decision, saying they had been in communication over the last few weeks. 
Adams told the Lantern he had also spoken with Comer the week of the picnic. 
“We’ve talked quite a bit, and I have a great comfort level with him,” Adams said. “I do sincerely think he’s the best candidate we’ll have. I think he is perfectly prepared for this job. He’s done so many other things that make him prepared for this position”
‘Where’s Mitch?’ ‘Where’s Beshear?’
Even though Beshear and Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell were not present at the picnic, their names came up repeatedly as the butt of jokes. Early on in the afternoon’s program, Democrats on one side of the pavilion began chanting, “Where’s Mitch?” In response, the Republicans said, “Where’s Andy?” 
Beshear said the picnic conflicted with his son’s final travel baseball tournament of his high school career. McConnell has been embroiled in the national spotlight as he was hospitalized in June and has not since been voting in the Senate. He said in a statement he would not attend the picnic this year as he was undergoing “intense physical therapy.” 
Charles Booker, the former state representative who is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate this year, said that he wanted everyone to get “the same health care Mitch McConnell is getting right now.” 
Meanwhile, U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, the Republican nominee, said despite his absence this weekend, Beshear is quick to find podiums and put on his emergency management jacket when there is an emergency. 
“You know he loves that jacket so much, he has pajamas just like it,” Barr said. 
Even a Democrat poked some fun at Beshear’s absence. Coleman said she had attempted to convince Beshear to go to the picnic this year. 
“I even told him Fancy Farm was in New Hampshire,” she said. That’s a state with an early Democratic presidential primary in 2028. 
Dave Baker, a WKYT anchor who was the emcee of the picnic, said that Beshear had probably figured it would be “a safe bet” to avoid standing on this stage between Coleman and his former senior adviser, Rocky Adkins, who is also running for governor. At that, Coleman and Adkins shared a laugh on the stage.
Before the picnic
Hours before the stump speeches began at the picnic, Comer and Barr were among speakers at the annual Graves County GOP Breakfast in Mayfield. There, they framed the November elections as Republican values versus “socialism.” 
Comer, who has gained national attention as the chairman of the fiery House Oversight Committee, said Democrats have gained “energy now that they haven’t had in a long time” and said it’s the “young socialist movement that’s taken over the National Democrat Party.” He pointed to elected Democratic Socialists of America candidates in Kentucky on the Louisville Metro Council and in the General Assembly.
Barr called his opponent, Booker, “the Mamdani of Kentucky,” likening him to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is a DSA member and defeated former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo by about nine points last fall. 
“If we lose this seat in the Senate in Kentucky, we will lose the Senate, and if we lose the Senate, we will lose our country. That is literally what’s on the line,” Barr said. “So, join me in fighting the socialist crazy.” 
Supporters cheered for Republican Congressman James Comer who is up for re-election this fall, but is considering a run for governor in 2027. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
The night before, Democrats gathered at the Marshall County Democrats’ Mike Miller Memorial Bean Dinner, where Booker spoke, as well as Adkins and Coleman. Throughout the evening, speakers’ remarks largely focused on opposing Republicans at the state and federal levels. 
“When we win this year, we will be shining a light that the country needs to see because democracy is being torn apart in our faces,” Booker said. “The Constitution is being trampled on at this very moment, and the idea that our children can have a better future than we have experienced —all of that is in question right now.” 
Adkins said he thinks Kentuckians “are tired of the political divide” and care about whether or not they have jobs, good roads, hospitals and public schools. 
“We’re about helping people. We’re about making sure organized labor has the work that they need to be able to put food on the table and a roof over their head,” Adkins said. 
Coleman, who touted recent endorsements from labor unions, said Kentuckians “are tired of the same old, same old.” 
“They want a governor who will continue to fight for them and against the chaos and corruption that we have coming out of Washington, D.C.,” she said. “They want people who will talk about people and not politicians.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Public march counters pro-deportation event in central Indiana
description: About 1,000 Hoosiers supportive of immigrants marched through Fishers on Saturday — a counter protest to a pro-deportation event planned for the city with remarks from two statewide elected officials.  The private mass deportation event was unexpectedly moved to Greenfield, according to an unconfirmed email sent to attendees, beginning at 6 p.m. Two outlets[...]
text:
Pro-immigrant protesters line up to march in Fishers on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)About 1,000 Hoosiers supportive of immigrants marched through Fishers on Saturday — a counter protest to a pro-deportation event planned for the city with remarks from two statewide elected officials. 
The private mass deportation event was unexpectedly moved to Greenfield, according to an unconfirmed email sent to attendees, beginning at 6 p.m. Two outlets had exclusive media access to the event headlined by former Border Patrol leader Greg Bovino, said Daniel Poynter, executive director of Save Heritage Indiana. He declined to name the outlets.
Under light rain, thunder and a billowing American flag, Fishers protesters gathered in front of the Nickel Plate District Amphitheater for speeches. Organizers concluded the protest, though, after lightning was spotted within five miles.
Among the attendees was Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis, who likened the mass deportation rally to the activity of the Ku Klux Klan, which had a stronghold in Indiana in the early 20th century.
“They are replacing slogans, uniforms and messages, but they are using the same playbook that played in Indiana over 100 years ago,” Qaddoura told protesters. 
A pro-immigrant protester with an “Ind 4 All” sign marches with a child through Fishers on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Rabbi Aaron Spiegel, executive director of the Greater Indianapolis Multifaith Alliance, said immigrants are just the latest in a series of groups to be scapegoated for societal problems.
“We have a moral and ethical duty to say ‘No, we will not dehumanize anyone,’” Spiegel said.
Attendees’ signs expressed support for immigrants and took aim at officials, including Bovino, President Donald Trump and Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith.
One masked person held a sign reading “preserve American demographics,” but protesters lifted signs of their own to block out the message.
Others on Saturday sought to emphasize Fishers as a city welcoming to immigrants.
“We live in a diverse neighborhood,” said Christine Winger, who wore a shirt reading “Fishers is for everyone.” 
“Our neighbors are from Ukraine, and from Japan and from all over the world, and they are welcome to be my neighbors, and I support them being here in Fishers, Indiana, because they are an important part of our community,” she said. 
Kelley Curran, another attendee, said she suspected the deportation event was moved out of Fishers in response to the showing of support for immigrants. 
Curran was there with Joe Hauptmann, who was encouraged by the turnout in a politically conservative state. A former chair of the Indiana Libertarian Party, Hauptmann said he’d often aligned with Republicans but was disappointed by their approach on immigration. 
“I feel very used because what I thought, when we were talking about freedom, we meant for everyone, and it turns out most of our allies meant only for themselves,” Hauptmann said.
Few details shared on pro-deportation event
Many of the specifics of the private pro-deportation event, with a $50 general admission fee for the evening and requirements of suits and ties for men and dresses for women, remained undisclosed.
Poynter said on X that it was sold out but refused to say how many people would attend. 
Save Heritage Indiana planned to release videos of the event, Poynter said. It was set to wrap up after 9 p.m.
The event ultimately ended up being in Greenfield, according to an unconfirmed email sent to attendees Saturday, with ID checks required for entry. But even before then, Save Heritage Indiana opted not to publicize the location. The group wrote on X that was to avoid harassment from “those who oppose free speech” and because of violent threats. 
Ashley Elrod, spokesperson for Fishers Mayor Scott Fadness, previously told the Capital Chronicle he hadn’t been contacted by the organizers and didn’t plan to attend. Elrod added local police wouldn’t provide private security for the event or a potential counterprotest. 
Gregory Bovino, former U.S. Border Patrol “commander at large,” stands in the street after exiting his vehicle in Minneapolis in January 2026. Bovino oversaw controversial immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis that resulted in the shooting deaths of two Americans before being reassigned. (Photo by Julia Rendleman)
“Fishers did not ask to be a part of this debate, but today, people have chosen to express their constitutional right to free speech and assembly in our city,” Fadness said in another statement Saturday.
Save Heritage Indiana’s event was headlined by Bovino. Once the face of President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign, he retired in March months after being demoted amid backlash to two fatal shootings by federal agents during operations in Minneapolis. 
The event advertised Bovino disclosing real truths about the number of people in the United States illegally after he was silenced by the establishment. 
“This gathering is for people who have decided that the time for polite silence is over. Commander Bovino will speak directly — unfiltered, unrehearsed, and accountable to no handler,” the website said.
According to promotional material, other speakers included Rep. Jim Lucas, R-Seymour, and Rupert Lowe, a British politician who founded Restore Britain, a political party supportive of mass deportations in the country.
Beckwith and Attorney General Todd Rokita each recorded messages to be played at the event, its website said. The Capital Chronicle requested the video remarks from Beckwith and Rokita on Thursday. Beckwith’s office insisted on a formal public access request and did not provide the video as of Saturday. Rokita’s office didn’t respond. 
Neither Gov. Mike Braun nor U.S. Sen. Jim Banks sent a video, Save Heritage Indiana said. The group slammed the Republicans in a message to its mailing list, saying the two “deserve the stocks” if they couldn’t voice support for immigration law enforcement.
“This rally is no more radical than that,” read the message, which was accompanied by an colonial America-era image of a man in stocks.
The critique of Banks led Nathan Roberts, co-founder of Save Heritage Indiana and Turning Point Action operative, to exit the group. On X, Roberts called Banks “the best senator in the country on” immigration policy, including for his efforts to end birthright citizenship.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Coloradans celebrate 150 years of statehood on a historic Colorado Day
description: Coloradans young and old spent a hot, sunny day in downtown Denver celebrating 150 years of Centennial State history with cake, sing-alongs, art projects, Legos, lowriders and even a square dance routine in the halls of the Capitol. After a pancake breakfast, Gov. Jared Polis, dressed head to toe in a red-white-and-blue cowboy getup, kicked […]
text:
Gov. Jared Polis shakes hands with Jerry Clayton, a Capitol volunteer dressed as Colorado's first governor, John Routt, during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Saturday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Coloradans young and old spent a hot, sunny day in downtown Denver celebrating 150 years of Centennial State history with cake, sing-alongs, art projects, Legos, lowriders and even a square dance routine in the halls of the Capitol.
After a pancake breakfast, Gov. Jared Polis, dressed head to toe in a red-white-and-blue cowboy getup, kicked off festivities outside the History Colorado Center Saturday morning, introducing musician Isaac Slade, a Boulder native who led the assembled crowd through a sing-along rendition of  John Denver’s “Rocky Mountain High.”
Polis, Lt. Gov. Dianne Primavera and other state officials later gathered on the steps of the state Capitol to cut Colorado’s 150th birthday cake. Polis shook hands with Jerry Clayton, a Capitol volunteer dressed as Gov. John Routt, Colorado’s first chief executive, who performed a reenactment of the reading of President Ulysses S. Grant’s proclamation of Colorado statehood on Aug. 1, 1876.

Grant’s order ended a years-long effort by territorial leaders to secure Colorado’s admission as the 38th state in the union. Coming less than a month after the nation commemorated 100 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the proclamation’s timing ensured that Colorado would be known by the nickname that a Denver newspaper had first suggested a year earlier — the Centennial State.
Saturday’s festivities across Colorado followed nationwide commemorations of the semiquincentennial on the Fourth of July. The state’s America 250-Colorado 150 commission was established by the Legislature in 2022 to coordinate the celebration of the twin anniversaries, dubbed the “sesquisemiquincentennial.”
“Our birthdays are always linked — we’re a little bit like a kid with a birthday on Christmas Day,” Polis joked. “Everybody’s celebrating the big America one, but don’t forget us, it’s also our birthday.”
Musician Isaac Slade, far right, led the crowd in a sing-along of John Denver's "Rocky Mountain High" during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Crowds gathered in downtown Denver for Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Gov. Jared Polis addresses the crowd at an event commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Lowriders were parked outside the Colorado State Capitol during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Gov. Jared Polis cuts a ceremonial birthday cake during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)State Rep. Brianna Titone, left, inspects a Lego-brick recreation of the Colorado House of Representatives chambers during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)A square dance performance was held inside the State Capitol building during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)A proclamation of Colorado statehood signed by President Ulysses S. Grant in 1876 is pictured on display at the History Colorado Center during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the proclamation's 150th anniversary on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Angel Vigil, an author and educator, is pictured dressed as early Colorado figure Casemiro Barela during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Inside the Capitol, artists premiered a “Colorado Past, Present, Future” themed exhibit, while members of the Colorado Square Dancing Association joined some enthusiastic newcomers in a dance in the building’s north foyer. The Denver Lego Users Group showed off scale recreations of the Capitol’s legislative chambers and invited attendees to help assembling a Lego-brick mountain landscape mosaic.
Celebrations were planned in communities across the state on Saturday, from an airshow at the Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport in Broomfield to a rock concert in Colorado Springs. As part of an initiative sponsored by the America 250-Colorado 150 commission, teams of climbers ascended nearly all of Colorado’s “14er” mountain peaks, though several of the climbs had to be scrapped amid an active wildfire season.
“This day represents years of planning and partnership by communities across Colorado,” Timothy Wolfe, the commission’s co-chair, said in a press release. “While today marks an important milestone, it is also an opportunity to reflect on our shared history, recognize those whose stories have shaped our state, and recommit ourselves to building a Colorado where every community sees itself in the next 150 years.”
Other commission initiatives include a documentary film series, a new historic marker program, a “digital passport” program to encourage travel and tourism around the state, and “A Portrait of Colorado at 150,” a collection of oral histories from at least 150 living Coloradans. Its website includes an expansive list of events commemorating Colorado’s 150th anniversary throughout the summer.
To escape the heat, crowds enjoyed free admission to the History Colorado Center, the Denver Art Museum and other institutions downtown. At a History Colorado exhibit, “38th Star: Colorado Becomes the Centennial State,” Angel Vigil welcomed museumgoers in costume as Casemiro Barela, a founding father of Colorado and longtime state senator from Las Animas County.
Angel Vigil, an author and educator, is pictured dressed as early Colorado figure Casemiro Barela during Colorado Day celebrations commemorating the 150th anniversary of statehood on Saturday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
An author and educator at History Colorado, Vigil performs in-character as Barela and other “Hispano men who have been marginalized, erased, or forgotten by history, but actually lived epic lives,” he told Newsline.
“Hardly anyone knows about him, but he lived an important life during his time and made huge contributions for 40 years,” said Vigil.
Barela was one of three Hispano delegates to the Colorado Territory’s constitutional convention in 1875 and 1876, and was instrumental in enacting a requirement that all state laws be published in Spanish for the benefit of the large Hispano community in southern Colorado. He and other framers of the state constitution wrestled with how to address hot-button issues like women’s suffrage, public education, corporate regulation and much more. They succeeded — though several previous efforts at statehood had failed.
“It was not automatic that we become a state,” Vigil said. “We had to work over 17 years to fix all the issues required to become a state, so that took dedication and perseverance, to keep going for it.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 9 Senate candidates make stump speeches to voters ahead of SC GOP special primary
description: Republican hopefuls seeking the party’s nomination for the Senate seat previously held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham make their pitch to voters.
text:
More than 400 people gathered Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at River Bluff High School in Lexington, to hear from the nine certified Republican candidates vying to succeed the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)LEXINGTON — Four days before the start of early voting, Republican hopefuls seeking the party’s nomination for the U.S. Senate seat previously held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham made their pitch to voters at a Lexington County high school.
More than 400 attendees filed into the auditorium of River Bluff High School Saturday to hear from the crowded slate of nine candidates:

Walterboro attorney Duke Buckner
U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, who represents the 7th Congressional District
Sen. Darline Graham, sister of the late Lindsey Graham
Spartanburg businessman Mark Lynch
former Myrtle Beach Mayor Mark McBride
U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, who represents the 5th Congressional District
retired Air Force officer Glenda Gail Parker
former congressman and Gov. Mark Sanford
Lexington County scientist and inventor Sam Shepherd

Candidates spoke separately, with the order predetermined through a drawing Friday. Each had 6 minutes to make a campaign speech and answered one question from a high school student.
Nearly all the candidates used part of their time to stress their support of the Trump administration’s crackdown on people living in the country illegally. They also talked about the need to rein in federal spending, which appealed to attendees.
Only two candidates pushed back against the Trump administration by opposing how it’s handled the war in Iran.
Sanford said the president should come to Congress to ask for permission. McBride said he thinks the United States needs to get out entirely.
That would be a sharp contrast to Lindsey Graham, who touted his influence on Trump’s decision to attack Iran.
Norman took a more Graham-like approach, calling for a well-funded military and peace through strength. Shepherd said the U.S. should not be providing humanitarian aid to other countries but also said he supported Israeli troops in the Israel-Hamas war.
Buckner said he wants to ban all foreign nationals from owning land in the United States and thinks people should have to show proof of citizenship before buying a house or renting an apartment.
Following the event, 265 attendees participated in a straw poll. The top vote-getters were Darline Graham, with 25% of the vote; Fry, with 23%; and Norman, with 20%.
Viewers statewide can watch five of the candidates who met the state GOP’s polling criteria debate Monday night.
Voters’ takeaways
For Neil Derrick, a 74-year-old retired personal fitness business owner from Columbia, it’s Darline Graham who has risen to the top. Sworn in July 14 to fulfill the remainder of her brother’s fourth term, which ends in January, Graham decided to enter the race for the next six-year term at the urging of President Donald Trump.
“She was thrust into this position,” Derrick said, but she answered the call.
Derrick thinks she stands the best chance of following in the steps of her older brother, who died unexpectedly of a ruptured aorta on July 11 in Washington, D.C.
Derrick said he didn’t always agree with the late senator.
“But he was solid, whether you liked him or not,” Derrick said.
He noted that Darline Graham has the support of her brother’s longtime staffers, who remain in the office.
That wasn’t enough, however, to sway Melodie Ingwersen.
“We don’t really know her personality,” Ingwersen said of Darline Graham.
Instead, the 75-year-old former toy shop owner from Columbia is leaning toward supporting Norman.
“It comes down to who can carry the weight of the job,” she said. “Norman already has experience in Congress. Plus, he hasn’t been there forever, so he’s still in tune with South Carolina.”
Norman, of Rock Hill, has represented the 5th District since 2017. Anchored in York County, the district covers the fast-growing Charlotte suburbs south to Kershaw and parts of Sumter County.
Ingwersen’s greatest concerns are the growing size of the national budget and passage of the SAVE America Act, which adds voter ID requirements nationwide and requires proof of citizenship when registering to vote. Lindsey Graham co-sponsored and advocated for the measure, which has stalled in the U.S. Senate after passing the House.
It was the first measure Darline Graham signed on to after being sworn in. And Norman has made its passage a central part of his message.
Like REAL ID, a federal bill could require proof of identity. Here’s how to get the documents in SC.

“It’s so important to have someone who can make grounded, wise decisions, not just sound bites,” Ingwersen said.
Leigh Parker, a 59-year-old business analyst from Aiken, said she voted for Lynch in his run against Lindsey Graham and she’s sticking with him in the special primary.
It’s Lynch’s embrace of Christianity following a battle with addiction that has earned her support.
“If we don’t come back to Christian values, nothing can save us,” she said.
Many others walked away from the event still undecided.
That included Scott Reagan, a 45-year-old software salesman from Lexington, who said he was still trying to make up his mind between two or three candidates.
Aiken County Republican Party Secretary Denise Brown and her husband, Joe Brown, said they came in weighing their choice between two candidates, but after hearing from some of the lesser-known people in the race, their list expanded to three or four.
The Browns said the economy, immigration and government spending and oversight are top issues for them.
Watch the candidates
The five candidates selected for Monday’s televised debate are Fry, Darline Graham, Lynch, Norman and Sanford. The one-hour debate starts at 7 p.m. and will be broadcast and streamed live across Gray Media stations in the state.
Chairman Drew McKissick said it gives voters statewide a chance to hear directly from the leading candidates.
“As Republicans consider who should represent us on the ballot and represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate for the next six years, it’s critical that they have an opportunity to compare the candidates on the issues and how they communicate their ideas to the public,” he said in a statement.
The special primary is Aug. 11, with a runoff likely on Aug. 25.
A three-day window of early voting starts Wednesday.
The winner of the contest will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas GOP state Rep. Austin McCollum arrested on domestic battering charges
description: Republican state Rep. Austin McCollum was arrested Saturday on domestic battering charges, prompting Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to call for his resignation and House Speaker Brian Evans to strip his leadership positions. McCollum was being held without bond in the Benton County jail on 3rd degree domestic battering charges, an online inmate roster[...]
text:
(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Republican state Rep. Austin McCollum was arrested Saturday on domestic battering charges, prompting Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to call for his resignation and House Speaker Brian Evans to strip his leadership positions.
McCollum was being held without bond in the Benton County jail on 3rd degree domestic battering charges, an online inmate roster showed. 5News reported he was also being held on aggravated assault and first-degree false imprisonment charges.
Details of what led to his arrest and a copy of the incident report were not immediately available. 
McCollum and a spokesperson for the Benton County Sheriff’s Office did not immediately respond to emails and phone messages seeking comment Saturday afternoon. It was not immediately clear when McCollum’s first court appearance would be.
McCollum has served in the state House since 2017 and represents House District 8 in Benton County. He won the Republican nomination for Benton County judge in March.
“The allegations against Representative McCollum are appalling, and I’m praying for his wife and children,” Sanders said in a statement. “I absolutely condemn violence of any form, and if these credible, sickening allegations are accurate, I call on him to immediately resign his office and drop out of the race for county judge.”
Rep. Austin McCollum (Arkansas Secretary of State)
Evans said he would strip McCollum, who serves as vice chair of the House Advanced Communications and Information Technology Committee, of his leadership positions. The Republican speaker from Cabot said he would call on McCollum to resign “or convene the House to take the necessary actions” if the lawmaker is convicted.
“Domestic violence is a serious offense that shatters families, harms victims, and erodes the trust that public servants are expected to uphold,” Evans said in a statement. “Every allegation of abuse must be treated with the seriousness it deserves.”
Attorney General Tim Griffin and Lt. Gov. Leslie Rutledge, both Republicans, also called for McCollum to resign and said he should drop his bid for county judge.
McCollum, a former House majority leader, has sponsored several bills that have become law including measures last year banning ranked-choice voting and 2023 legislation creating an election integrity unit in the attorney general’s office. In 2021, he was the lead sponsor of a bill that would have ended Confederate Flag Day. The House passed that measure, but it died in the Senate.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Lawmakers send Healey bill governing library book access
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: As they wrapped up a host of priorities on the last day for major new business, legislators gave final approval to a measure aimed at preventing politically charged book bans.
text:
THE LEGISLATURE on Friday sent to Gov. Maura Healey’s desk legislation that establishes guidelines for how schools and public libraries make decisions about the availability and appropriateness of books. 
“Together we are setting forth a bill to protect free expression and intellectual curiosity and every person’s right to free expression. Massachusetts has long been a national leader in education and learning. We are home to the nation’s first public library and first public school. In this commonwealth, we have long appreciated that unabridged access to knowledge is a key to finding opportunity and fulfillment,” Sen. Julian Cyr said during Thursday’s Senate session when the chamber advanced the legislation. “This legislation builds on that proud longstanding tradition by ensuring that decisions about library collections are made by trained professionals through a transparent process, not by political pressure or intimidation.”
The bill (S 3241) outlines criteria for school library teachers to use while determining whether materials are appropriate for a library including whether it is age appropriate, serves an educational purpose and is “based on the teacher’s or employee’s professional training and not on personal, political or doctrinal view.” Employees responsible for library materials can still remove items that are outdated or to accommodate new items.
Attempts to ban books, largely ones dealing with race, gender and LGBTQ+ identities, have been on the rise across the country. In 2025, 4,235 different titles were challenged – second to only 2023 when there were 4,240 challenges, according to the American Library Association’s Office for Intellectual Freedom, which noted that not all book challenges are reported. In 2025, 33 public libraries reported formal challenges – more than seven years combined – to materials and 86 libraries faced a total of 3,093 informal challenges, according to the Massachusetts Board of Library Commissioners. 
Under the bill, materials can only be removed from a school library after a vote by the school committee, or board of trustees if it’s a charter school. Before that vote, there must be a public hearing and determination from a review committee that the material “taken as a whole, based on clear and convincing evidence” does not have any educational, literary, artistic, personal or social value or is not age appropriate. Only school employees, parents or guardians or students enrolled in the school can lodge challenges. Students, parents and guardians may also appeal a decision to remove materials from the library to court. 
Residents of the municipality where a free library is located may challenge the selection of materials. And if materials are removed, that decision can be challenged by the material’s author or creator or residents of the municipality.
Employees are protected from retaliation based on their selection of library materials so long as their decision was made “in good faith” and followed the required criteria.
“At a time when the loudest and most extreme voices too often dominate, this bill helps ensure that libraries will remain quiet spaces where curiosity is encouraged, knowledge is accessible, and free expression is protected across the Commonwealth,” Rep. John Francis Moran of Boston, House sponsor of the bill, said in a press release.
The bill also directs school districts, charter schools and local education agencies to file an annual report with Department of Elementary and Secondary Education including information on all complaints and challenges seeking to remove or restrict materials. The Board of Library Commissioners is also required to file a similar report with the Legislature.
The House enacted the legislation on a 152-1 vote and senators enacted the bill on a voice vote. Rep. John Gaskey cast the sole vote against enacting the bill. Gaskey, a Carver Republican, in June spoke about his ill-fated amendment to repeal a provision shielding schools, libraries, employees and others from being convicted for sharing materials that are harmful to minors.
“We know what this bill is all about. That the ideological activists have decided to attack local school boards for simply daring to protect children from state-sponsored pornography. The outcome of this vote, I know, has already been preordained by our leadership, and we know exactly what the orders have said for you guys to do,” Gaskey said at the time. “But I did not run for this office to sit here quietly while the body systematically strips away parental rights and protects government employees from the very laws that every ordinary citizen must follow.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Maryland Sen. Alsobrooks campaigns for Scott Colom in Jackson, focuses on healthcare
description: Democratic U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, left, speaks with Nadia Colom, wife of Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom, in downtown Jackson on Aug. 1, 2026, on the importance of maternal health.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, a Democrat from Maryland, campaigned with Scott Colom, Mississippi’s Democratic Senate nominee, in Jackson on Saturday, where she encouraged voters to support Colom because he will prioritize access to affordable healthcare. 
“I feel every single seat is important in our country right now, as we’re trying to get back to a place where we are focused again on the middle class in this country,” Alsobrooks told Mississippi Today in an interview. 
Alsobrooks joined Colom and several healthcare advocates at the Capital Club in downtown Jackson on Saturday morning, where they pointed to Mississippi’s dire maternal health metrics, which are some of the worst in the nation, as a need for a senator who will vote to protect against cuts to Medicaid. 
Around a dozen people shared stories about their struggles obtaining affordable health care and about family members who have died giving birth in Mississippi. 
“We reject as a premise that we should ever accept that you cannot afford healthcare,” Alsobrooks said. 
Colom has made health care a central focus of his campaign and has pointed out that thousands of Mississippians have dropped health insurance plans they had through the Affordable Care Act. 
Active enrollment in the plans fell by about 70,000 people in Mississippi between February 2025 and February 2026, a nearly 25% drop, according to new federal data. People are dropping their plans because enhanced federal tax credits, which made health insurance more affordable for 22 million Americans, expired in December. 
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks in Jackson on Aug. 1, 2026.
Congress first authorized the expanded subsidies in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Mississippi was one of the states that benefited the most from the increased federal support. 
Both Colom and Alsobrooks criticized Colom’s opponent, Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, for backing the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill that slashed Medicaid benefits and largely gave tax breaks to higher-income earners. 
Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, told Mississippi Today in a statement that he encourages the Colom campaign to “continue campaigning on raising taxes and giving illegal immigrants free healthcare.” 
“Both issues that may sell to his Massachusetts supporters, but not in Mississippi,” Monssen said. 
Colom and Alsobrooks also planned to speak at a town hall in Jackson on Saturday evening about voting rights, alongside Mississippi Congressman Bennie Thompson and Mississippi NAACP Director Charles Taylor. 
Alsobrooks is the first U.S. senator to campaign for Colom. She is the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Maryland and is the third Black woman elected to the U.S. Senate.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Democrats in Kansas governor’s race debate Gov. Laura Kelly’s role in primary campaign
description: The final debate among Democratic primary candidates for governor in Kansas centers on claims tied to Gov. Laura Kelly's involvement in the contest.
text:
State Sens. Ethan Corson and Cindy Holscher, pictured together in April, joined Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog in a debate Friday on Fox 4 television featuring questions about Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly's influence in the primary gubernatorial campaigns of Corson, Holscher and Skoog. Kelly endorsed Corson. The primary election is Tuesday. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Democratic gubernatorial candidates Cindy Holscher and Ethan Corson tangled during a Friday debate about rival interpretations of conversations with the office of Gov. Laura Kelly about who should run to replace the popular two-term governor.
Kelly met privately with a cluster of prospective Democratic candidates in 2025, a list that included Johnson County state Sens. Holscher and Corson. Kansas Reflector reported in August 2025 that Holscher had expressed concern through texts sent to the governor’s office that Kelly might wade into the primary in a way designed to damage Holscher’s prospects.
Fox 4 Kansas City anchor John Holt, who moderated the televised debate ahead of Tuesday’s primary election, asked both candidates about a recent Kansas City Star report in which Kelly’s chief of staff, Will Lawrence, alleged one of Holscher’s texts to the governor’s office could be viewed as “blackmail.”
The Star reported Lawrence was convinced that Holscher threatened to disclose the governor’s then-unreported divorce if Kelly put her finger on the scale in the Democratic primary.
“That’s an absolutely ridiculous accusation,” Holscher said in response to Holt’s question. “It’s a last-minute attempt by insiders, the establishment, to try to prop up their candidate. I’m not tied to the establishment. I’m tied to the working people. I’m everything that often this party says what it wants, somebody who rose up out of poverty, a female, someone who fights for working families, from a military family and a union family. But, at times, the establishment just doesn’t want to embrace someone like that.”
Holscher said texts she sent to the governor’s office were about the governor’s potential involvement in the Democratic primary and inspired by her frustration with a political environment in Topeka layered with “bullying and coercion.”
In June 2025, Kelly publicly endorsed Corson. Kansas Reflector published a story in July 2025 in which Kelly confirmed her divorce from retired physician Ted Daughety had been finalized in October 2024.
Holscher claimed Kelly requested that she, Corson and Senate Minority Leader Dinah Sykes stay out of the Democratic gubernatorial race so the governor’s preferred candidate, Lawrence attorney Chris Mann, could run. Mann chose to seek the Democratic nomination for attorney general instead.
Holt asked Corson why he declined to respond to Holscher’s request that Corson disavow the attack by the governor’s chief of staff.
“We didn’t comment on that because that story had nothing to do with my campaign,” Corson said. “I’m really focused on addressing the issues that Kansans want to hear from all of us about healthcare, education, jobs, affordability. I put together really detailed plans for how to address all of those. And I, frankly, think that hearing from us on those issues is what the voters want and what the voters deserve.”
Holt sought clarification from Corson about Holscher’s claim the governor pressured Senate Democrats to clear a path for Mann.
“I think Governor Kelly has been clear from day one that she believes I’m the only Democrat who can win in November, that she believes that I’m the only Democrat who can put together the coalition that we need of Democrats, unaffiliated voters and moderate Republicans to hold this governor’s office,” Corson said.
In response to a question about Democratic Party unity, both Holscher and Corson said they would endorse the primary winner.
Holt asked Curt Skoog, the Overland Park mayor who entered the Democratic race for governor in June, if Kelly discouraged him from running for governor.
“The governor made it clear to me that she was supporting Ethan Corson,” Skoog said.
Skoog said he decided to run for governor because Holscher’s positions on issues made her unelectable in the November general election. Skoog said Corson failed to connect with Kansas voters despite funding for campaign ads and endorsements from Kelly, former Gov. Kathleen Sebelius and a collage of labor organizations.
“I am connecting with Kansans,” Skoog said. “I am the one who can win independent and moderate Republicans, and win at the end of the day.”
When Skoog launched his candidacy, Kelly issued a statement describing Skoog’s bid as a “thrown-together, last-minute, opportunistic attempt” to win the Democratic nomination.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Surpluses prove state lawmakers’ eyes are bigger than their stomachs
description: There are two times a year when you can count on South Dakota politicians getting a little pumped up about their performance and taking a victory lap.  One is at the end of the legislative session when lawmakers pat themselves on the back about their ability to produce a balanced budget. They’re right to take […]
text:
Jeff Mehlhaff, of the Legislative Research Council, presents fiscal year 2026 and 2027 revenue projections to the legislative Joint Appropriations Committee on Feb. 11, 2026, at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)There are two times a year when you can count on South Dakota politicians getting a little pumped up about their performance and taking a victory lap. 
One is at the end of the legislative session when lawmakers pat themselves on the back about their ability to produce a balanced budget. They’re right to take pride in their work. There are currently 10 states that run budget deficits. Balancing a budget is something that continues to elude the U.S. Congress. 
On the other hand, a balanced budget is mandated by the state constitution. By balancing the budget, legislators are simply following the law. It’s like they’re congratulating themselves for driving the speed limit. 
The other time you can count on a politician taking a bow is at the end of the state fiscal year in June. That’s when the amount of the budget surplus is announced. It doesn’t matter who is in the governor’s office. The announcement of the surplus will be lauded as that administration’s dedication to government efficiency. That’s what happened this year when Gov. Larry Rhoden greeted the news by saying it was the result of “good stewardship of taxpayer dollars.” 
Governor celebrates surplus as Democratic lawmaker says state missed opportunities to help people

This year, a $69 million budget surplus came from $30 million in higher than anticipated revenue, including $17 million in extra sales and use taxes. Another $39 million came from underspending by state agencies. 
The excess revenue may be a sign of a more robust than expected economy. It’s disconcerting, however, that the state budget process, with dueling theories from the Legislature and the executive branch, goes to a great deal of trouble to predict how much revenue will be coming in. In this case, the state’s budget experts looked into their crystal balls and managed to miss their target by $30 million. 
The $39 million that went unspent by state agencies included $32 million from the Department of Social Service. This raises the question of whether the people in society who need help the most are getting short shrift from the state agency specifically designed to help them. 
That’s not the case, according to Jim Terwilliger, commissioner of the state’s Bureau of Finance and Management. In a South Dakota Searchlight story, Terwilliger said the department’s underspending was the result of fewer than expected Medicaid patients and less use of substance abuse and mental health services at the Human Services Center in Yankton because it’s understaffed. 
“We’re trying to predict how many people come to the hospital with various acute conditions and so on and so forth,” Terwilliger told the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee. “So it’s not something that’s easy to predict going forward.”
Granted, predicting the state’s economic future is hard work. The $69 million budget surplus is less than 3% of the $2.5 billion state general fund budget. The $32 million returned to state government by the Department of Social Services represents less than 5% of the state general funds in the department’s budget. Still, make $69 million worth of budgeting errors in the private sector, and that thumping sound would be caused by heads rolling. 
This year’s $69 million budget surplus is on the low end compared to the surpluses in the past five years. There was a surplus of $63 million in 2025, $80 million in 2024, $96.8 million in 2023, $115 million in 2022 and $85.9 million in 2021. Some of that may be due to the increase in federal money during the pandemic. Still, there has to be a better way to ensure that the money in the budget has a chance to be spent for the betterment of South Dakotans or, if it’s not needed, doesn’t get put in the budget in the first place.


Let us know what you think...


 

A state government known for its conservatism, both in the Legislature and the executive branch, should have a better budgetary record. Each year since 2001, the last time there was no surplus, appropriators’ eyes have been bigger than their stomachs. They either budget more than they can spend or miss the clues about how revenue will play out in the coming year. Then in June, they declare the budget surplus is due to government efficiency. Government efficiency should start with a budgeting process that works, not end with an embarrassingly large surplus.
The matter-of-fact nature of the explanation of this year’s budget surplus to the Appropriations Committee belies the fact that mistakes were made. It wasn’t just a matter of the state departments’ underspending. It certainly looks like it was a matter of the citizens of South Dakota being overtaxed. Now $39 million that was earmarked for services for South Dakotans will instead linger in state government’s budget reserves, which have swelled to a record $325 million. 
On some level it’s reassuring to note that taxpayer dollars in the budget reserve may be used as one-time funds in state projects. However, it would do so much more to boost confidence in state government if lawmakers and the bureaucrats who work with them would just get the budget right the first time. That’s something that’s worthy of a victory lap.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi financial literacy mandate increases economic knowledge statewide
description: Senate Bill 2294, first taken up in the Senate Education Committee during the 2026 regular legislative session, became law July 1, 2026. Known as the Mississippi Math Act, it includes new requirements for financial literacy, computer science, and civics education.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi educators are preparing for new financial literacy, computer science and civics requirements under Senate Bill 2294, a wide-ranging education law that took effect July 1. 
Many of the classroom requirements of the Mississippi Math Act will be phased in over the next several years. The bill incorporates the J.P. Wilemon Jr. Financial Literacy Act, which failed to pass as a standalone measure in previous legislative sessions. 
Beginning with the 2027-28 school year, Mississippi public schools will be required to provide financial literacy instruction for students in grades 6-8. The curriculum will cover topics including income, budgeting, financial services, postsecondary education financing and consumer rights. The law also establishes new computer science and civics education requirements that will be implemented on separate timelines.
The Canton Public Schools district office will work throughout the year to prepare for the curriculum change during the 2027-28 school year. Credit: Allyson Cole/RHCJC
At Canton Public School District, financial literacy has traditionally been taught through partnerships with community organizations. Candra Nelson-Scott, assistant superintendent of curriculum and instruction, said outside educators provide students with practical lessons on managing money. 
“They talk about banking, savings accounts, investment accounts, budgeting, as well as informing (students) about loans, interest rates and principals,” she said. 
Nelson-Scott said the new law will establish consistent statewide expectations while giving districts flexibility in how the curriculum is delivered. She said district leaders and teachers will help determine whether financial literacy is offered as a standalone course or integrated into an existing class. 
Teacher training is expected to begin in summer 2027 as districts prepare for implementation.
Heather Morrison says the Department of Education is working with educators to prepare them for the new curriculum. She hopes parents will take the initiative and have open conversations with their students about financial literacy.  Credit: Mississippi Department of Education
Heather Morrison, director of P-20 Partnerships for the Mississippi Department of Education and the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning, said the department is working with partners across the state to prepare educators. 
“For the high schools, the teachers are going to have to earn an endorsement,” Morrison said. “For middle school, there’s no technical endorsement (requirement) yet.” 
Morrison said any educator may add a personal finance endorsement to a teaching license by completing a Mississippi Council-approved economics education course. 
She also said students entering seventh grade in the 2026-27 school year — the graduating Class of 2032 — will be the first required to earn a personal finance credit before graduating from high school. 
“Kids who take (College and Career Readiness courses) meet that personal finance requirement,” Morrison said. “If they don’t take that class, then they have to take the personal finance class.” 
Morrison said financial literacy is a life skill that should extend beyond the classroom and encouraged parents to reinforce those lessons at home.
Canton High School will incorporate financial literacy as a graduation requirement in future years. Credit: Allyson Cole/RHCJC
“I would hope parents are having these conversations with their students at home and make it a real-life conversation … having these conversations at home about budgeting, student loans, student debt,” Morrison said. “I definitely think it’s a positive (way) to spur conversation.” 
Nelson-Scott agreed, saying early exposure to financial concepts can better prepare students for adulthood. 
“I’m speaking from personal experience,” she said. “I can’t remember having that conversation (about financial literacy). Giving students this information early… gives them an early start.” 
Students and parents can expect financial literacy instruction to begin in Mississippi middle schools during the 2027-28 school year as districts implement the new requirements.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Woman detained by ICE released from KY jail after family speaks about her lack of care
description: A woman who was detained by federal immigration agents at the Louisville airport a couple of weeks ago has been released from custody Friday.  A federal judge ordered the release of Sarafinah Bukirwa and her family paid her bond, according to media reports. Earlier this week, Bukirwa’s brother, Isaac Kabunga, appeared with Democratic U.S. Rep. […]
text:
From left to right, U.S. Reps. Delia Ramirez, Gwen Moore and Morgan McGarvey go to a Northern Kentucky jail to see conditions for people being held by ICE. (Photo provided by U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey's office)A woman who was detained by federal immigration agents at the Louisville airport a couple of weeks ago has been released from custody Friday. 
A federal judge ordered the release of Sarafinah Bukirwa and her family paid her bond, according to media reports.
Earlier this week, Bukirwa’s brother, Isaac Kabunga, appeared with Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey and said he witnessed ICE agents detain her at the Louisville airport on July 22. He dropped her off as she was heading to a conference on sickle cell anemia. Bukirwa has the disease and operates a nonprofit focusing on support for those who have it, Sarafinah Sickle Cell Society.  
Under a visa, she came to the U.S. from Uganda to expand her work and applied for asylum. McGarvey said she was “doing everything the way that the rules and the laws have been laid out for her to do.”  
Kabunga said his sister was not receiving proper medical care while she was detained at the Graves County Detention Center. The jailer there, Jason Woosley, said Bukirwa “is receiving all prescribed medication.” 
“I’m so relieved Sarafinah is finally getting the care she needs and this nightmare is behind her, but so many families are still going through it,” McGarvey said in a statement Friday evening. “As long as this cruel administration continues its campaign of terror in our communities, we have to keep standing up for our neighbors.”
Days ago, McGarvey joined Democrats U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, of Illinois, and U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore, of Wisconsin, at the Campbell County Detention Center to get a closer look at jail conditions for ICE detainees there.  
According to data from Relevant Research, the Grayson County Detention Center is holding 168 people on behalf of ICE, and of that, 138 of those people are in the non-criminal population. Throughout Kentucky, about 10 jails are housing about 1,200 people for ICE. They typically receive federal funding for housing the detainees.
