name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Supreme Court sides with Nessel, overrules cases curtailing consumer protection law
description: In a 4-3 decision Friday, the Michigan Supreme Court rejected a lower court’s decision preventing Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel from moving forward with a price-gouging investigation against a major insulin manufacturer. Nessel, in 2022, filed an investigation into Eli Lilly and Company looking to investigate price disparities between its branded ver[...]
text:
Michigan Supreme Court / Hall of Justice | Photo by Jon KingIn a 4-3 decision Friday, the Michigan Supreme Court rejected a lower court’s decision preventing Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel from moving forward with a price-gouging investigation against a major insulin manufacturer.
Nessel, in 2022, filed an investigation into Eli Lilly and Company looking to investigate price disparities between its branded version of insulin injections and the generic version. Nessel also filed a complaint with Ingham County’s 30th Judicial Circuit Court, asking the Court to determine that the investigation was not subject to an exemption in the Michigan Consumer Protection Act.
Following a request from Eli Lilly, Nessel’s complaint was dismissed, prompting an appeal to the state Court of Appeals, and the Michigan Supreme Court when the lower court’s decision was upheld.
However, Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh, and Justices Noah Hood, Elizabeth Welch and Kimberly Thomas, all nominated by Democrats, agreed with Nessel’s arguments that two previous court cases – Smith v. Globe Life Insurance Company and Liss v. Lewiston-Richards Inc. – had improperly interpreted the exemption, preventing the Michigan attorney general from taking action against companies for deceptive business practices and price gouging if that business holds a license or other authorization from a state or federal agency.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In an opinion authored by Hood, the court overturned its decision in the two previous cases, and remanded the matter of Nessel’s investigation back to the 30th Circuit Court for further proceedings.
“The Michigan Consumer Protection Act was once the envy of consumer protection efforts across the nation, and today we can once again claim that mantle with these two abhorrent decisions off the books,” Nessel said in a statement. “Now, our extraordinary Consumer Protection Team can go back to helping residents who have been deceived by licensed businesses.”
Justice Kyra Harris Bolden, writing in a dissent joined by Justices Richard Bernstein and Brian Zahra, the lone Republican-nominated judge, argued that the attorney general lacked standing to bring the claim.
State Sen. Sam Singh (D-East Lansing), who has introduced legislation to bolster the Michigan Consumer Protection Act, also cheered the decision, calling on the Republican-led House of Representatives to pass his Senate Bill 134. 
In a statement, a Lilly spokesperson said they were “disappointed that a divided Michigan Supreme Court set aside longstanding precedent requiring termination of the Attorney General’s investigation.”
“We are proud of our strong record of insulin affordability solutions that have made a real impact for Michiganders and all Americans.” the statement said. “Lilly was the first company to cap what patients pay at $35 per month for all our insulins, we cut insulin prices by 70%, and in 2024 the average monthly out-of-pocket cost for Lilly insulin was less than $15.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Feds reject Arkansas’ request to renew Medicaid expansion program
authors: Andrew DeMillo, Ainsley Platt, Tess Vrbin
description: The Trump administration has rejected Arkansas’ request to renew its hybrid Medicaid expansion, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ office said Friday, creating uncertainty about the future of a program providing insurance to more than 200,000 low-income people.  Sam Dubke, a spokesperson for the Republican governor, said the federal Centers for Medicare and Medica[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)The Trump administration has rejected Arkansas’ request to renew its hybrid Medicaid expansion, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ office said Friday, creating uncertainty about the future of a program providing insurance to more than 200,000 low-income people. 
Sam Dubke, a spokesperson for the Republican governor, said the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services verbally confirmed the decision to the state and that officials expect a formal, written notification soon. 
“The administration is in discussions with CMS about a temporary extension to ARHOME to ensure impacted Arkansans maintain access to quality, affordable healthcare during this transition period,” Dubke said in an email. 
The state’s current waiver for the ARHOME program, which was established in 2013, ends Dec. 31. The state had requested to continue the program through 2031. Barring a special session, lawmakers aren’t set to meet again until the regular session in January. 
“Looking ahead to the next legislative session, CMS has provided the state with an opportunity for bold, conservative healthcare reform, and the governor will work with her partners in the legislature to build a sustainable model that maintains the same high quality of care and saves taxpayer dollars,” Dubke said.
Arkansas Explained: What’s happening to the state’s Medicaid expansion?

The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette first reported on the federal agency’s decision earlier Friday.
Arkansas was the first Southern state to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, but used a first-in-the-nation model that used expansion funds to purchase private insurance for those eligible.
The decision to not renew the program comes less than a month after Centene, one of two insurers providing coverage through ARHOME, announced it would not participate in the program next year. 
Gavin Lesnick, the spokesperson for the Arkansas Department of Human Services, said “changes are in store” for the ARHOME program, but the changes would not be immediate. Those with insurance plans through ARHOME do not need to do anything right now, he said, and the department will provide “frequent updates.”
“We look forward to robust discussions with a wide range of partners as we develop the next evolution of this program in a way that is functional, practical, and sustainable,” Lesnick said in a statement. “While it’s too early to know specifics of how this new approach will look, our commitment to connecting eligible Arkansans to effective health care will remain our guiding principle at the core of this work.”
The move also comes as the state has been preparing to impose work requirements for people on the expansion program, required under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“It sounds like our Medicaid expansion is seriously at risk going forward,” House Minority Leader Andrew Collins, a Democrat from Little Rock, said. “And it’s gravely concerning because this program was one of the things that helped Arkansans get access to health care, helped keep our provider network healthy and helped keep our state budget afloat for many years.”
Health experts have credited Arkansas’ expansion for a drop in the state’s uninsured rate and for a reduction in hospitals’ costs for treating patients without insurance. 
Camille Richoux, health policy director for Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families, said losing Medicaid expansion would be “devastating” for Arkansas.
“It would be devastating for individuals who would lose access to health care, for an already struggling health system, for rural hospitals, for our health workforce who rely on that revenue. We would see a huge increase in uncompensated care and a loss of all the gains in health that we’ve had due to more Arkansans having access to health care for the past 12 years.”
In 2026, the average monthly insurance premium in Arkansas for a medium-level silver plan purchased through Affordable Care Act marketplaces was $774, according to KFF — a $301-a-month jump from 2025.
Senate President Pro Tempore Bart Hester, a Cave Springs Republican, said he wants clarity from the federal government about whether the state needs to be ready to transition ARHOME enrollees to non-expansion Medicaid by Jan. 1.
Hester said he doesn’t believe the Legislature will support continuing Medicaid expansion in the 2027 session that starts in January. He expects the state to put Medicaid recipients in fee-for-service or managed care coverage instead.
“The feds can’t afford it. We can’t afford it,” Hester said. “It’s just not the government’s role to provide healthcare to people, outside of those that are the absolute [neediest].”
Arkansas adopted the hybrid model as a conservative alternative to Medicaid expansion when state government was divided between a Democratic governor and a Republican Legislature. 
The program has survived multiple attempts to kill it, winning reauthorization each year despite the three-fourths vote needed in the House and Senate. The program easily won reauthorization in the Legislature earlier this year.
Republican Sen. Jonathan Dismang of Searcy, who was an architect of the state’s hybrid expansion model, said he did not believe scrapping the program was on the table, but agreed that the form it takes going forward will likely change. The Joint Budget Committee co-chair said he didn’t know what a workable plan for the program could look like yet, and that a “lot of energy” needs to be spent in “a very short period of time” to figure out a solution .
“It’s going to be a massive thing for the next session, and something we shouldn’t take lightly. I can’t think of a more significant decision that we’ve got to make,” Dismang said. “I don’t think we can understate the significance of the decision that’s ahead for the administration, the legislative body, in how we move forward.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado inspection law unfairly singles out ICE detention center, operator’s lawyers say
description: Lawyers for the private company that runs Colorado’s only immigration detention center told a judge Friday that a new state law is unfairly discriminatory and should be struck down. The GEO Group sued the state over House Bill 26-1276, a new law that requires more frequent health and safety inspections inside immigration detention centers and […]
text:
A view of the Alfred A. Arraj U.S. Courthouse in downtown Denver on May 30, 2023. (Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Lawyers for the private company that runs Colorado’s only immigration detention center told a judge Friday that a new state law is unfairly discriminatory and should be struck down.
The GEO Group sued the state over House Bill 26-1276, a new law that requires more frequent health and safety inspections inside immigration detention centers and allows the state to impose civil penalties for noncompliance. GEO operates the facility in Aurora under a contract from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“This (case) isn’t about the general background of public health laws. This isn’t about creating a new inspection authority. This is about a state’s attempt to directly and specifically regulate, through targeted legislation, a single facility in the state,” Fred Yarger, one of GEO’s lawyers, told U.S. District Court Judge Daniel Domenico during a hearing Monday morning.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Yarger said that because there is only one facility in the state subject to the “bespoke” new law, it is discriminatory. The new regulations, he said, present an additional burden outside of existing public health inspection laws.
“It’s not simply the same (inspection) regime as before. If it was, the General Assembly would not have passed (the law),” he said.
GEO Group sues over new Colorado law requiring immigration detention center safety inspections

The state cannot regulate the federal government, Yarger said, but it is circumventing that restriction by regulating the government’s contractor instead. The law specifically carves out facilities directly operated by the federal government and it instead applies to contractor-operated facilities that “house or detain individuals who are noncitizens for purposes of civil immigration proceedings.”
That can only apply to the GEO site in Aurora.
GEO is asking the court to issue a preliminary injunction against the new law, which Democrats in the Legislature passed this year. It sets a minimum number of yearly health and safety inspections at the facility, requires GEO to pay for those inspections and lets the attorney general bring civil penalties against the company for noncompliance. Its provisions also cover how minors can be detained, mental health worker staffing minimums and annual reporting requirements.
Yarger argued that the law directly conflicts with the detention center contract GEO has with ICE. That contract requires that medical workers, including mental health professionals, are available at all times, but the new law states that someone must be physically on site. The contract also requires that GEO abide by ICE’s determination about access. Domenico questioned why he shouldn’t assume those contractual provisions with ICE include the expectation that GEO will comply with state and local laws.
Yarger said “the notion that through this contract, the (U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security) consented to any state law … it’s not a fair reading of the contract.”
Concerns are speculative
Talia Kraemer, representing the state, contended that there are no current or imminent threats to GEO, because the parts of the law that impose new requirements, such as around medical workers, have not undergone the rulemaking process through the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. That could take many months and would include an opportunity for input from GEO. The company’s concerns are speculative, she said.
Kraemer said the state only views the section related to inspections as in effect. In fact, state lawyers said, GEO has had favorable treatment historically because it has faced fewer required inspections than other penal facilities like state prisons and county jails.
“The fact the General Assembly has imposed a minimum inspections … does not indicate that Aurora has been singled out,” state lawyer Gabriel Podesta said.
Domenico asked the state’s lawyers where the constitutional line is when it comes to regulations of federal contractors.
“What if the regulations the state wanted to impose were so onerous that, maybe it didn’t make it impossible, but … that would make it effectively that nobody could profitably operate one of these?” he said. “Does it make sense to say ‘Well, the federal government contracts, and they’re allowed to comply with their contractural provisions, and anything beyond that is interfering with the federal government’s chosen methods?”
Domenico said he will issue a written order on the matter “as soon as possible.”
Tuberculosis case
The litigation coincides with GEO and ICE refusing to comply with a public health order issued by the Adams County Health Department around a confirmed tuberculosis case at the detention center. Federal officials are refusing access to local public health inspectors to complete an investigation that’s required by law.
“Adams County’s legal counsel, alongside the Colorado Attorney General’s Office, is actively working to preserve public health authority and ensure ACHD can continue fulfilling its statutory responsibilities in litigation arising from challenges brought by The GEO Group,” ACHD Executive Director Kelly Weidenbach said in a statement. “While that legal process moves forward, ACHD’s responsibility remains unchanged. We will continue to follow the science, apply Colorado’s public health laws consistently, and work with our partners to protect the health of every person and every community we serve.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: WPRI debate showcases a crowded, but not contentious, Democratic primary for lieutenant governor
description: By Rhode Island standards, the Democratic primary for the lieutenant governor’s job is a packed one. Yet the five-candidate contest for the seat currently occupied by Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos has received somewhat scant attention, WPRI 12 politics editor Ted Nesi remarked to four of the candidates shortly before the cameras rolled on a debate […]
text:
Democratic candidates for lieutenant governor, from left, former state Sen. Cindy Coyne, Newport City Councilor Xay Khamsyvoravong, Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos and Providence City Councilor Sue AnderBois stand behind WPRI 12’s new podiums during a debate taped in East Providence on Friday, July 31, 2026. (Photo by James Bartone/WPRI 12)By Rhode Island standards, the Democratic primary for the lieutenant governor’s job is a packed one.
Yet the five-candidate contest for the seat currently occupied by Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos has received somewhat scant attention, WPRI 12 politics editor Ted Nesi remarked to four of the candidates shortly before the cameras rolled on a debate taped Friday morning at WPRI’s studios in East Providence. 
As if to commemorate the occasion of their first televised debate, the TV station had recently purchased a new set of podiums with animated monitors on the front. Xay Khamsyvoravong, a Newport city councilor and former mayor of the City by the Sea, joked that the podiums were “custom designed for our respective heights.” 
From behind those new podiums, the candidates — Matos, Khamsyvoravong, Providence City Councilor Sue AnderBois and former state Sen. Cindy Coyne — mostly stood on common ground. 
 

 How to watch

The debate premieres Friday, July 31, at 6:30 p.m. on Fox Providence, with additional airings over the weekend, including Sunday at 10 a.m. in the usual “Newsmakers” time slot. You can also watch it online.



The four Democrats unanimously supported the state’s new millionaires’ tax. All four said they preferred Rhode Island’s 2033 deadline for achieving 100% renewable electricity, rather than set a new deadline of 2050 as Gov. Dan McKee has suggested. 
None offered an endorsement in the Providence mayoral race when asked. 
And the quartet agreed McKee was right to sign the charter school moratorium. 
The sharpest disagreement may have jutted out from the candidates’ different ideas about what a good relationship between governor and lieutenant governor should look like in a state where the two officeholders are elected separately.
Who wants to be a ‘shadow governor’? 
Early in the McKee administration, Nesi noted, press releases shared news from the “McKee-Matos administration,” a label that fell into disuse “a long time ago.”
“Do you still consider yourself Gov. McKee’s partner today?” Nesi asked Matos.
Matos acknowledged that this previously united front was mostly due to how she obtained the office, having applied for the position when McKee opened it to contenders in 2021. 
But Matos said the state must “change the way we elect the lieutenant governor.” 
Her solution, which she said she’d work on instituting if elected, would adopt a model closer to that of Massachusetts, in which the governor and lieutenant governor run separately in the primary but on a combined ticket in the general election.
“It’s a challenge for a governor, lieutenant governor, to be able to have that relationship because they’re not elected together,” Matos said. “There’s always going to be people around the governor that only want one governor. The governor doesn’t want a shadow governor, nor (do) the people around him want a shadow governor.”
She also said that a lieutenant governor who completes the remainder of a governor’s term should not be permitted to run immediately for a full term. 
Nesi pivoted to Khamsyvoravong next about the office’s needs, which the Newporter described as “clear scope, clear support, a clear plan for what you’re doing.” 
He offered as an example the relationship between former Gov. Gina Raimondo and then-General Treasurer Seth Magaziner, calling it “the best relationship between a governor and a general officer that I have seen in my lifetime.”
Raimondo defined a mission for Magaziner to find school construction funding, and that led to billions for the state, Khamsyvoravong said. 
“That is the type of relationship that should exist between the lieutenant governor and the governor,” he added.
Matos chimed in briefly, citing that example as an unequivalent one.
“A lot of the work that the governor does depends on also having a good relationship with the investment that the state is making with the treasurer,” Matos said. “So there’s always going to be a better relationship between the treasurer and the governor than with the lieutenant governor and the governor.”
Four Democrats paint their views for the ‘entrepreneurial’ lieutenant governor’s office

Coyne said eight years in the state Senate taught her the path to get legislation from “a piece of paper to the governor’s office” is knowledge that’s “not in a book anywhere,” and it’s knowledge she’d share with the governor’s team. 
Nesi countered that McKee wanted a similar rapport when he was lieutenant governor, but that “it wasn’t on offer from Governor Raimondo.” 
“Well, we try to collaborate as best as we can,” Coyne said, adding one can still use the office as a “bully pulpit” or reroute legislative priorities through teamwork with the General Assembly.
AnderBois described herself as “radically collaborative,” pointing to her experience coordinating work across state agencies as Rhode Island’s first director of food strategy.
Still, AnderBois warned: “I’m very collaborative and very friendly, but you can’t push me around.”
WPRI 12 investigative reporter Tim White, right, speaks with Democratic candidates for lieutenant governor, from left, former state Sen. Cindy Coyne, Newport City Councilor Xay Khamsyvoravong, Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos and Providence City Councilor Sue AnderBois before taping a debate at the station’s East Providence studio on Friday, July 31, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Seven successions in state history
Rhode Island’s lieutenant governor has fewer constitutional duties than those in other states. 
But one big responsibility remains, as prescribed in the state constitution: If the governor should “die, remove from the state, refuse to serve; become insane, or be otherwise incapacitated,” the lieutenant governor steps up to the plate.
“The importance of this office is not lost on anyone,” WPRI investigative reporter Tim White said at the start of the debate. He noted that McKee became governor after his boss Gina Raimondo left for a job in Joe Biden’s administration.
A 2021 analysis in the Boston Globe showed that a lieutenant governor taking over for the governor of Rhode Island has only happened seven times since the Constitution’s ratification in 1842. 
Still, it does happen. And it can bring an unwelcome inheritance, White noted. In McKee’s case, it would be the Washington Bridge debacle, he posited. 
“If you suddenly found yourself in that chair, name one specific thing you would have done differently at the start of the bridge crisis,” White asked the four candidates. 
All agreed McKee was wise to close the bridge’s westbound span. They differed on the details. 
Khamsyvoravong said the state should have concentrated its resources on repairing the bridge, comparing McKee’s response to Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s response to the 2023 collapse of an Interstate 95 overpass.
Matos said she would have routed financial assistance to affected businesses faster.
AnderBois said she would have accepted responsibility from the outset rather than blaming previous administrations, and pondered “more creative solutions to get people from one side of our state to the other, not just ‘how many cars can we pack on that bridge?’”
East Bay resident Coyne said the administration’s communication needed improvement. 
“I’m still waiting for the day of reckoning,” Coyne said, recalling McKee’s March 2024 promise to hold accountable those responsible for the bridge’s failure. 
There was almost unanimity again on the question of whether former Rhode Island Department of Transportation (RIDOT) Director Peter Alviti Jr. should have been removed sooner.
Coyne, Khamsyvoravong and AnderBois said they would have removed him from his role.
Matos, meanwhile, said she would not have replaced Alviti “in the middle of the crisis.” 
“I think we needed his expertise and the knowledge that he had in order to get through the crisis,” Matos offered. “It’s very difficult when we just shut down a bridge [and] make changes in an organization like DOT that touches so many other projects that are happening right now.”
The candidates also debated abolishing ICE (Matos and AnderBois supported the idea, while Khamsyvoravong and Coyne favored reform), clean energy guidelines (all four agreed to keep the renewable energy deadline at 2033, with Matos noting this was one of her diversions from McKee), and the charter school moratorium’s legal aftershocks. AnderBois and Khamsyvoravong were broadly curious about how the legislation came to affect De La Comunidad, the school which was prevented from opening and is now suing McKee. But all four candidates echoed one after the other that it’s now a matter for the courts.
The fifth candidate for LG, Ross McCurdy, did not participate in the debate. Per the rules of WPRI’s parent company Nexstar Media, candidates for statewide office must have reported at least $100,000 in campaign contributions, with at least 25% raised in-state, to participate in televised debates.

title: National Weather Service says nine tornadoes hit WV last week
description:
The National Weather Services has now confirmed that nine tornadoes touched down in West Virginia during the storms on July 21 and 22.

The Weather Service’s office in Charleston confirmed six within the West Virginia portion of its forecast area while the Baltimore and Washington, D.C. office confirmed three tornados in Eastern West Virginia: one at Highvie[...]
text:
Jane Lew, West Virginia, flooded during the storms July 21 and 22. (Photo courtesy of Andrew McDonald)The National Weather Services has now confirmed that nine tornadoes touched down in West Virginia during the storms on July 21 and 22.
The Weather Service’s office in Charleston confirmed six within the West Virginia portion of its forecast area while the Baltimore and Washington, D.C. office confirmed three tornados in Eastern West Virginia: one at Highview, in Hampshire County; another at Seneca Rocks and a third that traveled from Kiser Gap, W.Va. to Criders, Va.
An EF2 tornado hit southeast Ritchie County. Two EF2 tornadoes started in Washington County, Ohio and traveled more than 12 miles into Pleasants County, West Virginia.
Another EF1 tornado started in Washington County, Ohio and traveled 24 miles into Raven Rock, W.Va. and through Pleasants, Tyler and Ritchie countiesy before lifting in Arnolds Creek Road, in Doddridge County, according to the Weather Service. 
Two other tornadoes — rated EF0 and EF1 — traveled less than a mile in Barbour and Randolph counties. 
The EF, or Enhanced Fujita Scale, rates tornadoes based on windspeeds, with EF0 denoting speeds of 65-85 miles per hour and EF5 marking speeds in excess of 200 miles per hour. 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey declared a state of emergency Tuesday evening for all 55 counties in the state because of the storms, which also brought straightline wind and dumped 5 to 7 inches of water, causing severe flooding to parts of the state. 
No injuries or deaths have been associated with any of the twisters. The storms tore the roof of the St. Marys home of former West Virginia Del. Donna Boley, according to reporting by Ogden Newspapers. 
Upshur, Lewis and Pleasants counties in North Central West Virginia were among the hardest hit. 
Two deaths have been associated with the storms. James J. Harper, 61, and Judy A. Young, 59, of Upshur County, were found dead inside a vehicle that was recovered from the Stonecoal Lake area of Upshur County, officials say.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘My thoughts were distorted’: Woman gets at least 10 years in Rutland fatal shooting
description:
Courtney Samplatsky, initially charged with second-degree murder in the June 2022 killing, pleaded guilty Friday to a reduced charge of voluntary manslaughter.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘My thoughts were distorted’: Woman gets at least 10 years in Rutland fatal shooting.
text:
Judge Cortland Corsones presides in Rutland County Superior criminal court in Rutland in Jan. 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

RUTLAND – A judge has approved a plea deal and sentenced a Rutland County woman to at least 10 years in prison for fatally shooting a man inside an apartment four years ago stemming from a drug-related dispute.
Judge Cortland Corsones handed down the sentence to 39-year-old Courtney Samplatsky during a hearing Friday in Rutland Superior criminal court. 
Samplatsky, formerly of Fair Haven, had initially been charged in 2022 with second-degree murder in the fatal shooting of Sincere Johnson, 46, of New York City, inside a Baxter Street apartment in Rutland. In addition, Samplatsky was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for allegedly pointing a firearm at another man in the aftermath of the shooting.
As part of a deal, Samplatsky pleaded guilty Friday to a lesser charge of voluntary manslaughter as well as the aggravated assault charge. 
Under the agreement, Samplatsky received a sentence of 14 years and 11 months to 20 years in prison, all suspended on probation except for 10 years to serve. 
“This is a situation of either a drug deal having gone bad or a drug robbery having gone bad,” Corsones said, adding that the result was Samplatsky shooting and killing Johnson. “It was a horrific crime, we can’t lose sight of that.” 
The judge said in accepting the plea deal he was taking into consideration several factors, including that Samplatsky had no prior criminal history and suffered from substance use disorder and mental health challenges. 
Corsones called the agreement “fair and appropriate.” 
Jamal Johnson, Sincere Johnson’s brother, had earlier spoken during the hearing by video.
“This lady has taken away a part of us, a part of our family. She’s ended a life,” Jamal Johnson said. “Not only did she end a life, the life she ended affected so many other people – daughters, sons, mothers, brothers, cousins.” 
Jamal Johnson called the sentence too lenient. 
“Hopefully,” he added, “God gives me the grace to understand this because right now I don’t have it.”

READ MORE

Samplatsky also spoke. She told the judge she didn’t have the words to express the remorse she felt. 
“My thoughts were distorted and my actions were wrong,” Samplatsky added. “I’m very sorry for the pain that I caused.”
Rutland County State’s Attorney Ian Sullivan, the prosecutor, said in court Friday that in reaching the plea deal he weighed the risk of taking the case to trial with the certainty of the sentence under the deal.
Attorney Marshall Pahl, representing Samplatsky, told the judge that his client had worked a great deal while incarcerated awaiting resolution of the case to address her substance use disorder and mental health challenges. Also, Pahl said, Samplatsky has served as a mentor to other incarcerated people dealing with similar issues. 
According to charging documents, police were called to an apartment building on Baxter Street on June 11, 2022, for a report that a man had been shot and killed. Police later found Johnson dead inside an apartment, the documents stated. 
During the police investigation, according to the documents, witnesses reported that Samplatsky and a man had plans to “rob a drug dealer” and that Samplatsky “shot the drug dealer in the face” during a dispute.
Samplatsky was arrested in New Hampshire shortly after the shooting along with her husband at the time, Michael O’Brien. Samplatsky had denied killing Johnson in speaking with police, charging documents stated. Samplatsky made racist comments about Johnson, the documents stated, and a hate crime enhancement had been filed in the case but was not included as part of the plea deal.
O’Brien had been charged with aiding in the commission of second-degree murder. However, after litigation and a ruling that called into question the strength of the evidence against him, Sullivan dismissed the charge.
Samplatsky, currently held at the Chittenden Regional Correctional Facility in South Burlington, has been in custody since her arrest in 2022.

title: New Mexico environment officials propose another delay on heat safety protections for workers
description: The New Mexico Environment Department has proposed delaying the process to create and adopt rules aimed at protecting workers from heat-related illness and injuries to early 2027.
text:
The New Mexico Environment Department recently filed a motion to postpone rulemaking on worker heat safety to early 2027. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The New Mexico Environment Department has proposed delaying the process to create and adopt rules aimed at protecting workers from heat-related illness and injuries to early 2027.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a recent filing with the state’s Environmental Improvement Board, NMED lawyers wrote that it hasn’t been able to reach consensus on the proposed heat protection standards with the many stakeholders on this issue — including labor organizations, employers and public health advocates — ahead of the current rulemaking hearing, which had been scheduled to begin Sept. 21.
State environment officials first proposed the rulemaking in early 2025 and floated the possibility of requiring employers to provide rest periods, shaded areas and drinking water in hot conditions. Within months, however, the rulemaking was postponed.
Groups representing a number of industries — including livestock, oil and gas and utilities — have pushed back on some of the proposed rule’s requirements.
The latest delay is the fourth since the rulemaking was announced.
Environmental advocates lamented NMED’s latest filing and pointed to the region’s recent bout of triple-digit temperatures as evidence that workers need heat-related protections as soon as possible.
“Regardless of whether a job is in the field or the classroom, heat has the same impacts on the human body. All workers need protections,” Healthy Climate New Mexico Senior Program Consultant Shelley Mann-Lev said in a statement.
The state Environmental Improvement Board is made up of seven members who are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the state Senate. If the rulemaking advances in March, as NMED requested, New Mexico’s next governor will have a chance to install the board overseeing the proceedings.
“As the state moves forward under a new administration, we hope we will see new standards forworker protections adopted,” Conservation Voters New Mexico Chief Operating Officer Molly Taylor wrote in a statement. “Federal worker heat safety standards stalled under Trump. We believe this is an opportunity for New Mexico to lead the nation and show that we can protect our people in the wake of climate change.”

name: VTDigger
title: Regulators reject Route 100 quarry in Morristown
description:
The regional Act 250 commission called the quarry “offensive and shocking.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Regulators reject Route 100 quarry in Morristown.
text:
A 12-acre hill along Route 100 in Morristown. Photo by Gordon Miller/Stowe Reporter

This story by Patrick Bilow first appeared in the News & Citizen on July 30, 2026. 
After a two-year deliberation, the state Act 250 commission has rejected a Morristown business’s proposal to build a quarry operation on land across Route 100 from the Morrisville-Stowe Airport.
Garret Hirchak, CEO and founder of Manufactured Solutions Inc., has for years been trying to build an industrial park on the 89-acre property. The project’s initial phase — and the cause of consternation among Morristown residents and some town officials — would have entailed extracting rock from a wooded knoll at a rate of 35,000 tons a year over 10 years.
According to application documents submitted by MSI, the quarry is incidental to the project, meaning the knoll must be removed to make way for buildings, but it’s also a revenue driver meant to help fund the industrial park.
Several Morristown residents have protested the project throughout the duration of its Act 250 review. Their main concern is silica, a hazardous dust the quartz rock in the knoll would produce if crushed, according to Act 250 documents. Opponents argued it could lead to dangerous lung diseases, including silicosis, if inhaled by humans.
The District 5 Act 250 commission, in its written decision about Hirchak’s project delivered July 24, determined the quarry would be “offensive and shocking.”
The commission stated that “removal of an 8.5-acre rock hill over a decade cannot be determined to be ‘incidental’ in the plain meaning of the word.”
It added that a quarry is not permitted in that area of Morristown, according to the town’s rules, and noted the operation would pose negative health impacts as well as constant noise and traffic associated with crushing and transporting material.
“The proposed continuous cycle of industrial activity will be maintained for a decade,” the commission’s letter reads. “When contrasting the existing surroundings with the impacts associated with the proposed disturbance, the Commission finds the project is offensive and shocking.”
While the commission rejected the proposed quarry operation, it did not reject the industrial park. The property can still accommodate most of MSI’s plans with the knoll intact.
However, it’s unclear whether MSI will move forward without the quarry, and Morristown Zoning Administrator Tyler Machia was unclear on Tuesday whether the project would appear again before the town Development Review Board.
Hirchak did not respond to a request for comment before publication.
Some in town have expressed support for an industrial park without a quarry. The park, which would be the largest of its kind in the region, according to zoning officials, has been touted for its potential to create jobs and drive the local economy.
“I supported the industrial park, but I did not support the gravel extraction,” selectboard chair Don McDowell said in an interview this week. “In my mind, the intent of the town plan was to restrict gravel extraction and those activities to the Route 15 corridor, not to the Route 100 corridor.”
The selectboard last year penned a letter to the Act 250 commission condemning the quarry and urging the commission to consider the project carefully. The letter was sent at the behest of several members of the public who spoke at well-attended board meetings over the last year.
Hirchak or a representative from his company was scheduled to attend one of those meetings in February, and dozens of community members showed up with signs that read “Stop MSI Quarry,” but no one from the company showed up.
Thea Alvin, a Morristown resident who lives on Route 100 near MSI’s property, has been a prominent opponent of the quarry. Last August, she and another resident, Kristin Fogdall, gave a thorough presentation to the selectboard about the negative impacts of the project.
“I’m excited but holding my breath,” Alvin said this week, of the quarry’s rejection. “The Act 250 process is over. We won. We achieved our goals. But now we wait to see what their next step will be.”
Local ruling
The Act 250 commission’s decision supersedes the Morristown Development Review Board’s 2023 approval of the quarry and industrial park. Despite the project pushback from residents even three years ago, the board approved rock extraction as incidental to development, and an application was forwarded to Act 250 officials the following year.
In the wake of more recent opposition, the selectboard and planning commission have embarked on a process to tighten the town’s zoning language pertaining to rock extraction. They are paying particular consideration to terms like “incidental,” which town leaders agree is open to wide interpretation during the review process.
That topic was the subject of a recent joint meeting between the selectboard and planning commission.
“The planning commission is working on language that they will bring back to the board to entertain sometime in the future,” McDowell said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Kanawha County Commission wants more information as WV DEP considers permit for Clean Seas
description: Members of the Kanawha County Commission sent a letter to the state Department of Environmental Protection this week urging it to refrain from issuing an air quality permit for a proposed “advanced recycling” plant until the company behind the project can provide more details to confront concerns raised by residents.
text:
Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who is concerned about the proposed Clean Seas project, speaks at the Kanawha County Commission meeting on July 23, 2026. Caruthers — along with several of his neighbors — delivered a petition signed by nearly 1,000 residents opposing the pyrolysis plant to commissioners Ben Salango and Natalie Tennant. (Photo by Caity Coyne | West Virgina Watch)
Members of the Kanawha County Commission sent a letter to the state Department of Environmental Protection this week urging it to refrain from issuing an air quality permit for a proposed “advanced recycling” plant until the company behind the project can provide more details to confront concerns raised by residents.
A public comment period for the project — which, as proposed by company Clean-Seas West Virginia, would build a plastics pyrolysis facility at the old 84 Lumber building near Belle, in eastern Kanawha County — was closed on Monday. The DEP has already granted a draft permit for the facility, which would operate by burning plastic feedstock to create pyrolysis oil, synthetic gas and solid residue to be used and sold for petrochemical manufacturing purposes.
Residents in the region have been sounding the alarm on the project — and the company proposing it — for nearly a year. They worry about potential emissions particularly as the proposed location sits only a few hundred feet from Riverside High School, Midland Trail Elementary School, residential neighborhoods and a new offroad trail system meant to increase tourism opportunities in the region.
Last week, several residents appeared at the Kanawha County Commission meeting. Armed with a petition signed by nearly 1,000 residents, they asked commissioners Ben Salango and Natalie Tennant to hear their concerns and let Clean Seas know residents are not happy with the way they’ve operated and are deeply concerned about the potential health and community impacts, especially for vulnerable populations.
“My son is a combat veteran who suffers from COPD from his time in Iraq, and he lives right behind me. This is going to hurt him. It’s going to hurt me as an older person. It’s going to hurt little children,” said Laura Wellstead, who lives a few miles down the road from the proposed plant in London. “What we’re asking you is to stand up for those of us who do not have access to people who wield the levers of power and authority in this state. To stand up for us in Kanawha County, to stand up for the elderly and the children and the disenfranchised, so that we can be proud of our state and say, ‘Come here! It’s beautiful. The air is fresh, and we welcome you, as West Virginians, to our community.’”
Several residents made similar requests at that meeting. They spoke about how difficult it’s been to get answers from the company about the proposed project. They cited Clean Sea’s previous, mostly failed, attempts at building similar facilities in other places. They raised alarms about the company’s questionable financials and what impact such a project could have on a community that’s attempting to rebrand itself as part of the tourism “gateway” to the New River Gorge National Park.
Salango, president of the Kanawha County Commission, told members that while he shared their concerns, the powers of the commission were limited. He cited a policy implemented about 40 years ago that stops the county from enforcing zoning in unincorporated areas, which includes most of eastern Kanawha County.
“So we can’t zone. We can’t. Commissioner Tennant and I couldn’t come up with an ordinance right now that says no plastic emissions or no recycling plants in that zone if we wanted to,” Salango said. “They took that away from us. That was the voters.”
In the letter to the DEP, Salango and Tennant — the third position on the Kanawha County Commission is currently vacant — pushed the DEP to evaluate several factors before moving forward with permitting, including:

Whether the air dispersion modeling provided by Clean Seas reflects potential worst-case operating conditions
If emissions estimates included in the air quality permit application are based on reliable data that is comparable to other, similar facilities
Whether the pollution control measures touted by Clean Seas are sufficient enough to protect children at the nearby schools and those who live in neighboring communities
What enforcement measures exist to verify actual emissions after the plant begins operations

Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who has taken the helm of organizing his community to seek these answers and more about the proposed plant, said it’s critical not only for those who live nearby but the region as a whole to ensure that Clean Seas would bring a net positive to the area.
Based on what they know so far, though, that doesn’t seem to be the case.
“We all want economic development. We want jobs, we want new industries and opportunities. We just aren’t convinced that this kind of development will be good for us — or anyone,” Caruthers said. “We’ve done our research and we have a lot of concerns. This isn’t the first time this company has tried to open something like this, and they don’t really have a track record with projects that we can trust. On top of that, what they’re proposing to bring here — it really could harm us. We don’t need more polluters in a place already known as ‘Chemical Valley’.”
A report published this week by the Ohio River Valley Institute lays out several of the concerns shared by Caruthers and his neighbors about previous ventures taken on by Clean Vision Corporation, which is Clean Seas’ parent company.
Per the report, Clean Vision has proposed opening at least 14 plastics pyrolysis facilities worldwide since 2020. As of December 2025, only two of those operations were functional. Filings indicate that the ones that were operational have also scaled back services due to infrastructure needs and a lack of interested funders.
In those projects and in West Virginia, Clean Vision has repeatedly realigned projects, walking back previously promised timelines, changing the proposed scopes of projects and, in many cases, abandoning them altogether, per the report.
Caruthers said this doesn’t inspire hope for how they would operate in Kanawha County if they’re given approval to move forward.
“We want stable jobs. If we’re going to bring new industries, new companies here, we want to make sure that they’re stable and coming from (a company) that has experience and knows what it’s doing and can handle its financials,” Caruthers said. “No one that I know has seen that kind of evidence or assurance come from Clean Seas.”
Clean Seas initially came to West Virginia in 2023, when then-Gov. Jim Justice entered the state into a memorandum of understanding with the company, which promised to invest $50 million to build up the pyrolysis plant. Around that time, the company was making similar agreements with governments in Massachusetts, Arizona, Michigan and Puerto Rico. 
None of those other projects appear to have advanced, per the ORVI report. 
In 2023, the company asserted that operations at the Belle facility would be running by 2024, where it would process 100 tons of plastic per a day with plans to eventually scale up to 500 tons per a day. 
By 2024, the plant was not yet operating. The company had yet to start the permitting process necessary to begin operations. That July, however, the West Virginia Economic Development Authority granted a $15 million bridge loan to Clean Seas to get the facility off the ground.
Throughout 2025 and into 2026, the project saw delay after delay announcement come from the company. The proposed scale of the project — as well as its predicted start date — changed almost quarterly.
Financially, the ORVI report paints an overall concerning picture for Clean Vision. The company currently has two operational pyrolysis facilities: one in India and another in Morocco. Since operations began at those locations in 2023, filings with the federal Securities and Exchange Commission show the company has generated less than $614,000 in revenue from pyrolysis activities, with the income shrinking year over year. Meanwhile, it’s accumulated nearly $58 million in deficits due to operational losses and other growing expenses.
Morgan King, the climate manager for West Virginia Citizen Action Group, said the company’s financials and the fact that taxpayer dollars have gone to this project raise grave concerns for residents in eastern Kanawha County.
“People don’t want their tax dollars going to a company that can’t even really prove it knows what it’s doing,” King said. “They’re really frustrated, and they do want to see new things come to the area but not like this, and not as some kind of experiment.”
And on top of being concerned over the financials, King said there are residents who — because of broken promises from numerous would-be developers in the past — don’t believe the pyrolysis plant will really happen.
“They’ve seen this before, so many times. Someone comes in promising jobs and a new industry, whatever that industry is, and it just never happens,” King said. “There are a lot of residents who don’t really believe this is real, but don’t want to see any more taxpayer dollars going toward it either way.”
For Caruthers, it’s difficult to ignore the history of Kanawha County’s “Chemical Valley.” The region was once thriving — nearly a metropolis in West Virginia terms. Chemical manufacturers like DuPont dominated the region, giving hundreds of locals good-paying jobs and contributing to building up the community through investing in local schools, roads and other amenities.
But over the years, Caruthers said, operations shrunk. Job opportunities dwindled. When the economic boons slowed, residents were left in communities with little else to show for that boom period other than poor air quality and manufacturing and chemical “eye sores.”
Now, he said, residents want to ensure they’re not watching history repeat itself. For the past few years, investments have come to the communities off the Midland Trail that gave residents hope.
The new Appalachian Outlaw Trails are paving the way for a new tourism-based economy. There are discussions occurring about how to capitalize on the region’s proximity to the New River Gorge and other tourist attractions. 
A pyrolysis plant, Caruthers said, puts the potential benefits of these investments at risk.
“No one wants to see something like that right off the road, next to two schools, when they come to enjoy outdoor tourism,” Caruthers said. “The company is not cleaning the area up, they’re just coming inside and adding equipment, so it’s going to be an eyesore. It’s going to be a smell sore. It’s going to be a chemically-induced emissions sore. You’re going to have people coming to the trails, getting exposed to this, and then not wanting to come back.”
And further, Caruthers doesn’t feel that his community should be used as an economic experiment for alleged recycling technology brought by a company that has a questionable background in successfully running such endeavors. 
“That’s not the kind of economy or investment that we’re asking for down here, and we deserve better than being guinea pigs for this company that hasn’t made any real effort to talk to us about our concerns or provide information that we can trust,” Caruthers, 45, said. “Since as long as I can remember, it’s felt like it’s just one bad thing after another for this portion of the county and we’re tired of it. We don’t want to live with the fallout of something we don’t support, so we need people to hear us and join this fight.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Former state agency directors call new Medicaid fraud task force a ‘sham’
description: Two former directors of the state agency that oversees Medicaid fraud investigations said Friday that Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird’s newly formed fraud task force is “political theater.” Dean Lerner and Kevin Techau, who served as directors of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under Democratic governors Tom Vilsack and Chet Culver, said Bir[...]
text:
Two former directors of the state agency that oversees Medicaid fraud investigations are raising objections to a new Medicaid fraud task force led by Attorney General Brenna Bird. (Stock photo by zimmytws/Getty Images)Two former directors of the state agency that oversees Medicaid fraud investigations said Friday that Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird’s newly formed fraud task force is “political theater.”
Dean Lerner and Kevin Techau, who served as directors of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under Democratic governors Tom Vilsack and Chet Culver, said Bird, a Republican, is “leaving millions of dollars on the table” by not working to fully fund Iowa’s existing Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.
Bird, who is seeking reelection this year, heads the newly formed, 11-member Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force, which was created to develop recommendations on how to reduce fraud to stop incidents of fraud in the taxpayer supported healthcare program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Kim Reynolds signed an executive order July 1 creating the task force, which is expected to produce a final report that will be submitted by Oct. 29, 2026.
Dean Lerner, left, and Kevin Techau have each served as director of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals. (Photo by Clark Kauffman/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Techau, who has served as the U.S. Attorney for Northern District of Iowa, and Lerner held a press conference Friday at which they described the task force as a “sham.” The two said Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, which was created in the 1970s and operates within the state agency they once headed, is best suited to address Medicaid fraud — in part because 75% of the cost of its operations is funded by the federal government.
Also, Techau said, for every dollar the unit spends, it generates $4 to $5 in revenue that’s collected through reimbursements and civil and criminal penalties.
Calls and emails to Bird’s office were not returned Friday.
Lerner said Friday that part of the problem is that Iowa has chosen not to fully staff its Medicaid Fraud Control Unit. That decision, he said, limits the number of cases that can be investigated and the amount of taxpayer dollars that can be recovered.
While each of the 50 states has its own Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, a 2024 report from the Office of Inspector General at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says that Iowa has a history of providing far less funding for its MFCU than states with comparable levels of Medicaid spending.
Data from the National Association of Medicaid Fraud Control Units indicates there were five states that in 2022 had Medicaid budgets within $1.5 billion of the $8 billion spent by Iowa Medicaid that year.
All five of those states had MFCUs with budgets that were two to four times that of Iowa’s unit. In fact, some states with far smaller Medicaid budgets than Iowa spent significantly more on their fraud control units.
The latest data from the national association is from 2025, and indicates Iowa still lags behind many states with similar or smaller levels of Medicaid spending:
Iowa: 10 MFCU staffers to oversee $8.3 billion in Medicaid spending.
Arkansas: 23 MFCU staffers to oversee $8.9 billion in Medicaid spending.
Kansas: 16 MFCU staffers to oversee $6.5 billion in Medicaid spending.
Mississippi: 35 MFCU staffers to oversee $7.7 billion in Medicaid spending.
Utah: 22 MFCU staffers to oversee $5.3 billion in Medicaid spending.
Kentucky: 16 MFCU staffers to oversee $6.4 billion in Medicaid spending.

Commentary: Don’t create political theater — fund the Medicaid fraud fighters

Techau: Better data analytics can uncover fraud 
In 2022, the inspector general reviewed the work of Iowa’s MFCU and praised it for operating effectively but noted the unit was leaving positions vacant and was not maintaining its own approved staffing levels.
The inspector general said adding more staff “would ultimately enhance the unit’s ability to protect the Medicaid program and its beneficiaries,” but state officials disagreed and argued current levels of staffing were adequate.
“Iowa doesn’t need another task force to tell us how to fight Medicaid fraud,” Techau said Friday. “We already have trained investigators, a Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, the Iowa False Claims Act, whistleblower protections and experienced federal, state and local law-enforcement partners. The question is whether Iowa is willing to adequately fund them and aggressively use the tools we already have.”
Lerner and Techau made several recommendations on how Iowa could better combat Medicaid fraud, including:
— Staffing: Fully fund Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit with the full number of authorized qualified investigators and staff.
— Analytics: Modernize investigative technology and data analytics to better detect suspicious billing patterns that point to Medicaid fraud.
— Hotline: Restore and actively promote a statewide Medicaid Fraud Hotline.
— Partnerships: Fully empower the Iowa Auditor of State and other independent agencies to investigate fraud.
Fraud investigations, Lerner said, are built by experienced investigators using whistleblower information, audits, referrals and sophisticated analysis of billing data. “Iowa should invest in the people and tools that actually do that work,” he said.
Techau and Lerner also questioned the “political” nature of the new task force, noting that Bird, whose office doesn’t handle Iowa’s Medicaid fraud investigations, heads the panel, while Auditor of State Rob Sand, a Democrat now running for governor, was not given a seat on the task force.
