name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan sees further increase in cyclosporiasis cases amid ongoing state and federal investigations
description: Michigan has documented 10,773 cases of cyclosporiasis, according to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, up from the 8,176 cases reported last Friday. The department is issuing daily updates on the number of documented cases with weekly updates on hospitalizations, as well as cases recorded in each of Michigan’s 83 counties. A total […]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. Michigan health officials say lettuces and salad greens are emerging as a likely source in the nationwide cyclosporiasis outbreak, which has sickened thousands of people across the country. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Michigan has documented 10,773 cases of cyclosporiasis, according to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, up from the 8,176 cases reported last Friday.
The department is issuing daily updates on the number of documented cases with weekly updates on hospitalizations, as well as cases recorded in each of Michigan’s 83 counties.
A total of 193 people have been hospitalized with cyclosporiasis, up from 160 reported last Thursday.
Cyclosporiasis cases continue to rise, as Michigan remains hardest hit state

Cyclosporiasis has been detected in 72 counties. Wayne, Oakland, Washtenaw, Ingham and Genesee counties have the highest number of reported cases.
The state health department announced on July 1 that it was investigating the outbreak, which is caused by the microscopic Cyclospora parasite and spreads through contaminated food or water. Symptoms can emerge two days to two weeks after exposure and include watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, cramping, bloating, increased gas, nausea and fatigue.
As of Thursday, the state’s investigation remained ongoing, pointing to lettuce and salad greens as a potential source of the outbreak. However, DHHS could not completely rule out other types of produce, or identify a specific grower or supplier as a source of the outbreak.
On July 17, Taylor Farms De Mexico issued a voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico. On July 24, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said it is continuing its investigation into infections linked to iceberg lettuce from the region along with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state and local health departments.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The CDC is issuing weekly updates on cyclosporiasis cases, documenting 6,707 cases as of July 28, with 11,500 cases – mostly stemming from Michigan and Ohio – yet to be confirmed through laboratory testing.
The federal agency notes its reports do not include probable cases, which may result in lower case counts than those reported by state health departments. 
The CDC is investigating multiple clusters of Cyclospora cases including a multistate outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce affecting nine states: Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
Michigan remains the hardest hit state, with the CDC recording between 1,000 and 4,000 cases.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Democrat Jasmine Thomas hopes lived experience will propel her to Oklahoma Senate seat
authors: Sabrina Thaler, KOSU, Natalie Armour, KOSU
description: In an Aug. 25 runoff election, Oklahoma voters will choose the Democratic nominee to replace Markwayne Mullin in the U.S. Senate after his March appointment to lead the Department of Homeland Security. In the June primary, N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas led the five-way Democratic primary with 45% of the vote, and Jim Priest followed with nearly […]
text:
N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas on April 3, 2026 at the Capitol files to be a Democratic candidate to be Oklahoma's next U.S. senator. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)In an Aug. 25 runoff election, Oklahoma voters will choose the Democratic nominee to replace Markwayne Mullin in the U.S. Senate after his March appointment to lead the Department of Homeland Security.
In the June primary, N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas led the five-way Democratic primary with 45% of the vote, and Jim Priest followed with nearly 24%. State law requires a runoff when no candidate in a primary earns more than half the vote.
The winner of the runoff will face Republican Kevin Hern in the general election in November. Hern has served as the Congressman for Oklahoma’s first district since 2018 and swept the Republican primary in June.
Neither Thomas nor Priest has held elected office before. Priest, a lawyer and nonprofit executive, ran in 2010 to serve as state Attorney General and lost to Republican Scott Pruitt. Thomas is a nurse.
Both candidates would face an uphill battle in November. Oklahoma has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1990, and Hern alone received more votes in the Republican primary than every Democratic candidate combined. President Donald Trump endorsed Hern shortly after Mullin’s cabinet appointment, a decision the New York Times wrote “all but assured” Hern would take the seat.
Hern has also raised significantly more money than either Democratic candidate, including more than $5 million he personally loaned his campaign.
KOSU interviewed Priest and Thomas about how they would approach a race against Hern, their attitudes toward the President and what their priorities would be in Congress. KOSU’s interview with Jim Priest was published Thursday.
Sabrina Thaler, KOSU reporter: Why are you running for Senate?
Jasmine Thomas, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate: I’m running because there has never been any kind of representation on the federal level here in Oklahoma. I have never seen anyone who looked like me, walked like me, talked like me, or who has lived like me in these positions. I have seen countless people who are exactly the opposite of me. And I just thought that it was my time to actually step up.
I have a son with autism. Oklahoma didn’t have the resources for us to be able to give him the ABA, the speech language pathology, the OT, and the Army saved us. And I just thought, well, who’s saving the Oklahomans? So when I went to go look at all of the legislation that was in the Senate or even in the state House. I said, you know what? Like there’s no priorities here. None, zero, zilch. And none that actually benefit the working class. But then one day I just so happened to wake up and see Markwayne Mullin. And I was just like, man, this guy is a real… he’s interesting. Like, what does he actually do? So I just went back and I looked at all of his track record of any legislation that he’s passed and just noticed that none was conducive to the Oklahomans. Everything just benefited him in some odd capacity. But the U.S. Senate was not the first thing that I thought that I would ever run for, for sure, but I’ve always wanted to be a legislator.
Thaler: You don’t have conventional political experience, but what experience of yours do you think makes you qualified to be a Senator?
Thomas: My lived experience. I believe that most public servants… I don’t believe that we should be called politicians, because politicians obviously have a different kind of interest versus a ‘public servant.’ I’m a nurse. I’m an active duty military spouse. I’m an advocate. I’m a mom with a child with special needs. So disability rights has been something that I’ve advocated heavily on. The veterans, VA and also military spouse issues that we face within our community. I’ve advocated on behalf of. And also nurses, nursing unions, making sure that we actually have a lunch, we get paid for the time that we’re on the clock, not being able to take a break because we have so many patients to one nurse. I’ve also done education advocacy, because my son is in a special education class. I’ve done IEP, 504 and the IDEA. It’s all a big cluster of things.
I believe that you don’t necessarily have to have political experience. You have to have that lived experience or else you won’t know how to serve your community at the end of the day. You just won’t, when you’ve never been from, a certain area or you’ve never been having to scrounge up change to eat or trying to figure out where you’re going to get formula from, or sitting in an IEP meeting, or wondering how you’re going to pay certain bills, what kind of workforce you have you’re having to go into because there’s hospitals closing down in rural areas.
Someone’s not prioritizing the people. They’re not prioritizing the people. And that’s just not what we need on a federal level. We need someone who’s going to stand up and who’s going to actually make things change. We need to have someone who can get up there and say, listen, I’ve touched the hands of the rural community, the urban communities, the Black, brown, the disability community. We need people who are actually public servants.
Thaler: Oklahoma hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1990. And the state has also struggled with low voter turnout. In June, less than a quarter of registered voters cast ballots. If you win this coming runoff, how do you plan to reach Republican and independent voters?
Thomas: We ended up shutting the independents out of our voter bloc anyway, and so with closed primaries for our independents who are normally some of our solid voters, it really kind of put that damper. I understand that we have over 200-and-something thousand Democrats that are registered, but the thing is, they needed something to vote for. And that’s why I decided that I would get into this as well. We’ve seen the same people run over and over and over again, and we’ve seen nothing change. So I was out there getting people registered. I was out there getting motivated, activated, feet on the ground.
I can reach across the aisle. I’m not a difficult person. One thing about me is that I’m not a yes-man. I tell people that I’m kind, not nice. Kindness is standing up to the oppressor and saying no when everyone else is saying yes. But being nice is being the yes-man and not going against the grain and taking the path of least resistance.
Thaler: As a senator, how would you translate Oklahomans everyday concerns into federal policy, and what are those policies that you would propose?
Thomas: I have a few policies, and some of them are very detailed, and they’re very centered to the people. We see a lot of issues every day that do not get addressed, because I know that corporations are being put over the people. So one thing that I would make sure of, is I’d codify our civil rights. I think civil rights are super important, and I think when anyone is walking that line where they can just delineate our rights, they need to be codified, 100 percent.
When I get up there, I’m going to make sure that we start funding and putting in the resources into our hospitals, getting their funding for their research, such as cancer, autism or any other, any other health ailment.
My job is to not keep rebuilding onto the cracked foundation that we’re at right now. It’s not. My job is to reconstruct, rebuild. That’s not getting rid of the Constitution. That’s not taking away what the Founding Fathers have done. At the end of the day, the Founding Fathers founded this land of freedom, justice, and the pursuit of happiness, and that’s what we need to get back to. But we can build a better America by actually starting with the people.
Thaler: If you win August’s runoff, you would face Representative Kevin Hern in the general election. He swept the Republican primary, and his campaign has also raised over $9 million. And that includes $5 million of Mr. Hern’s own investments. How do you plan to bridge that gap and face Kevin Hern in the general election?
Thomas: The thing is, we’re seeing a whole new generation of campaigning. I have piloted the online campaigning here in Oklahoma. We’re seeing a new generation of campaigning and we’re seeing that money really doesn’t matter. It just doesn’t. Money is the root of all evil right now. So we’re seeing people, when you reach out to them, you touch them, you actually go into the communities and actually talk with them, you’re seeing their minds change. So even with $9 million, a handshake is worth more than that.
I believe that I can beat Kevin Hern because Kevin Hern has a different type of interest that should not interest anyone who actually cares about Oklahoma. He swept this because of the fact that people know who he is. Our Republican counterparts, even our moderates know — and most of them are actually going to vote blue – they voted for the most extreme to make the Democratic candidate look more appealing and appeasing. But that’s giving us a better strategy that I don’t want to give out too much, because the thing is, I can’t give it away, or else someone else is going to try to take it from me.
Thaler: Representative Hern has been a fierce champion of President Trump, and he received the president’s endorsement in this race. Your potential predecessor, Markwayne Mullin, left his post in the Senate to join President Trump’s cabinet. As a Senator, how would you approach a working relationship with the president?
Thomas: Like I said, I’m kind, not nice. So I will make sure that I work as diligently as I can to make sure that within my first 100 days that we impeach, remove, and convict. They will have to pry that pen out of my cold, dead hands before I go any further with allowing this administration to continue doing what they’re doing. So, I mean, hopefully that’s a good answer. But I am going to remove, impeach, remove and convict. That’s it. Like that’s all. That’s the answer.
And we can take back the Senate. We just have to keep giving people something to vote for, something to look forward to. Because if we don’t do that, our younger generation, that’s who we’re depending on.
We know that our regular voters, the ones that come out every election, can help, but the youth and also our Black and brown communities, they are going to carry this. And also our moderates, I love my moderate Republicans. But our super MAGA Republicans, our job is not to change their mind. We’re not going to switch that. I am very, very well aware of that. It’s just not going to happen. Now, can they have a coming to Jesus? Absolutely. I applaud them for that. And I actually would encourage that. But that’s not going to be our main base. We’re going to actually get our disengaged and apathetic. We’re going to get our younger voters. We’re going to get the people who are against or not wanting to vote or that don’t want to be political because of, you know, certain beliefs that maybe the political system does not actually work for us, it works against us. Well, who can work against us if your voice is casted and you get someone that you believe in? We just have to give the people something to believe in.
Thaler: What makes you different from Jim Priest, your opponent in this race?
Thomas: I’m not a career politician. I am a mom of a son with autism. I am an active duty military spouse that understands what it’s like to organize and to be resourceful, and also who knows how to be very reasonable, because that life is hard. But also, I’m a nurse. I do this caring thing for people daily and we need someone like that. We need people who have lived experiences. And I don’t believe that that’s what Jim has.
No shade to Jim, or maybe all shade, because I cannot fund myself $50,000 to put into my campaign. Right. I cannot even put that into my kids’ accounts right now. I live the same working class life that everyone else does, still to this day. My campaign finances. I beat him by a 21% margin with less than $50,000. And that all came from my community. It came off of my community. But the thing is, I cannot fund my kids’ future tomorrow. But he could step away from this today and fund his grandkids’ future. I cannot rely on leaving this, and just going to kick back and relax and have a great time. I’m going to have to get back to work after this because life is not free. And the thing is, that should not have to be our first thing that we have to think about when we’re trying to be public servants. It should be, ‘Hey, you’ve been campaigning for X amount of time, take two weeks off,’ you know? But no. I have to get right back to work. And that’s something that my opponent does not have to worry about. He does not.
I just want to say, vote for me. I have the grit. I’ve shown the stamina and I’ve shown how hard I work. And I outwork everyone. And if that wasn’t the truth, then I wouldn’t be in this position right now. I am the candidate. I am the girl for this job. And I know that I can beat Kevin Hern because Kevin Hern has already beaten himself.
We don’t need two of the same going against each other. That’s a bore. Let’s live it up for once. Let’s have something that Oklahoma can actually be proud of, but also let Oklahoma finally have some eyes on them outside of Thunder. We can do this. It’s going to be an uphill battle. It’s going to be David and Goliath. But the thing is, David still beat Goliath at the end of the day.
This transcript has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.
This article was originally published by KOSU.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas Explained: What is the back-to-school sales tax holiday?
description: It’s not Black Friday or the holiday season, but expect Arkansas stores to be more crowded than usual this weekend.  Saturday and Sunday mark the state’s annual sales tax holiday, created by lawmakers 15 years ago to provide a tax break to families during back-to-school shopping. Arkansas is among 20 states that have enacted “holidays” […]
text:
Saturday and Sunday mark Arkansas' annual sales tax holiday. The holiday was created in 2011 to coincide with back-to-school shopping. (Jon Cherry/Getty Images)It’s not Black Friday or the holiday season, but expect Arkansas stores to be more crowded than usual this weekend. 
Saturday and Sunday mark the state’s annual sales tax holiday, created by lawmakers 15 years ago to provide a tax break to families during back-to-school shopping.
Arkansas is among 20 states that have enacted “holidays” when items like clothing and school supplies are exempt from sales taxes. Experts have debated over the effectiveness of such laws. 
Navigating the laws and figuring out which products will be exempt from sales taxes can be tricky. Here’s a guide to the sales tax holiday and its rules:
Why does Arkansas have a sales tax holiday?
The Arkansas Legislature and then-Gov. Mike Beebe in 2011 approved the measure creating a sales tax holiday for certain items during the first weekend in August. 
This year, the sales tax begins at 12:01 a.m. Saturday and ends at 11:59 p.m. Sunday. During that time, eligible items will be exempt from the state’s 6.5% sales tax as well as city and county sales taxes.
Supporters of the 2011 noted that states adjoining Arkansas had similar tax holidays tied to the start of the school year, and said Arkansas was losing revenue because of residents traveling out-of-state for deals.
Beebe had been hesitant to the idea of a sales tax holiday but agreed to sign it as part of a $35 million package of tax cuts enacted that year.
What items are exempt?
The state Department of Finance and Administration provides a list of items that are exempt during the sales tax weekend.
The items have changed little since 2011, though the Legislature in 2021 expanded it to include cell phones, laptops, tablets and computer monitors. There’s not a limit to the price or number of electronic items for the exemption.
The exemption applies to school supplies, including book bags, Crayons, lunch boxes, art supplies and pencils.
Clothing items that are less than $100 are exempt. That applies to individual items, so someone could buy as many shirts as they want that cost $99 or less and not pay sales tax, but if they buy a shirt for $101 they’d have to pay tax on that item.
Clothing accessories or equipment, including briefcases or jewelry, qualify for the exemption if they’re less than $50 per item. 
Navigating the rules isn’t always easy. While belts are eligible for the exemption, belt buckles sold separately aren’t. Sneakers qualify, but cleated athletic shoes don’t. Diapers and wedding attire are also considered eligible clothing items for the holiday.
And the exemption covers reference books and textbooks, but it won’t cover the latest bestsellers by Stephen King or John Grisham. 
Sorry, gamers, the holiday doesn’t apply to gaming systems.
What if I want to shop online?
Eligible items purchased online also qualify for the tax holiday as long as it’s delivered to an address in the state. It can arrive anytime, but the purchase must be made Saturday or Sunday.
What’s the impact of the tax holiday?
Department of Finance and Administration spokesperson Scott Hardin said the agency doesn’t have specific estimates on the impact since retailers are not required to submit figures on the tax-free sales.
“However, we can say conservatively that Arkansans are saving several million dollars this weekend,” Hardin said in an email.
When the sales tax holiday was approved in 2011, finance officials estimated it would cost the state about $2.1 million the first year.
Experts, however, have questioned the value of tax-free weekends and holidays like Arkansas’. The nonprofit Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy has said the holidays don’t address the “inherently regressive” nature of sales taxes.
“In the long run, sales tax holidays leave a regressive tax system unchanged, and the benefits of these holidays for working families are minimal,” the group said last year.
The Tax Foundation has also criticized the holidays, calling them an “inefficient vehicle” for tax relief or creating additional economic activity.
“They inject unnecessary instability into government and business revenue streams; create administrative and compliance costs for businesses, governments, and consumers; and do not promote long-term economic growth,” the group said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ wants semiautomatic rifle ban to remain in effect as it seeks Supreme Court review
description: New Jersey said an appeals court ruling striking its ban on certain semiautomatic weapons should be paused as the state appeals.
text:
A July 17 Circuit Court ruling found New Jersey laws banning certain semiautomatic rifles and magazines that can hold more than 10 rounds were unconstitutional. (Photo by Aristide Economopoulos/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey asked the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals to pause an order striking the state’s ban on certain semiautomatic weapons while the state seeks to bring the case before the U.S. Supreme Court.
In a court filing entered Friday, attorneys for the state argued the appeals court has routinely stayed orders while litigants sought certification before the highest court in the land and pointed to contrary rulings from six other circuit courts that upheld similar bans.
“That nearly thirty appellate judges across the ideological spectrum agree with the State’s arguments suggests at least a ‘reasonable possibility’ that five Justices would ultimately do the same,” New Jersey attorneys said in the filing.
The appeals court’s ruling also struck down New Jersey’s ban on high-capacity magazines.
In Friday’s filing, the state cited a three-pronged test to back its request.
New Jersey argued courts have historically allowed struck laws to persist if there was a reasonable probability that the Supreme Court would take up the case, that five justices would reverse the lower court’s ruling, and that a litigant would face irreparable harm if a law was struck.
The Supreme Court has already taken up Viramontes v. Cook County, an Illinois case that asks whether the Second and 14th Amendment rights permit ownership of AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, so it would likely take up New Jersey’s case, the state argued.
Three justices — Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch — voted to take up a case challenging magazine capacity limits last year.
Rulings from the 1st, 2nd, 7th, 9th, and D.C. circuit courts have upheld semiautomatic weapon bans or magazine capacity limits, and New Jersey argued the justices could agree with those decisions rather than the one issued by the 3rd Circuit.
And they said New Jersey would be harmed if the law were to lapse, both because states always face irreparable harm when a court blocks a law and because even a temporary break to the nearly 40-year-old ban would have permanent consequences by allowing the sale of firearms that could later be declared illegal again.
“Law enforcement would not know who now possesses such weapons in New Jersey, and thousands of individuals may be subject to criminal exposure for continuing to possess weaponry they understood to be lawful when initially purchased,” New Jersey’s attorneys wrote.
A state exhibit showed at least three instances where New Jersey arms dealers had sold high-capacity magazines following the ruling.
“Absent a stay of the mandate, thousands (or more) of such sales could take place in the State, a bell state and local law enforcement could not soon un-ring,” the state said.
New Jersey’s so-called assault weapons ban dates to 1990 and bars ownership of 66 listed rifles and shotguns and similar firearms plus those with certain characteristics, like a pistol grip, a threaded barrel meant to accept muzzle devices like flash hiders and suppressors, or folding or telescoping stocks.
Its high-capacity magazine ban bars any magazine that can hold more than ten rounds of ammunition.
The National Rifle Association, which funded and argued the case, and the Association of New Jersey Pistol and Rifle Clubs, which brought it, did not immediately return a request for comment.
Gun owners have also challenged a more recent New Jersey law that bars firearms in an array of locations. A divided three-judge 3rd Circuit panel upheld most of the law but gun owners want the court’s full panel of judges to rule on their challenge.

title: Health advocates raise alarms about Nebraska’s ‘rushed’ implementation of Medicaid work requirements
description: LINCOLN — After Nebraska implemented new Medicaid work rules eight months ahead of a federal deadline, Angela Lindstrom with the Health Center Association of Nebraska said some residents have waited up to 90 minutes on the state’s phone line to get their questions answered. “As you can imagine, our certified application counselors are sitting with […]
text:
A sign in front of the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services' Lincoln Public Assistance Office on Oct. 30, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — After Nebraska implemented new Medicaid work rules eight months ahead of a federal deadline, Angela Lindstrom with the Health Center Association of Nebraska said some residents have waited up to 90 minutes on the state’s phone line to get their questions answered.
“As you can imagine, our certified application counselors are sitting with a patient — they don’t have 90 minutes to sit there and wait,” Lindstrom said. “A lot of times these people have a lot of barriers just to be able to get to the appointment.”
Lindstrom was one of several health advocates that shared concerns about what they called a “rushed” implementation of new federal work requirements for Medicaid participants in Nebraska. The Friday discussion was hosted by watchdog group Nebraska Appleseed. Several speakers said the added complications are deterring overall participation in Medicaid, and noted there remains a list of questions state officials have yet to answer.
Nebraska was the first state in the U.S. to comply with new work requirements for Medicaid participants added under the “One Big Beautiful Bill” Congress passed last year. Under the new rules, most able-bodied Medicaid participants between 19 and 64 must show they’ve worked a minimum of 80 hours per month, or show they have earned at least $580 each month.
Sarah Maresh, Appleseed’s program director for health care access, estimated the new rules will apply to roughly 70,000 Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska.
Nebraska becomes first state to add new Medicaid federal work requirements

States are required to implement the changes by Jan. 1, 2027, but Nebraska began requiring new enrollees to comply on May 1. Starting Aug. 1, the rules will apply to existing enrollees, meaning that some current participants could lose coverage.
The one exception in Nebraska is Dawson County, which was approved for a temporary exemption as the county struggles with a high unemployment rate following the closure of the Tyson Foods plant.
In an interview with nonprofit news organization Tradeoffs, Nebraska’s Director of Medicaid and Long-Term Care Drew Gonshorowski estimated that about 200 Nebraskans will lose Medicaid coverage starting Aug. 1, under the new rules. While Maresh said this was lower than she was expecting, she noted that the new rules will be applied to existing enrollees at their monthly renewals, so she wasn’t anticipating an immediate steep drop-off in participation.
Maresh added that remaining unanswered questions include:

How many applicants have been denied Medicaid coverage since May 1?
How are some of the temporary exemptions being defined, such as work that requires employees to travel?
When will the state be publicly sharing data related to the Medicaid changes?

Officials with Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Maresh said it was contradictory for Gov. Jim Pillen to expect Nebraskans to comply with the new work requirements when he recently called for a hiring freeze within state agencies in a memo he released earlier this month.
Lindstrom said the changes have not only confused Medicaid enrollees and applicants, but also some state workers charged with implementing the changes. She shared an instance of one pregnant applicant who was denied coverage despite being eligible, simply because the state missed that she was pregnant on her application.
In addition to long wait times on the state’s standard phone line, Lindstrom said there have been bigger issues for the state’s hotline for Spanish speakers. She said the Spanish line was out of commission for more than six weeks between May 15-July 1.
Megan Word, Nebraska government relations director for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, said the changes will likely increase the chance of Nebraskans delaying healthcare treatments, which in turn will increase their likelihood of needing more costly emergency care.
Cheri Stollar, a Lincoln-based therapist and single mother of five, backed up Word’s point. She said she went uninsured for most of her life, and as a result she held off seeking treatment for a collection of medical issues until some of them became life-threatening.
Stollar qualified and enrolled in Medicaid last year, and said she’s offended by the stigma that enrollees are “lazy.” As a therapist, Stollar said she’s encountered people with mental health issues so severe that they aren’t capable of working on a daily basis.
Stollar said she feels like the Medicaid changes are “kicking people when they’re down,” as many Medicaid participants are low-income or struggling with severe and ongoing health issues.
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha, a mental health professional who sits on the Nebraska Legislature’s Health and Human Services Committee, said the disruption the Medicaid changes can cause to patients could amount to more than “just a paperwork delay.” In some cases, he said it could cause medical crises that otherwise would have been preventable.
Fredrickson highlighted that implementing these changes ahead of schedule was a choice from the governor, and not a requirement, which he found troubling.
“It’s really not the badge of honor that the governor and his allies in the Legislature seem to really think that it is,” Fredrickson said.

name: Delaware
title: The Lincoln Memorial “Undercroft” Opens – Attractions Available to Delawareans!
description: Beneath the Lincoln Memorial: A Hidden Space Opens to the Public After More Than a Century – The Undercroft One of the many benefits of living in Delaware is our access to varied sights and attractions.  We have the Beach, the Shore, the Poconos, Philadelphia, New York City and Washington D. C. all within a couple of hours or so.  ... Read More
text:
Beneath the Lincoln Memorial: A Hidden Space Opens to the Public After More Than a Century – The Undercroft

A Night View of the Lincoln Memorial, with Lincoln’s Statue in View Between the Columns.
The famous Abraham Lincoln Statue at the Memorial.
One of the many benefits of living in Delaware is our access to varied sights and attractions.  We have the Beach, the Shore, the Poconos, Philadelphia, New York City and Washington D. C. all within a couple of hours or so.  This past week, we journeyed down to Washington, D. C. to take in some of the usual sights – especially the National Mall area.  We were attracted to a brand new offering that opened just in time for the 250th celebration. For more than 100 years, millions of visitors have climbed the steps of the iconic Lincoln Memorial without realizing that a vast hidden chamber lies beneath their feet. That secret space—the memorial’s “undercroft”—opened to the public in June 2026 as one of the most significant enhancements to the National Mall in decades.
The new visitor experience offers a rare look inside the engineering that made the Lincoln Memorial possible while telling the evolving story of one of America’s most recognizable symbols of democracy, equality, and civil rights.
A Monument Built on a Swamp
Construction of the Lincoln Memorial began in 1914 on land bordering the Potomac River that was once marshland. Engineers faced a daunting challenge: how to support a structure weighing approximately 38,000 tons on unstable soil.
Their solution was remarkable. Workers drove deep foundations to bedrock and constructed an enormous structural chamber beneath the memorial. Inside, more than 120 massive reinforced concrete columns—each extending roughly 50 feet to bedrock—carry the weight of the marble temple above. The resulting cavern covers about 50,000 square feet, nearly twice the footprint of the memorial itself.
Although essential to the monument’s stability, the undercroft was never intended for public access. For generations it remained a little-known maintenance area visited only by National Park Service personnel, preservation specialists, and construction crews.
More Than an Engineering Marvel
Dedicated in 1922, the Lincoln Memorial quickly became far more than a tribute to the nation’s 16th president.
Its grand steps evolved into one of America’s most powerful civic stages. Among its defining moments:

In 1939, celebrated singer Marian Anderson performed before 75,000 people after being barred from singing in Constitution Hall because of her race.
In 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his historic “I Have a Dream” speech during the March on Washington.
The memorial has continued to serve as a gathering place for demonstrations, celebrations, protests, and national commemorations spanning generations.

Because of this history, the memorial has become as much a symbol of the ongoing pursuit of civil rights as it is a monument to Abraham Lincoln.
Delaware Shown on the Lincoln Memorial Frieze
A Delaware Connection at the Lincoln Memorial!
There are a couple of Delaware-related highlights at the Lincoln Memorial.  The design includes 36 columns around the exterior – symbolizing the 36 states in the Union at the time of Lincoln’s death.  These states are also engraved in “the Lower Frieze” that encircles the memorial, above the columns.  Delaware, as the “First State” is listed in the prominent position of top-right along this display!
Above that is “Attic Frieze”, which displays the 48 states that were present at the time the memorial was dedicated in 1922.
Transforming a Hidden Space
Planning to open the undercroft to visitors began nearly a decade before construction started in 2023. The $69 million project combined federal funding with substantial private support through the National Park Foundation.
Rather than converting the entire foundation into museum space, designers preserved the dramatic industrial character of the chamber. Approximately 15,000 square feet were developed into an immersive exhibition area while leaving much of the towering structural space visible.
A Model of the Lincoln Memorial “Undercroft”.
Visitors now encounter:

The soaring grid of exposed concrete columns supporting the memorial.
Interactive exhibits explaining the memorial’s design and construction.
Multimedia presentations tracing the monument’s changing role in American history.
Historic artifacts and construction remnants, including reproductions of workers’ graffiti discovered during restoration.
Improved accessibility features and educational displays for visitors of all ages.

Many visitors have compared the immense concrete chamber to the nave of a cathedral—an apt description for a hidden space that has quietly supported one of America’s most revered monuments for more than a century.
Opening Ahead of America’s 250th Birthday
The undercroft officially opened to the public on June 25, 2026, just ahead of nationwide commemorations of the United States’ 250th anniversary. The timing reflects a broader effort by the National Park Service to enrich the visitor experience across the National Mall while preserving its historic landmarks.
Admission is free, although timed-entry tickets are required because visitor capacity is limited. Advance reservations are available through Recreation.gov for a nominal reservation fee, while a limited number of same-day tickets are distributed daily by the National Park Service.  Access to the Undercroft is to the right of the main stairway of the Memorial, where you present your timed-entry ticket and pass through a security checkpoint.
A New Perspective
For visitors, the undercroft provides something unusual: an opportunity to appreciate both the physical and symbolic foundations of the Lincoln Memorial.
Above ground, visitors encounter Daniel Chester French’s towering marble statue of Abraham Lincoln and inscriptions from the Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural Address. Below ground, they discover the hidden engineering that made the monument possible and learn how the memorial itself has become a stage for defining moments in American history.
The result is more than a museum. It is an experience that reminds visitors that great monuments are supported not only by stone and concrete, but also by the generations of Americans who have continually redefined the ideals they represent.

title: US Senate panel advances bill to reject Education Department transfers
text: WASHINGTON — A bipartisan effort to rein in President Donald Trump’s efforts to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education has cleared its first major legislative hurdle in a bipartisan U.S. Senate committee vote. The measure, approved by the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee in a 13-9 vote Thursday, represents the most sweeping attempt from Congress so far in rejecting some of the interagency agreements, or IAAs, Education has signed with other departments as part of the administration’s push to eliminate the 46-year-old agency. The Senate bill, sponsored by Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, with GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska as original co-sponsors, would block IAAs that transfer programs regarding special education, elementary and secondary education, postsecondary education and Native American education.Part of the measure takes aim at Education’s efforts announced in June to outsource programs under its Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, or OSERS, to the Department of Health and Human Services. OSERS is responsible for administering the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA, which guarantees a free public education for students with disabilities.Education has so far entered into agreements with HHS, along with the departments of Labor, Interior, State, Treasury and Justice, to offload several of the department’s core responsibilities to those agencies.Collins, Murkowski join DemsCollins said the “straightforward” bill “keeps the administration of important landmark education programs at the Department of Education — where Congress specifically put them and where they belong.”All Democrats on the panel voted to advance the measure. They are: Kaine, Patty Murray of Washington state, Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, John Hickenlooper of Colorado, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Andy Kim of New Jersey, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland.Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, ranking member of the panel who caucuses with Democrats, also voted to advance the bill. Collins and Murkowski were the only GOP members to join Democrats. GOP Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky did not vote. The panel’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy, voted against the bill, saying that while he opposes the transfer of special ed programs to HHS, he is open to moving OSERS to the Labor Department. “I don’t oppose all of these IAAs,” the Louisiana Republican said. “I do think the administration should be allowed to pilot how to address inefficiencies and the potential for efficiencies by operationalizing these IAAs.”The other GOP members who voted against the measure were Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas, Tim Scott of South Carolina, Josh Hawley of Missouri, Tommy Tuberville of Alabama, Jim Banks of Indiana, Jon Husted of Ohio, Ashley Moody of Florida and Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma. ‘Show us the price tag’ The panel also approved an amendment to the bill from Murray that would require Education Secretary Linda McMahon to report to Congress on the cost estimates for each of the IAAs her agency has signed with other departments. “My amendment is very simple — it asks one thing: Tell Congress and the public what these interagency agreements actually cost taxpayers,” Murray said. “If you’re proud of this deal, show us the price tag,” she added. “What do you have to hide?” Education Department defends transfersTrump has sought to take an axe to the Education Department in his quest to send education policymaking “back to the states.” That push continues despite much of the oversight and funding of schools already occurring at the state and local levels. Savannah Newhouse, an Education Department spokesperson, said “the era of coddling a failed status quo must end,” in a statement to States Newsroom Thursday.“Secretary McMahon promised Congress a proof of concept that is currently underway and delivering results across our partner agencies, and it is entirely premature to sabotage this effort before it has the chance to eliminate bureaucratic barriers and fully deliver the results that our students, families, and educators deserve,” Newhouse added. McMahon, along with the heads of the six departments involved in the IAAs, defended the agreements in a letter sent to the GOP and Democratic leaders in the House and Senate the same day the Senate panel advanced the bill. “Misconceptions have circulated about our fourteen IAAs,” McMahon and the leaders of the agencies wrote. “Since these agreements were signed, however, they have demonstrated measurable results by driving stronger grant competitions, streamlining government operations, and producing better outcomes for Americans.”The Senate measure sharply contrasts with a package that advanced out of a House education panel this month that would greatly reduce the department’s responsibilities.

title: Veteran Dave Graham seeks Republican nomination for Delaware attorney general
description: Former Army and Delaware National Guard member asks state GOP leaders to place him on November ballot David Graham, a U.S. Army and Delaware National Guard veteran with decades of experience in state government and public finance, announced Thursday that he is seeking the Republican nomination for Delaware attorney general. Graham made the announcement July[...]
text:
Former Army and Delaware National Guard member asks state GOP leaders to place him on November ballot
David Graham, a U.S. Army and Delaware National Guard veteran with decades of experience in state government and public finance, announced Thursday that he is seeking the Republican nomination for Delaware attorney general.
Graham made the announcement July 30 during an appearance on “The Rick Jensen Show” on WDEL. He said he has asked Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono to nominate him as the party’s candidate for the statewide office.
Graham’s military service is expected to be a central part of his appeal to Republican leaders and voters. He has served in both the U.S. Army and the Delaware National Guard and has presented his candidacy as one rooted in service, accountability and respect for the rule of law.
The announcement does not yet make Graham the official Republican nominee. As of Friday, the Delaware Department of Elections did not list a Republican candidate for attorney general. The regular candidate filing deadline was July 14.
Republican leaders could still have a path to nominate a candidate for the general election, subject to Delaware election law, applicable deadlines and the filing of required documents.
Graham’s effort has a precedent in Delaware political history, although the election rules and circumstances are not identical.
In 1976, Democrats concluded their state convention without nominating a candidate for state treasurer. Tom Carper, then a 29-year-old employee of the Delaware Office of Economic Development, subsequently entered the race, secured the Democratic nomination and won the general election.
The victory began a nearly five-decade career in elected office that included service as state treasurer, congressman, governor and U.S. senator.
Graham is similarly asking party leaders to consider him after Republicans did not produce a candidate for attorney general through the regular filing process. His supporters could cite Carper’s experience as evidence that a candidate who emerges after the regular process can still mount a serious statewide campaign.
There is also no requirement in the Delaware Constitution that the attorney general be a licensed lawyer.
The state constitution establishes the attorney general as an elected statewide officer serving a four-year term, but it does not list a law degree, bar membership or prior legal practice among the qualifications for the office.
Although Delaware’s attorney general leads the Department of Justice and serves as the state’s chief law enforcement officer, voters are not legally limited to choosing candidates who are practicing attorneys.
Graham is expected to point instead to his military service, government experience and background in financial oversight as qualifications for managing the department and promoting accountability within state government.
Truono, who became state Republican chairman in August 2025, has not publicly confirmed that the party will nominate Graham. The Delaware GOP had not announced a decision following Graham’s radio appearance.
Graham would give Republicans a candidate in a race currently centered on a three-way Democratic primary.
Incumbent Attorney General Kathy Jennings is seeking another term and faces challenges from Dwayne Bensing and Patty Rickman in the Sept. 15 Democratic primary. No Republican filed for the office before the regular deadline.
In addition to his military service, Graham has worked for the Delaware Department of Finance since 2003. Before joining state government, he spent approximately 25 years as a certified public accountant, giving him experience in public finance, financial oversight and government operations.
Graham has sought statewide office several times and has frequently presented himself as an outsider focused on accountability, government integrity and responsible management.
He ran as a write-in candidate for governor in 2012 and as the Independent Party candidate for attorney general in 2014. Graham received about 2.1% of the vote in the 2014 general election, which was won by Democrat Matt Denn.
In 2020, Graham sought the Republican nomination for governor but lost in the party’s primary.
His entry would offer Delaware voters a contrast between a veteran with experience inside state government and candidates with more traditional legal backgrounds. It would also prevent Republicans from leaving the attorney general’s race uncontested in November.
Delaware’s attorney general leads the Department of Justice, which oversees criminal prosecutions, consumer protection, civil litigation involving the state and other legal matters.
The general election is Nov. 3.
TO GO

What: 2026 election for Delaware attorney general
Candidate: David Graham, a veteran of the U.S. Army and Delaware National Guard
Democratic primary: Tuesday, Sept. 15
General election: Tuesday, Nov. 3
Republican status: Graham has asked the Delaware Republican Party to nominate him, but he was not listed Friday as an official candidate by the Department of Elections.
Candidate qualifications: The Delaware Constitution does not require the attorney general to be a lawyer or member of the Delaware Bar.
Historical precedent: Tom Carper entered the 1976 state treasurer’s race after Democrats initially left the nomination open and went on to win the general election.
Learn more: Candidate and ballot information is available through the Delaware Department of Elections.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Election officials unfazed by Trump administration monitoring primaries in Manchester and Nashua
description: New Hampshire election officials say they’re unconcerned after the Trump administration announced it will send election monitors to watch September’s primaries in Manchester and Nashua — a longstanding practice that has drawn partisan suspicion amid the president’s recent actions on elections. The U.S. Department of Justice announced earlier this month it’s[...]
text:
New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, the state’s chief elections official, said his office learned of the monitors at the same time the public did. (Photo by Kate Brindley/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire election officials say they’re unconcerned after the Trump administration announced it will send election monitors to watch September’s primaries in Manchester and Nashua — a longstanding practice that has drawn partisan suspicion amid the president’s recent actions on elections.
The U.S. Department of Justice announced earlier this month it’s sending monitors to 15 jurisdictions in six states. In addition to Manchester and Nashua, the DOJ plans to send monitors to Boston and New Bedford in neighboring Massachusetts. Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, and Virginia are the others.
“We’re sending the monitors into cities and counties where there may have been some problems in recent elections,” Assistant U.S. Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said in a video posted to social media. “So this is something that DOJ does routinely.”
Dhillon said the goal is to ensure people with disabilities and language barriers are able to vote, but also to “make sure that our voting is accurate so that every citizen who votes has their vote counted equally without being canceled out by somebody who shouldn’t be voting.”
New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, the state’s chief elections official, said his office learned of the monitors at the same time the public did.
“In New Hampshire, we have a tradition of letting people observe our election process,” Scanlan, a Republican, said. “It doesn’t matter whether they’re from New Hampshire, from the federal government, or international observers. Those individuals do not have a role in the election process, and the expectation is that if people representing the federal government are here, that they are not going to get in the way of our election officials doing their job.”
Manchester City Clerk Matthew Normand, who runs the Queen City’s elections, also said he’s ready to welcome monitors.
“We have them at every election at all the polls generally,” Normand said. “So I don’t really have a reaction other than they’re welcome to come and watch what we do here in Manchester.”
The DOJ asked Manchester to provide it with information about its precinct locations and other election-related matters. Normand said the city will respond by the DOJ’s Aug. 8 deadline.
Normand said he met with the Secretary of State’s Office and New Hampshire Attorney General’s Office last week. He said they’ve promised “additional guidance” and that local moderators on his team will have a chance to meet with the New Hampshire Attorney General’s team to ask questions about what the federal government may be doing.
Both Scanlan and Normand said they weren’t concerned about September’s elections. Nashua City Clerk Daniel Healey did not respond to the Bulletin’s request for comment. 
Asked what problems with Manchester’s recent elections the federal government may be referring to, Normand said he was unaware of any.
The DOJ declined to answer the same question. Instead, it wrote in an email: “Election monitoring is a longstanding DOJ practice that has continued under presidents of both parties. In 2022, DOJ sent monitors to nine jurisdictions during the primaries, and 27 jurisdictions in 2024. It helps ensure compliance with federal voting laws and strengthens public confidence in the process.” 
Indeed, presidential administrations from both parties have monitored elections in previous elections to ensure compliance with federal laws. However, the Trump administration’s monitors come amid the president’s repeated claims that American elections are rife with fraud. 
At the heart of those claims is Donald Trump’s 2020 election defeat, which he unsuccessfully attempted to overturn and still claims — falsely — was stolen from him. In January, the FBI conducted a search warrant on a Fulton County, Georgia, election center at the heart of Trump’s claims, seizing boxes of 2020 ballots. Additionally, earlier this year, Trump called to “nationalize” elections in some states, ostensibly because the states are allowing undocumented immigrants to vote in high numbers. That kind of federal intervention runs counter to the U.S. Constitution, which specifies states determine the “times, places, and manner” of elections in a purposefully decentralized system.
“I’ve heard comments that the administration has made,” Scanlan said. “I don’t think that they have been particularly helpful in establishing the confidence that voters should have in the election process. Anybody that participates in New Hampshire elections knows that they are fair and accurate and well run, and that just means that we have to be more vigilant in keeping our voting population informed about how our elections operate.”
The DOJ also sent a letter to Scanlan threatening him with “criminal liability” if he knowingly allows noncitizens to vote. The same letter was sent to chief state election officials across the country.
“I have not yet reacted to the letter,” Scanlan said. “It did not get me very excited. I’m not concerned about criminal prosecution because we are not engaging in vote manipulation.”
The letter, sent on July 7, asked for a response within five days. Scanlan said he has not responded.
“I’m in no hurry,” he said.
Gov. Kelly Ayotte also chimed in on the election monitors, telling reporters Wednesday: “I would welcome anyone that wants to come to New Hampshire and see how we do elections. I think we do them well, and so if they want to come and observe how we do elections here in New Hampshire, I think they will see that we conduct our elections in a fair, transparent way.”
The decision to send monitors to New Hampshire comes in the wake of the Trump administration’s defeat in federal court last month over its attempt to force New Hampshire to hand over sensitive voter data. The administration ordered all 50 states to provide their voter registration records. When many states — mostly Democratic led — refused, including New Hampshire, the administration sued. Scanlan said New Hampshire state law intended to protect citizen privacy prevented him from releasing certain information, such as partial Social Security numbers and driver’s license numbers. In June, U.S. District Court Judge Joseph Laplante ruled federal attorneys hadn’t established a sufficient legal basis to compel Scanlan to turn over the voter database. The Trump administration has suffered similar defeats in other states. The federal government still has the opportunity to appeal the decision.

title: DM schools fired a secretary for allegedly accessing principal’s work-authorization records
description: A former Des Moines Public Schools employee who was fired for allegedly having and sharing photos of a school principal’s passport and employment-authorization records is entitled to jobless benefits, a judge has ruled. State records indicate Laura Shockley worked for the school district, most recently as an executive secretary, from Sept. 15, 2025, until Ma[...]
text:
A former employee of Lincoln High School in Des Moines, who was fired after being accused having and showing photos of a school principal’s passport and employment-authorization records, has qualified for unemployment benefits. (Photo via Google Earth)A former Des Moines Public Schools employee who was fired for allegedly having and sharing photos of a school principal’s passport and employment-authorization records is entitled to jobless benefits, a judge has ruled.
State records indicate Laura Shockley worked for the school district, most recently as an executive secretary, from Sept. 15, 2025, until May 21, 2026, when she was fired.
On July 17, 2026, Administrative Law Judge Stephanie Adkisson presided over a hearing on Shockley’s request for unemployment benefits. According to Adkisson’s recently published decision in the case, one of Shockley’s coworkers reported to the district on May 6, 2026, that Shockley had on her personal cellphone photographs of documents belonging to her supervisor, Lincoln High School Principal Praveen Bannikatti.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The documents included Bannikatti’s I-9 form, which is a work-authorization record used to establish individuals’ employment eligibility in the United States, and his passport. The complaining employee alleged Shockley had showed the photographs to another employee of the district and indicated she had also overheard Shockley discussing the documents.
Several months prior to that alleged incident, Ian Roberts, then the school district’s superintendent, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for being in the United States without legal work authorization. Roberts, whose case garnered national media attention, is now serving a two-year prison sentence on immigration and firearms charges.
According to Adkisson’s findings in Shockley’s unemployment case, Bannikatti, who has been with Des Moines Public Schools since 2008, asked Shockley whether she had cellphone photos of his personal documents. Shockley stated she did not, adding that she did not know where such records were even kept by the district.
After that conversation, the district placed Shockley on administrative leave and, according to Adkisson’s findings, interviewed both the complaining coworker and the other employee who asserted she had seen the photos. On May 21, 2026, district officials interviewed Shockley about sharing confidential personnel information with the staff and running personal errands during work hours — allegations that Shockley denied, Adkisson stated in her findings.
State records indicate the district concluded Shockley was not being truthful and that she could not be trusted with confidential information. After giving Shockley the opportunity to resign, which she declined, the district fired her.
At Shockley’s subsequent unemployment hearing, Shockley testified district officials had previously met several times with her two accusers due to concerns that they were not treating Shockley with respect. One of the coworkers had allegedly been passed over a promotion that was given to Shockley, Adkisson noted in her findings.
In ruling that Shockley was eligible for unemployment benefits, Adkisson stated she found Shockley’s version of events to be “more credible” than that of the district.
The school district, she noted, provided no written investigatory documents or decision-making records related to the allegations or Shockley’s dismissal. The district provided only witnesses “with second-hand information and did not make the witnesses who allegedly witnessed the incident available for the hearing, nor did they provide their written statements,” Adkisson reported.
Shockley, she added, “credibly testified she did not have the photos the coworkers accused her of having.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Shockley, Bannikatti or the school district’s communications staff for comment Thursday afternoon.

title: A Louisiana law change will erase an ethics fine for just one person
description: The Louisiana Legislature voted for a law change that benefits only one person, state Rep. Steven Jackson, D-Shreveport, by erasing a $1,000 ethics fine he faces.
text:
The Louisiana Legislature voted for a law change that benefits only one person, state Rep. Steven Jackson, D-Shreveport, by erasing a $1,000 ethics fine he faces. (Allison Allsop/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Legislature voted for a law change that benefits only one person, state Rep. Steven Jackson, D-Shreveport, by erasing a $1,000 ethics fine he faces.

Act 777 will likely force the Louisiana Board of Ethics to revoke a financial penalty Jackson has been fighting for years. 
“When we went through our cases to see what this [new law] would affect, there’s only one potential late fee that this affects, and it’s by Rep. Steve Jackson,” Ethics Administrator David Bordelon said at the board’s July meeting. 
As recently as June, the ethics board voted unanimously to enforce the $1,000 penalty over Jackson’s objections. But Bordelon said in an email this week that he believes the new law will compel board members to revoke the fine regardless of what they desire.  
A spokesperson for Jackson, Ashley Crawford, questioned whether he really was the only person who benefited from the law change. 

“[A]ny assertion that no other individual may be affected is mere speculation unless every potentially impacted matter has been reviewed,” Crawford wrote in an email Thursday. “If such a comprehensive review has been completed, we would expect that effort to be reflected in the Board’s upcoming annual audit or otherwise documented by the Board.”

Jackson was first hit with the fine in 2023 because he failed to submit a personal financial disclosure form required from candidates running for the Louisiana Legislature. He didn’t turn in the paperwork until January 2026, when the ethics board threatened to increase his fine if it wasn’t filed immediately. 
This $1,000 fee is just one small part of a larger set of disputes Jackson has had with the ethics board going back to 2015 and his first race for the Caddo Parish Commission.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 
In January, Jackson told the ethics board he had paid between $10,000 and $15,000 in penalties over several missed deadlines for ethics and campaign finance reports required for political candidates and elected officials. That was before another $6,720 in fines was levied against him, including the disputed $1,000, for another set of violations earlier this year. 
One of the first pieces of legislation Jackson sponsored as a freshman legislator was a 2024 law that exempted political candidates from having to file personal financial disclosure forms if they had previously submitted the same form as an elected official. 
Had that statute been in place when Jackson first qualified as a Louisiana House candidate in 2023, he would not have accrued the fine he’s now seeking to vacate. At the time he signed up for the statehouse race, he was a Caddo Parish Commissioner. 
This year’s law change helps Jackson because it makes the law he sponsored and passed in 2024 retroactive to a time before he missed the deadline and was assessed his late fee. 

Sen. Katrina Jackson-Andrews, D-Monroe, added the amendment to Act 777 that is forcing the ethics board to rescind Jackson’s penalty. Jackson and Jackson-Andrews are not related. 
In an interview Thursday, Jackson-Andrews said she inserted the amendment at the request of another legislator but not Jackson. She doesn’t remember who the person was. The senator said she didn’t know the amendment would benefit Jackson financially until after the Legislature had approved it. 
“I wouldn’t have offered an amendment for a $1,000 fine,” Jackson-Andrews said. 

State Rep. Chris Turner, R-Ruston, sponsored the underlying legislation with the amendment that benefits Jackson. 

Turner said Jackson told him, during this year’s legislative session, that Jackson-Andrews had amended Turner’s bill. Turner said he didn’t know at the time the amendment helped Jackson specifically. 
“I did not know it would benefit him,” Turner said. 
At this month’s meeting, ethics board member La Koshia Roberts said legislators could have contacted their staff to ask about the effects of the bill before voting it into law. 

“I thought it was interesting that some of those legislators claim to not know that it would impact one of them individually yet not one bothered to call the staff to inquire about it,” she said. 
Bordelon said the ethics staff tries to make themselves available to answer questions about legislation before it becomes law. 
“We try to provide that information to know … what changes in law, how many cases this could affect, who it could affect,” he told the ethics board this month. “And just the way this bill was handled, that didn’t happen.” 

Turner said the ethics board could also have contacted him if they had concerns about the legislation.
The board is likely to take up the issue of Jackson’s late fee at their meeting on Aug. 7.

title: Many states expanded care for children, older adults and workers
description: Many states have made marked progress over the past two years in extending crucial care and benefits to children, workers and aging adults. But they will be hard-pressed to fill the void left by impending federal cuts to social services, according to a new analysis. A report released this week by The Century Foundation and […]
text:
A new report found that in the past two years, more than half the states expanded care for children and services for older adults and disabled people. But they will be hard-pressed to maintain funding in the face of federal cuts. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Many states have made marked progress over the past two years in extending crucial care and benefits to children, workers and aging adults. But they will be hard-pressed to fill the void left by impending federal cuts to social services, according to a new analysis.
A report released this week by The Century Foundation and Caring Across Generations found that more than half the states improved services for children, older adults and disabled people and made family and medical leave more available for workers.
The report ranks states on both their overall performance in those areas and highlights progress since the nonprofit groups began to grade the states in 2021. It gave top grades to California, Oregon, New York, Massachusetts and New Jersey. The lowest rankings went to Alabama, Mississippi, Wyoming, Florida and North Carolina.
But federal policy changes will have a major impact on state budgets, the authors note.
The broad tax and spending measure that President Donald Trump signed last summer imposed major cuts and eligibility changes to Medicaid, the public health insurance program for low-income people, and to the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (SNAP), commonly known as food stamps. Additionally, Congress allowed federal subsidies for Obamacare health care plans to expire at the end of last year, pushing millions off the program.
The report says cuts to Medicaid, Obamacare and the food stamp program “have left state budgets with constraints that will be difficult, if not impossible, to overcome.”
The report called out five states that saw the most improvement since the last evaluation in 2024: Virginia, New York, Nebraska, Michigan and Washington.
While the liberal-leaning groups gave their top marks mainly to Democratic-led states, they did highlight incremental progress in conservative Southern states. In particular, the study highlighted efforts to expand paid leave for state employees in Alabama, Georgia, Mississippi and Tennessee.
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

title: Local efforts to ban Flock cameras gain steam
description: As municipalities in Maine and across the country are increasingly relying on Artificial Intelligence for policing, some localities have made progress in removing surveillance cameras, foreshadowing forthcoming legislative fights over state-level restrictions.  As of Thursday, bipartisan Maine legislators who launched a petition to ban AI-powered Flock camer[...]
text:
A Flock Safety license plate-reading camera is seen at Colfax Avenue and Franklin Street in Denver on Aug. 5, 2025. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)As municipalities in Maine and across the country are increasingly relying on Artificial Intelligence for policing, some localities have made progress in removing surveillance cameras, foreshadowing forthcoming legislative fights over state-level restrictions. 
As of Thursday, bipartisan Maine legislators who launched a petition to ban AI-powered Flock cameras — automated license plate readers that store information in searchable law enforcement databases — in the city of Auburn have gathered more than enough signatures to do so.
The campaign submitted more than 1,800 signatures — hundreds more than the required 1,568 — to the city, which is now tasked with verifying the signatures. Once verified, the Auburn City Council can either vote to enact the ban or send it to the voters.
The city installed Flock cameras last summer, a decision that drew community uproar after it was done without public notification, as the Sun Journal reported at the time. 
State legislators start petition to ban Flock cameras

Auburn Police Chief Jason Moen pointed to the cameras helping solve several crimes when defending his department’s funding request to continue to use the cameras earlier this year. But, ultimately, the city opted not to not include funding for the cameras in its latest budget, declining to continue the contract with Flock. 
Artificial Intelligence in policing is not new, but as police departments accumulate growing volumes of digital evidence, AI is progressively being used to help sort, search and analyze that information, which is being accessed by federal immigration authorities as well. There is no consistent national framework to govern how AI can be used in public safety settings, and state-level approaches remain limited and uneven.
Auburn is not the only Maine city to take issue with the technology. South Portland disabled and removed its Flock cameras in June, following similar public concern about data sharing and surveillance. 
There remain dozens of Flock and other cameras in Maine, according to open-source tracking tools such as Don’t Get Flocked and DeFlock. 
Police use of artificial intelligence grows as rules lag behind

Efforts to limit this type of surveillance have garnered bipartisan support. 
The Auburn petition is endorsed by the entire legislative delegation in that region: Republican Reps. Laurel Libby and Quentin Chapman, Republican Sen. Bruce Bickford and Democratic Rep. Adam Lee.
Republican Rep. David Boyer, who lives in neighboring Poland, is also the lead sponsor of a proposed statewide ban on Flock cameras. While it won’t be considered until the Legislature reconvenes in January, Boyer submitted a bill to ban municipalities and police departments from using the cameras, except for those used for toll collection. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of Maine is also planning to push for state-level restrictions on law enforcement access to surveillance cameras next legislative session, policy director Michael Kebede said earlier this week.
