name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Dark-money complaint headed to Tennessee Election Finance Registry
description: Better late than never, Tennessee’s campaign finance watchdog will take up a sworn complaint against a dark-money group that’s been pounding U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn with a TV ad calling her “queen pharma mama.” The Registry of Election Finance is set to consider the complaint by Chip Buck of Pall Mall, a Blackburn surrogate, at […]
text:
The Tennessee Registry of Election Finance will  consider a complaint filed by a campaign surrogate for U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, photographed at a 2024 conference, over a dark-money ad targeting 
her in her race for the Republican gubernatorial nomination. 
(Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Better late than never, Tennessee’s campaign finance watchdog will take up a sworn complaint against a dark-money group that’s been pounding U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn with a TV ad calling her “queen pharma mama.”
The Registry of Election Finance is set to consider the complaint by Chip Buck of Pall Mall, a Blackburn surrogate, at a Sept. 15 meeting.
Falling five weeks after the Aug. 6 gubernatorial primary, the meeting won’t produce anything that would affect next week’s outcome. In fact, some might say the board’s decisions rarely produce anything other than coffee shop talk. But sometimes you gotta dance with what you got.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Buck’s complaint says Alexandria, Virginia-based American Exceptionalism Institute (say that three times fast) failed to register with the state even though it likely spent more than $5,000 to attack Blackburn, a violation of state law, and failed to disclose that it used artificial intelligence, or some other duping technology, in the ad. Buck told the Lookout he wasn’t connected to the Blackburn campaign, despite speaking on her behalf at a campaign event and wearing “Marsha Marsha Marsha” stickers in photos with her and his wife. He declined to say anything else to the Lookout but is seeking an investigation into the group that’s been running at least two sets of ads attacking Blackburn.
The “queen pharma mama” ad, a spoof that Blackburn’s attorney demanded be taken off the air this week for defaming her, harkens to the senator’s time in the U.S. House when she sponsored a bill — written by a pharmaceutical lobbyist — that was designed to make sure patients received their medication but wound up stopping DEA agents from intercepting large shipments of drugs that flooded small communities with opioids during a national epidemic. Blackburn, at that point, had accepted about $120,000 in contributions from pharmaceutical companies, and she’s up to about $560,000 these days, according to recent reports. All told, Blackburn has netted more than $23 million in fundraising while serving in Congress.
The Lookout hasn’t been able to turn up much about the American Exceptionalism Institute, other than it’s a nonprofit group that raises and spends money.
Blackburn backer seeks investigation into dark-money ads against gubernatorial candidate

Interestingly enough, Buck’s complaint, which was notarized July 10 and received by the Registry July 20, claims the group started running ads June 10, which appears to be long before the “queen pharma mama” ad came out.
Regardless of the time frame, this week’s mud-slinging ordeal is a bit perplexing. Attack ads are part of the game, but Blackburn’s people apparently felt this one was garnering too much traction as the race with U.S. Rep. John Rose tightens. (Oops, almost forgot to mention state Rep. Monty Fritts, who is busy trying to prop up Christianity.) 
Blackburn’s cease-and-desist letter put newfound focus on the ad and reminded everyone that her staff said she would find a way to deal with “unintended consequences” after the Washington Post and “60 Minutes” reported on the pharmaceutical law she co-sponsored.
No doubt, it was a calculated risk, as was filing the sworn complaint, which will keep the matter in the public eye for another two months, at least.
Then again, allowing the ad to keep running through Aug. 6 could have been the death knell for a campaign that once seemed to guarantee victory. In some instances, Blackburn has acted as if she’s already been sworn into office. Heck, somebody’s got to run the state — or not. We haven’t seen, or heard, much out of term-limited Gov. Bill Lee in months.
But getting back to the sworn complaint. If you’re hoping for some sort of penalty for the American Exceptionalism Institute, remember that the Registry’s investigation couldn’t turn up the North Carolina restaurateur named Brandon Crawford who purportedly made a $7,000 donation to the Faith Family Freedom Fund PAC that spent money to help state Rep. Todd Warner beat Republican Rep. Rick Tillis in 2020. Here’s a hint: Crawford’s existence is doubtable, at best.
The Registry dismissed a complaint by Tillis’s campaign manager about illicit collusion with the PAC.
Blackburn goes after dark-money group calling her ‘queen pharma mama’

Yet testimony showed former House staffer Cade Cothren ran the PAC secretly after persuading a former girlfriend to form it.
Cothren was pardoned by President Donald Trump after being convicted on federal fraud and conspiracy charges to secretly tap state lawmakers’ constituent mailer accounts.
The Registry board levied civil penalties totaling $80,000 against Cothren for misleading the state about the 2019 political action committee. His attorneys were expected to appeal, which is par for the course, because this stuff stretches on forever, forever, forever … .
It adds up
The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a clean-energy political action committee, is committing $700,000 to ads against U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles as he tried to fend off former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher in the newly-gerrymandered 5th Congressional District.
That brings the group’s spending to $2 million against Ogles, who received a Trump endorsement and is benefiting from spending to the tune of nearly $660,000 from the House Freedom Caucus.
On a rampage
Warner, who uses Cothren for campaign work, is trying to rebound from President Donald Trump’s endorsement of state Sen. Brent Taylor of Shelby County as they vie for the Republican nomination in the newly-gerrymandered 9th Congressional District.
The Marshall County farmer said people in the largely rural district stretching from Memphis along the southern Tennessee line to Williamson and Rutherford counties are “struggling” with the price of fuel and groceries and raised questions about Trump’s policies.
Rep. Todd Warner, pictured in his legislative offie with a cut out of President Donald Trump, said he’s unperturbed by Trump’s endorsement of Sen. Brent Taylor in the 9th Congressional District Republican primary. (Photo: John Partipilo)
“I don’t think he’s as popular as he was. You ain’t gotta quote me on that, or you can. I don’t care. It don’t matter at this point. I feel like his popularity is down,” said Warner, who remains a Trump supporter, keeps a life-size cutout of the president in his state office and sent at least one mailer saying the president needs his help to rebuild America.
Taylor said in a text statement that Warner’s “disparaging remarks” about the president and his agenda “reveal his true feelings about the America First movement.”
Also running in the primary are perennial candidate Charlotte Bergmann of Memphis and Jeremy Thompson, a retired U.S. Army sergeant.
“What’s your name …”
A perusal of Sen. Blackburn’s federal finance reports this week turned up a couple of interesting contributors. One guy named “Joseph Dimaggio” kicked in a little cash, and another named “Jesus Christ” of D.C. gave around $230 in small contributions during the latest reporting period. The cash apparently is coming in through the WinRed fundraising platform, which is a major money maker. Don’t worry, this reporter couldn’t make it through all 279,000 contributions.
What would Jesus do? A Washington, DC man named Jesus Christ has donated $230 to U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign. (Photo: Getty Images)
Anyone who’s ever followed baseball knows about the great Joe Dimaggio who led the New York Yankees to multiple World Series titles and holds the all-time record with a 56-game hitting streak. Now we know where you have gone, “Joltin” Joe.
But “Jesus Christ”? You just don’t see that name every day, unless you’re in constant repentance. 
Should someone have raised a red flag? For one thing, they tell me foreign nationals aren’t allowed to donate to federal campaigns, and he did come from Galilee. Blackburn could even be accused of accepting money from “immigrants.” Gasp. 
More than likely, this will never see any form of investigation, even if a Rose surrogate files a complaint. 
But considering Jesus could perform all sorts of miracles, including raising the dead, turning water to wine (one of my favorites) and feeding the 5,000 with a handful of fishes and chunks of bread, couldn’t he come up with more than a couple hundred bucks?
“I don’t care what they may say / Jesus is just alright, oh yeah.” *
*Doobie Brothers, “Jesus is Just Alright”

name: WyoFile
title: Shuttered National Park Traveler editor talks Trump pressures, media struggles
description:
After 21 years of leading the news outlet, Kurt Repanshek sat down to talk about the value of parks and what’s at stake under the current administration.
The post Shuttered National Park Traveler editor talks Trump pressures, media struggles appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When journalist Kurt Repanshek quit his Associated Press job in Wyoming in the ‘90s to freelance, he hoped to align his reporting with his environmental and public lands interests. 
He wrote wildlife pieces and national park guides. In August 2005, he launched a blog as a platform for his work. He soon found that readers were hungry for any bits of news on parks like Grand Teton, Acadia or the Great Smoky Mountains. 
“I think the first week I had over 400 readers, which I thought was amazing because I hadn’t told anybody about it,” Repanshek said, “and it kept growing and growing and growing.”
Two decades later, Repanshek’s National Parks Traveler had established itself as a one-stop destination for all things national parks — from enterprise pieces about climate change and invasive species to tidbits on Yellowstone bison gorings and watchdog journalism about staff morale under Trump administration cuts. The Traveler, which became a nonprofit in 2016, touted a global audience of more than 4 million readers and listeners in 2025. As the Traveler’s sole full-time employee, Repanshek wore many hats — reporter, editor, board meeting facilitator, podcast host, freelance content wrangler and flag-waving executive director. 
“In so many ways, I think what Kurt was doing was a calling and a vocation, more than a job,” said Katie Nyberg, executive director of National Parks Friends Alliance, who was a faithful reader. “I don’t know where he found the energy.”
When he turned the Traveler into a nonprofit, Repanshek said, he thought a board and mission would be beneficial. “I also figured that the readers would jump on board and shower me with donations to keep it running, which never happened.” 
Despite its impressive audience reach, vast archive and plaudits for public lands reporting, the publication never employed a full-time development person, which Repanshek said was its downfall. Funding sources including grants and private donations weren’t enough.
“I like to say that the Traveler was a journalistic success, but a financial failure,” he told WyoFile from his home in Park City, Utah, where he has spent recent weeks wrapping up his publication and adjusting to retirement. 
When he started considering hanging up his hat, Repanshek, who will turn 70 in November, said he hoped to hand the Traveler off to another entity willing to take it into the future. Efforts to secure that were fruitless, however. The site halted publication at the end of June.

National Parks Traveler Editor Kurt Repanshek talks with John Cely in Congaree National Park, South Carolina. Cely, a state biologist, helped found Congaree as a national monument 50 years ago. (Bob Janiskee)

The Traveler’s demise creates a void for people like Nyberg who strive to be up to speed on parks and public lands. 
“There was no better publication for me to basically have my thumb on the pulse of what was going on nationally,” she said. “It was a go-to resource for me, and still is.”
While other publications do spill ink about national parks, she said, the Traveler is the only one she knows that was entirely devoted to their sustained coverage.  
Talks of a new operator aren’t entirely closed, Repanshek said. And with pressures from the Trump administration to cut park service staff, remove exhibits and shrink national monuments, he added, it’s an especially critical time for journalists to hold leadership accountable and inform the public about government actions affecting public lands. 
The current state of the National Park Service is “a mess,” he said. “It’s a tragic derailment of the park service mission, the park service role, and I don’t know how long it’s going to take to recover.”
Repanshek sat down with WyoFile to talk about the value of American parks, the unique place the Traveler occupied in the mediascape and what’s at stake for America’s “best idea.” 
A critical chapter
A common misconception was that as editor of National Parks Traveler, Repanshek was often on the move to locales like Montana’s Glacier National Park or the Florida Everglades. 
Ironically, he wasn’t a big traveler. “Most of my stuff is over the phone, over Zoom, press releases, that kind of thing,” he said. “Just because, we never had a big budget to do a lot of travel.”
That said, a few field reporting trips stood out over the years. Repanshek went underground at Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota, snorkeled in Florida’s Biscayne National Park and toured ancient sites in Mesa Verde National Park that aren’t open to the public. 
People always ask him how many parks he’s been to. But for Repanshek, “it’s not about how many parks you’ve been to.” It’s more about the quality of the experience.
Lion Geyser eruption with a rainbow in Yellowstone National Park. (Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)
If properly appreciated, National parks, he said, “are so important in helping people reconnect with themselves, with forgetting about checking their email, checking their texts.”
And that’s only the beginning of their value. 
“I think they’re incredibly important for all the roles they serve, from preserving history and protecting history and interpreting history to preserving these incredible landscapes and these vistas,” he said. “And they play such vital roles for the environment, clean water and clean air, biodiversity.”
The role of the Traveler, he said, was to inform the public not only of the stories within the many and varied parks, but also how Congress and the park service have managed them. As a watchdog, the Traveler has always taken a hard look at the way the government stewards the lands, Repanshek said, and as a result has ruffled feathers in various administrations. 
The level of upheaval and uncertainty that has defined the most recent chapter, he said, is unprecedented. Along with park-service-specific tumult, attempts to roll back or alter federal regulations like the Roadless Act, Endangered Species Act and NEPA “all have ramifications for the national parks,” Repanshek said. 
With high burnout and low morale, he believes the park service is in danger of lasting. And because the agency has drastically scaled back communications, trying to report on it is very frustrating. It got so bad that Traveler reporters couldn’t even secure interviews on stories of park service successes, he said. 
While he’s no longer posting regular Traveler updates, Repanshek’s writing impulse is still kicking. “In fact, when I get off with you, I’m going to write a letter to our Congress folks,” he told WyoFile. “…the latest in a long-running series.”
Another loss
Over his 40-year journalism career, Repanshek has also watched the industry suffer as national and local newspapers shuttered or consolidated, newsrooms hollowed out and online changes further eroded quality.
“Certainly the state of the media industry in America is in dire condition,” he said. “There’s been a loss of so much.”

Kurt Repanshek, founder of the publication National Parks Traveler, peers out of Cunningham Cabin in Grand Teton National Park. (Marcelle Shoop)

The latest casualty is his own brainchild, which he said occupied a singular place as the clearinghouse for national parks news. Readers could learn about storm damage at their favorite park. They could dive deep into the history of tallgrass prairie ecosystems. Or they could read about Interior Department machinations that posed threats to endangered species. 
Repanshek was disappointed, he said, that the Traveler couldn’t find financial support among the outdoor recreation industry. With their products going out into America’s public lands, he said, “they should have vested interest in seeing accurate coverage of what’s going on in these places.”
The Traveler website is still up, and conversations about reviving it haven’t entirely ceased, Repanshek said. He likened it to the scene in “The Princess Bride” when Miracle Max says of Westley, “he’s not all dead. He’s only mostly dead.”
The post Shuttered National Park Traveler editor talks Trump pressures, media struggles appeared first on WyoFile .

title: ‘Where’s he at?’ WV flood survivor says government should do more to help
description:
WESTON, W.Va. —  On July 21, it took 45 minutes for flash floods to destroy three houses in Jason Mulholland’s family. The home he shared with his wife and the nearby homes of his two sons, 33 and 29, are all beyond repair.

text:
Jason Mulholland stands beside his home in Lewis County, W.Va. The house was destroyed by flooding last week. (Photo by Lori Kersey | West Virginia Watch)WESTON, W.Va. —  On July 21, it took 45 minutes for flash floods to destroy three houses in Jason Mulholland’s family. The home he shared with his wife and the nearby homes of his two sons, 33 and 29, are all beyond repair.
Mulholland had just returned from work and was making dinner when the water from the creek behind his home on Copley Road, near Weston, started to rise. He and his son started moving their vehicles out of the water’s path. He carried two of his grandchildren, 4 and 1, to safety from the rising water. 
“We stood in the middle of the road there in three feet of water and watched all this float away,” he said, gesturing to the ruined houses. 
His own home – a double-wide trailer that he’d recently remodeled – was knocked feet from its foundation. A porch and some cinderblocks are all that’s left from one of his son’s houses. Debris from the rest of it washed down the creek and tangled in nearby trees. 
Downed trees and housing debris sits on the Mulholland’s land on Copley Road in Weston. (Photo by Lori Kersey | West Virginia Watch)
Now, Mulholland is angry that the West Virginia and federal governments haven’t done more for his family and the rest of his community.
“He’s running this country,” Mulholland said of President Donald Trump. “He’s worried about what’s going on over here and overseas…but he’s not here worried about us, the people that voted him in office. My gripe is ‘where’s he at?’” 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey has requested an expedited major disaster declaration that would allow individual assistance and public assistance for Lewis County, where Mulholland lives, and six other counties hard hit by deadly storms and flooding on July 21 and 22. The Trump administration has not yet approved the declaration. 
Mulholland said a representative from the Federal Emergency Management Agency has been to his house and told him if the Trump administration approves the disaster declaration, they’ll offer him $48K for his home, which he’s put $300,000 into. The federal government could loan him money to rebuild, he said he was told.
“That’s not what us fellow West Virginians or fellow Americans want to hear,” Mulholland said. “They want to hear our president and our governor of West Virginia step up and say, ‘Look, guys, what can we do to help you?’ And they ain’t none of them doing that.”
Mulholland is also angry that Morrisey and Trump haven’t been to his neighborhood to see the damage and speak with affected residents. Morrisey has so far made four visits to flood-affected areas of the state, speaking to reporters twice from Buckhannon and once from Weston. He also visited St. Marys and Weston last weekend.
Mulholland said it’s sad that the state can spend $2 million on a festival and Ferris wheel for America’s 250th birthday, and the president can spend money on war, while neither the state or federal government are doing more for flood victims. 
“It don’t make a bit of sense,” he said. “And I will get out. I will get out to West Virginians, if I’ve got to go on every news station in the state of West Virginia. And until I see him or get some kind of assistance, I’m going to let fellow West Virginians know how he’s doing.”
What remains of one of three Mulholland family homes destroyed by last week’s deadly floods. (Photo by Lori Kersey | West Virginia Watch)
Lars Dalseide, communications director for Morrisey, said the governor understands the frustration that families are feeling after the devastating flood. He pointed out that during his four visits over the last week, Morrisey met with local officials, first responders, business owners, and residents. The governor, Dalseide said, has also directed state resources to support response and recovery efforts and requested the major disaster declaration from the federal government.
The West Virginia National Guard was deployed to assist in flood response, and the governor also sent in the state Department of Highways and the Department of Environmental Protection. 
“The administration remains focused on helping every affected community recover as quickly as possible,” Dalseide wrote in an email to West Virginia Watch.
Morrisey spoke to reporters about flood recovery Wednesday in Weston, where he celebrated the reopening of the Shop n’ Save grocery store. 
There, he told a reporter he’d been in touch with officials from the federal government about the state’s disaster declaration application and that he would continue to push “as hard as possible,” but said it could take time. 
The governor encouraged people to volunteer at construction and mucking projects in affected areas. West Virginia Voluntary Organizations Active in Disasters is coordinating volunteers. 
Morrisey also urged people to be patient. 
“It does take time to muck out the homes. It takes time to rebuild the bridges and the roads and do the things that are necessary for long-term recovery,” Morrisey said. “But the state of West Virginia is going to stand behind Upshur County. It’s going to stand behind Lewis County. It’s going to stand behind Pleasants County and all the counties and cities affected by Mother Nature’s wrath.”
Mulholland has lived on Copley Road for 50 years, and his mother has been there 73. Neither have experienced flooding like they did last week, even during a historic flood in 1985.
“In 85, when it flooded that bad, the water never got in that road,” he said. “It got up in here, but it was never in (the road).”
Floods – even deadly ones – are not uncommon in West Virginia. Last year, flooding hit several counties in southern West Virginia. A flood in northern West Virginia last summer killed several people in Ohio County. 
While Mulholland waits to know what assistance he can get from the government, he said he doesn’t plan to leave the land he lives on.
“I mean, will it ever happen again?” he said. “You don’t know. A person just doesn’t know if it’s going to happen. I mean, I would have never ever expected it to happen. But here we are.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Every state, including West Virginia, should ban child marriage to protect girls from harm
description: West Virginia has one of the weakest marriage laws in the region.  Currently, 17 states ban child marriage entirely. News flash: West Virginia isn’t one of them.  Thirty-three states still permit it with exceptions. Some still have no minimum age. That’s shocking. It protects predators over a girl’s safety.
text:
The West Virginia Legislature's 2024 regular session ended Saturday, March 9, 2024. (Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia has one of the weakest marriage laws in the region.  Currently, 17 states ban child marriage entirely. News flash: West Virginia isn’t one of them.  Thirty-three states still permit it with exceptions. Some still have no minimum age. That’s shocking. It protects predators over a girl’s safety. 
Virginia and Pennsylvania completely banned marriage for minors. In Ohio and Kentucky you can be as young as 17 with judicial approval. In West Virginia it is sixteen-year-olds with parental consent. 
Here’s the shameful reality: Republicans claim to protect children, but actions speak louder than words. They continue to thwart efforts to fully ban child marriage. Instead, they passed a compromise bill (HB 3018) that still legally allows 16 and 17-year-olds to be married off. 
Would more female legislators make a difference? Studies conducted by the nonprofit Unchained At Last say yes. They show a correlation between higher females in politics and stronger marriage laws. If you didn’t know, West Virginia has the lowest representation of female lawmakers in the nation. 
Del. Kayla Young (D-Kanawha) has been a lead sponsor of bills to ban child marriage. She told 13News: “I’ve had county clerks reach out to me to tell me like, ‘hey, this is still a problem because so many out-of-state folks are still coming here to get married because we’re a border state for so many other states who have banned child marriage.” 
Here’s an example to back that claim: you may have heard of the abusive home uncovered in Ohio this month dubbed “The House of Horrors.” Sixteen children were found starved in a room. Some wonder if the mother was also a victim, forced to give birth year after year. You see, at age 15, she was taken to Mason county WV, to wed where it was still legal. 
Does this sound like human trafficking to you? The United Nations says yes. Call it what it is. The UN considers child marriage a form of forced marriage because children lack the legal maturity to provide free and informed consent. 
The United States is the only UN member state that has not yet ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child which reaffirms that the minimum age limit should be 18 years for marriage.
Think about it: Minors lack full legal autonomy, making it difficult to leave abusive environments, sign leases, or access domestic violence shelters.  Also, teen brides  are often robbed the chance to finish school and have a higher risk of poverty. 
And in a world where the rapist is shamed less than the girl he raped, teen marriages often serve as a sinister rape loophole. Far more often than not, the bride is a teen and the man is an adult. A landmark joint study by McGill University and advocacy groups, found more than 66,000 U.S. child marriages since 2000 involved ages or age gaps considered sex crimes. 
Our leaders provide shameful examples:   President Donald Trump–and the richest man on earth–Elon Musk–have 19 children from 7 wives between them. And Trump has been accused of rape by well over a dozen women since the 1970’s including his ex wife Ivana in a sworn deposition. On this note, finally, in 2024, spousal sexual abuse in West Virginia was criminalized. Took a while…
The point is simple: our girls cannot wait. They are being harmed. 
In conclusion, I’ll share a true story: I was giving an elderly woman a ride in Kanawha County. I asked about her life. She shared she was raped as a young teen and pressured to marry the rapist. She is his care-taker 24/7. She only leaves the house to go to the grocery. They have one son. Sit with that for a minute. She was married off to her rapist. So many other West Virginia women are forced into the same horrific fate. 
Our girls deserve a better West Virginia. When will our legislators stand up to protect them? The time is now.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger administration seeks public input on new energy plan
description: Every four years, Virginia law requires the governor’s administration to develop a new energy plan outlining the commonwealth’s energy needs and how the state intends to meet its power generation goals. Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond, Secretary of Commerce and Trade Carrie Chenery and Department of Energy representatives have been hosting invite-only[...]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Every four years, Virginia law requires the governor’s administration to develop a new energy plan outlining the commonwealth’s energy needs and how the state intends to meet its power generation goals.
Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond, Secretary of Commerce and Trade Carrie Chenery and Department of Energy representatives have been hosting invite-only stakeholder meetings across the state to gather input on how the administration can shape its policies and how Virginia can meet its net-zero clean energy mark.
“It’s really just designed to basically provide a 10-year roadmap looking at how we’re going to hit the 2045 net zero (goals) across all sectors,” Allmond said.
A public meeting will be held in Petersburg on Aug. 3 at the public library at 5:30 pm. Comments submitted at the meeting, along with responses gathered through an online survey, will be considered as the administration drafts the plan.
“But our energy future should not — must not — just be written in Richmond,” Gov. Abigail Spanberger said in a news release. “I want to hear from Virginians across every corner of the commonwealth, and I encourage everyone who pays an energy bill in Virginia to make their voice heard.” 
In addition to public input, the governor’s plan is developed in consultation with the State Corporation Commission, the Department of Environmental Quality and other state agencies.
Spanberger is aiming to address high energy costs as demand for power continues to grow across the commonwealth. She has touted an “all of the above” energy strategy that includes renewable sources such as solar and wind, while also expressing interest in small modular reactors and maintaining fossil fuel sources when needed. 
To offset carbon emissions from natural gas generation, Spanberger pushed for and secured Virginia’s return to the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, a multi-state carbon allowance auction.
Unlike the Integrated Resource Plan that utilities must submit to the SCC outlining how they intend to build enough infrastructure to meet projected demand, the governor’s plan offers more flexibility in determining how to achieve the net-zero target established in state law, Allmond said.
Under the Virginia Clean Economy Act, the state’s major utilities are also mandated to retire their carbon-emitting power sources by 2050, with some exceptions to maintain grid reliability.
“The IRP is not strictly on getting to net zero by 2045. There’s still work arounds in the Clean Economy Act, and so they’ve been relying on that reliability exception,” Allmond said. “That doesn’t really exist here, and so, this is really showing ways to get to net zero.”
The final report on the 2026 energy plan will be released Oct. 1.

title: Virginia legislator was allowed to use campaign funds for her defense. So she did.
description: State Sen. Louise Lucas, the powerful Portsmouth Democrat, used $300,000 in campaign funds to contribute to her legal defense fund and hire a law firm following an FBI raid in May on her businesses in Portsmouth. That’s a sizable amount.  What The Virginian-Pilot article should have noted higher in the story was that Lucas was […]
text:
Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)State Sen. Louise Lucas, the powerful Portsmouth Democrat, used $300,000 in campaign funds to contribute to her legal defense fund and hire a law firm following an FBI raid in May on her businesses in Portsmouth. That’s a sizable amount.
 What The Virginian-Pilot article should have noted higher in the story was that Lucas was allowed to do this — since the payments occurred before July 1. That’s when a new state law prohibiting personal use of campaign funds took effect.
 The feds haven’t charged Lucas with any crime, though she remains under a cloud. The senator must pay to defend herself during the ongoing probe. She didn’t respond to my email and voicemail questions.
 A spokesperson with the Norfolk FBI office told me this week that, following U.S. Department of Justice policy, “the FBI does not confirm or deny the existence of an investigation, nor does it provide updates.”
 The lack of details, however, increases speculation the investigation is politically motivated, even though it reportedly began during the Biden administration. The former president is a Democrat, too.
 Virginia officials finally released a report on data centers last week, something they had withheld for more than six months. The Associated Press noted declines are likely to occur in an aquifer in the eastern region because of population growth and industrial use. Environmental scientists produced the report.
The commonwealth deserves the condemnation and scrutiny it’s getting over the issue of data centers, especially because of their impact on water and other resources. 
Are state leaders favoring the industry at the expense of residents? Many Virginians think so, in part since Northern Virginia is home to the world’s largest concentration of data centers. My commentary colleague Ivy Main has covered the controversy closely over the past several years.
As more details are released about a fatal car crash in Chesapeake, it’s amazing other people weren’t injured — or worse. Synclair Tyrone Mayes, 19, a Navy sailor, faces involuntary manslaughter charges in the death of landscaper Guadalupe Rivera, 60, who was working along the sidewalk on May 29 when the accident happened.
 Authorities say Mayes is now free on bond and can’t drive; the city’s top prosecutor, Matthew Hamel, told me his office opposed bond. Law enforcement officials say Mayes was traveling faster than 90 mph when his car first collided with an SUV and then struck and killed Rivera. The speed limit along that four-lane road is just 35 mph. No one else was seriously injured.
The initial collision dislodged the engine of the SUV and hurled it dozens of feet. I travel through that section of the city frequently, and I wrote about the case in June.
 Mayes’ attorney didn’t respond to my questions about his client. A preliminary hearing is scheduled Sept. 16.
 Who knew the state was home to such preferred, inexpensive lodging when parents spirit away their children for some fun? USA Today just ranked the Rochambeau Roadside Inn in Williamsburg as the No. 1 affordable family vacation stay. It topped the list of nine preferred places around the country to hit the pillows, relax and save a few bucks.
 The inn has 22 rooms and dates to 1954. The 6,000-acre Massanutten Resort in the Shenandoah Valley came in third on the list.
U.S. Sen. Mark Warner says if he wins in November, it will be his last term in the Senate. He’s been in the office since 2009 and is currently serving his third term in the chamber. The Democrat is 71 now and would be 78 by the end of a fourth, six-year term.
 Warner recently told a crowd in Staunton it’s time for younger people to have a chance for the office, but “I sure as hell was not going to quit while Donald Trump was sitting down the street,” The Virginian-Pilot reported. I wrote a few weeks ago that too many politicians at the local, state and federal levels don’t know when to quit. Was Warner heeding my advice?
“The senator assures me that the decision was based on a variety of factors, not a single well-timed column,” Warner spokeswoman Ruthanne Thongkai responded by email. “Though he appreciates you giving yourself that much credit!”
 President Donald Trump seems determined for Republicans to take it on the chin during the midterm elections this fall (except for touting his disingenuous SAVE America Act legislation, making it harder for people, including Republicans, to vote). 
You might not care a whit about the country’s war in Iran, or whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu snookered Trump into joining this war of choice.
 You do care about $4-a-gallon gas. Prices have risen dramatically since the war started Feb. 28. Virginia households have paid $573 more for gas since the war began, a recent congressional report found. It said Virginians have paid $1.8 billion more for gas since February.
 If you’re like me, you cringe every time you go to the pumps, and you think seriously whether you really need to get behind the wheel. 
The situation is especially galling since Trump, during the 2024 election campaign against Kamala Harris, had the temerity to say she would get the United States into World War III if she were elected president. 
The irony is probably lost on the current chief executive.

title: Online prediction markets rile up state lawmakers
description: CHICAGO — The escalating feud between states and online prediction markets was on full display at a summit of state lawmakers this week as legislators publicly scolded Kalshi and Polymarket, the two most prominent platforms. Prediction market platforms say they are like commodity markets that offer contracts to speculate on the future price of corn […]
text:
Online prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket are attracting scrutiny from state lawmakers, who argue the platforms are undermining state gambling regulations. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)CHICAGO — The escalating feud between states and online prediction markets was on full display at a summit of state lawmakers this week as legislators publicly scolded Kalshi and Polymarket, the two most prominent platforms.
Prediction market platforms say they are like commodity markets that offer contracts to speculate on the future price of corn or oil — not sportsbooks that allow gamblers to place bets. But many states reject those justifications, arguing the platforms are a backdoor to skirt state gambling regulations, particularly on sports.
The issue has sparked action from state regulators, new legislation, and a flurry of lawsuits from states, prediction markets, and the Trump administration, which has sought to sideline state oversight.
During a sometimes-heated panel discussion at the annual gathering of the National Conference of State Legislatures in Chicago, Iowa Republican state Sen. Dan Dawson told the audience that a group of students at his son’s high school recently enrolled in Kalshi to bet on World Cup matches. In Iowa, people must be at least 21 to participate in legal online sports betting.
“States are the ones that pick up the pieces,” Dawson said as a Kalshi executive looked on.
Dawson has previously raised concerns about the public health consequences of prediction markets. While an industry representative pledged to work with states, Dawson said a legislative subcommittee that recently studied the issue could not get even basic information from the prediction markets about their reach in Iowa.
“We couldn’t get one answer,” he said.
Kalshi and Polymarket are skirting laws on sports betting, states say

In March, Kalshi preemptively sued to block Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, a Republican, from taking civil or criminal enforcement action against it. In its suit, Kalshi claimed there was “a substantial risk that the attorney general of Iowa will bring an enforcement action.”
Regulation of prediction markets
Sara Slane, Head of Corporate Development at Kalshi, told lawmakers in Chicago that the company was committed to building relationships with the states. But she said the prediction markets are not subject to state oversight, as they are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates derivatives such as futures contracts on stocks.
She said prediction markets require a national standard rather than a “state-by-state regulatory patchwork.”
“This was exactly what the commodity exchange was set up for,” she said.
The five-member, presidentially appointed CFTC currently has four vacancies. But it has aggressively sought to exclude states from overseeing prediction markets, suing red and blue states alike to maintain its jurisdiction over the markets.
Earlier this week, a coalition of 44 state attorneys general wrote to the agency, arguing it does not have the power to regulate sports-related event contracts, which they say are subject to state gambling regulations.
In addition to encroaching on state-regulated and state-taxed sports gambling, states argue that prediction markets are subject to potential insider trading, lack consumer oversight and can fuel problem gambling.
Slane said her firm works to prevent money laundering and allows people who have problems with gaming to block themselves from the site. She said Kalshi also works with major sports leagues to prevent athletes and referees from trading on sports events.
“We take this very seriously,” she said. “We want to promote integrity around our exchange.”
But prediction markets continue to gain national attention for allowing people to unfairly bet on the outcome of events by leveraging nonpublic information.
This week, the White House announced the president’s teleprompter operator was no longer on staff after he was accused of using inside knowledge to make bets about presidential speeches on Kalshi.
Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz on Tuesday signed an executive order prohibiting state employees from using inside information to bet on prediction markets. At least eight states, including Arizona, California, Maryland and Wisconsin, have implemented similar restrictions.
Mick Mulvaney, executive director of the Gambling is Not Investing Coalition, said he was sympathetic to the argument that prediction markets want to avoid a regulatory patchwork across the states.
“That being said, there’ve been two areas where the states have almost always been entirely sovereign: That’s on booze and gambling,” he said.
Mulvaney, a Republican, represented South Carolina in the U.S. House and served as acting White House chief of staff during President Donald Trump’s first term. His organization argues that prediction markets should be subject to the same state and tribal regulations as other forms of gambling.
With litigation flying, he said there’s no question the debate is heading toward the U.S. Supreme Court. Mulvaney said it’s unclear how the conservative court will rule, given its recent decisions. Some of those rulings have allowed the expansion of federal executive power, while others have tilted toward the states.
“So that will be fascinating to see how it shakes out at the Supreme Court,” he told Stateline. “But I have every expectation that this is going all the way up.”
Threat to tribal casinos 
Casino gambling has been the sole economic engine for many Native American tribes for years, said Michael Hoenig, vice president and associate general counsel for gaming at the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation in Southern California.
He said tribes have built up the gambling industry over the last 40 years — sometimes in cooperation with states, other times “in friction with the states.”
“This is just a profound affront to tribal sovereignty, tribal self-government,” he said. “Tribes are supposed to have the sovereign right to decide who gets to operate gaming on their lands and who doesn’t.”
Aside from regulatory concerns, state leaders worry about how the rise of prediction markets may impact the financial and mental health of their residents. Since a 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling opened the door for states to legalize sports gambling, 39 states and the District of Columbia have done so.
Advocates, researchers and lawmakers are already raising alarms about how the burgeoning market could fuel gambling addiction and hurt household finances. 
Growth of sports betting may be linked to financial woes, new studies find

Aside from regulation, there is little difference between the potential impacts of prediction markets and online sports betting, said Rachel Volberg, a professor emerita of epidemiology at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
Volberg, who has studied gambling addiction for 40 years, told lawmakers in a separate presentation that the research is clear about how over involvement in gambling can hurt individuals and families. However, she told Stateline that legal sports gambling is too new for researchers to fully measure how much the high-speed and accessible world of online gaming has changed the dynamics.
In North Carolina, a new poll found that most people generally approve of sports betting, but a majority wants the state to ban prediction markets.
In the Meredith College poll released Tuesday, 51% of registered voters said they were satisfied with state regulation of sports gambling. Only 11% said they were dissatisfied, while 38% said they didn’t know.
In that poll, two-thirds of registered voters said they would support state legislation banning prediction markets, while 24% said they should be legal.
Though sports fans, policymakers and the researchers continue to grapple with the quickly evolving landscape, experts gathered in Chicago were clear that this industry is here to stay.
“It’s not going anywhere,” said Anthony D’Angelo, who leads responsible gaming efforts at Fanatics Betting & Gaming.
D’Angelo said his company’s sportsbook invests heavily in providing assistance for problem gamblers, flags potentially problematic transactions and incentivizes customers to set and stick to betting limits.
He said lawmakers can help keep people away from illegal and offshore betting platforms that have no oversight or consumer protections.
“We all want the same things to happen,” he said. “I think we want a sustainable, long-term industry where customers are protected.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: The childcare landscape can be challenging in New Hampshire. This agency is here to help.
description: Whether you’re a parent or provider, navigating New Hampshire’s childcare landscape can be tricky. With hundreds of programs and varying resources, it’s difficult to know where to start as a parent or provider. To help address those challenges, the state contracts with the Community Action Partnership of Hillsborough and Rockingham Counties, which provides s[...]
text:
The Child Development Center at the Community Action Partnership of Hillsborough and Rockingham Counties in Manchester. The organization holds the contract for Child Care Aware of New Hampshire, which delivers statewide childcare resource and referral services to families and providers. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/ New Hampshire Bulletin)Whether you’re a parent or provider, navigating New Hampshire’s childcare landscape can be tricky. With hundreds of programs and varying resources, it’s difficult to know where to start as a parent or provider.
To help address those challenges, the state contracts with the Community Action Partnership of Hillsborough and Rockingham Counties, which provides statewide child care resource and referral services through Child Care Aware of New Hampshire. Child Care Aware helps families, providers, and programs with various childcare-related issues, such as helping families find a childcare program, assisting with New Hampshire Connections, administering nationally registered early education apprenticeship programs, and more. 
Child Care Aware, which has offices in six communities across the state, also works with its parent agency, Child Care Aware of America, to oversee national surveys and collect state-based data. Every year, they serve more than 500 families and 2,700 childcare workers. 
The agency’s work is entirely federally funded, though it must be approved by the Department of Health and Human Services and the Executive Council before it is received. Last month, the Executive Council approved $3.4 million in federal dollars to fund the agency’s operations through June 2028. 
Dee Dee Thurber, program director for the agency, said the majority of the work with families is in helping them find childcare that fits their needs and in their preferred area. The agency makes a curated list of 5 to 15 program referrals — not recommendations — when families ask for assistance in finding a program that has capacity. They will also help families apply to the state childcare scholarship assistance program. 
The agency also helps families understand New Hampshire’s childcare rules and quality indicators, as well as prepare for what to look for during a facility tour. Thurber said that the agency takes on the research and education work “a lot of families don’t have time to do.” All services are free. 
“It would take them a very long time to pinpoint the childcare centers that are within their search radius. And we actually do that work for them, because we have the ability to use the database and do that,” she said. “We are a resource for them in helping them find childcare and helping them gain more knowledge.” 
Child Care Aware of New Hampshire also aids providers, the term used for childcare directors and teachers, through two main avenues: outreach and technical assistance. 
The agency helps the Department of Health and Human Services and other partners spread the message about their initiatives. Employees conduct campaigns via phone, email, and mail to make sure information is spread to over 700 programs. Recently, the team completed a big “outreach drive,” where they tried to contact all of the state’s programs via phone, email, and mail to make sure they updated their provider profiles on the state-run New Hampshire Connections Information System website.
“We realized that some providers don’t actually know how to get into the system,” Thurber said. “This was a great way to really reach out, and then when they needed help in the system, we can help.” 
Thurber said her team also helps programs with credentialing applications and Granite Steps for Quality, the state’s childcare quality improvement program. 
The agency also provides professional development help, resources, and training, both virtual and in-person. Based on feedback from the childcare community, Child Care Aware of New Hampshire provides curated development training on topics of interest, such as infant and toddler care or family child care. If a program requests specific training, agency specialists can travel to provide it. 
The 14 employees on Thurber’s team have over 400 years of combined experience in the childcare field, a fact Thurber is very proud of. Their experience, she said, makes them properly suited to handle their responsibilities. 
“The nice thing is that we bring lived experience to our jobs, and we also can bring authenticity because what we’re sharing is what we’ve experienced and what we lived,” she said. “We love what we do.” 
Scholarship and apprenticeship programs
Child Care Aware of New Hampshire also manages one national scholarship program and two apprenticeship programs, one registered by the U.S. Department of Labor and the other available to New Hampshire high school students. 
The Teacher Education and Compensation Helps, or TEACH Scholarship, provides money to early childhood educators while they are pursuing their child development associate or associate’s degree in the field. The scholarship covers 85% to 95% of tuition, books, release time (practical work in a program), and a stipend. The scholarship is national, and Child Care Aware administers it as a part of their duties as a resource and referral agency. 
They also run New Hampshire’s Early Childhood Apprenticeship Program. The year-and-a-half-long, U.S. Department of Labor-registered program recruits educators and connects them with a mentor at a childcare program to deliver support and on-the-job learning. 
Nicola Peno, child development director at the Community Action Partnership of Hillsborough and Rockingham Counties, said the apprenticeship program gives prospective educators a “guided structure” and “support” as they enter the field, making them more likely to continue once the program’s finished. 
“The apprenticeship program just really structures (students’) knowledge and those practice skills and experiences that they get,” she said. 
The new high school pre-apprenticeship program does the same but for high school students. If they decide to continue in early education upon high school graduation, the program leads into the apprenticeship program or TEACH Scholarship. 
Thurber said the most important service the agency provides is connections. 
“We’re a resource and referral agency, so I really do think that that’s the most important component,” she said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana tax amnesty program underway with prospect of collecting at least $100M
description: Inquiries about Indiana’s tax amnesty program are off to a quick start from businesses and individuals with overdue state taxes, according to state officials. The general public, however, won’t notice much promotion of the effort as the Indiana Department of Revenue is focused on directly notifying delinquent taxpayers about the chance to pay off those […]
text:
The Indiana Department of Revenue logo outside its State Government Center offices. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Inquiries about Indiana’s tax amnesty program are off to a quick start from businesses and individuals with overdue state taxes, according to state officials.
The general public, however, won’t notice much promotion of the effort as the Indiana Department of Revenue is focused on directly notifying delinquent taxpayers about the chance to pay off those bills without penalties.
The amnesty period opened July 15 for those with tax liabilities from before Jan. 1, 2024. They must agree on payment plans no later than Sept. 9.
Early online traffic about eligibility
More than 2,300 people had logged into the Department of Revenue’s online service portal to check on their amnesty eligibility and payment options as of this week, said Emily Wann, the agency’s executive director of operations.
Emily Wann, executive director of operations for the Indiana Department of Revenue. (Photo provided by Department of Revenue)
The department is using its Indiana Taxpayer Information Management Engine, or INTIME, as its principal way of processing actions for the amnesty program.
“Our customers can go to INTIME … and actually determine if they’re eligible for amnesty, look up any of their eligible liabilities, learn more information,” Wann told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “They can make direct payments through INTIME, or they could set up a payment plan.”
Indiana had similar amnesty programs in 2005 and 2015 that allowed those voluntarily pay their tax delinquency to avoid facing civil or criminal penalties, including late-payment fees, interest or collection fees. 
Those who took part in either previous amnesty aren’t eligible for the new period.
Direct contact rather than advertising
The Department of Revenue said it has about $465 million in delinquent taxes on its books. 
It estimates the amnesty period could yield between $65 million and $144 million, while the State Budget Agency has included $124 million of amnesty revenue into its 2027 fiscal year projections.
Those figures add up to collecting between 14% and 31% of the past-due taxes.


Amnesty details:

Offer is open to individuals and businesses with past-due taxes from before Jan. 1, 2024, who did not take part in Indiana’s similar 2005 or 2015 programs waiving penalties, interest and collection fees.
Individuals owing more than $100 and businesses owing more than $500 can set up payment plans, but those debts must be paid by June 7, 2027, to avoid incurring additional penalties.
More details available on the Department of Revenue’s Tax Amnesty 2026 webpage.



Indiana’s 2015 amnesty period collected $188.5 million, which a state report said amounted to 34% of the eligible liabilities.
Department officials decided against any mass marketing endeavors for the tax amnesty program, instead sending notices directly to the individuals and businesses with delinquencies.
So there will be no tax amnesty billboards or television ads, department spokeswoman Megan Kramer said.
“Instead of spending money on trying to get a percentage of people who aren’t actually eligible, we wanted to instead really focus our efforts on those who we know could benefit from this opportunity,” she said.
Where the money collected will go
Legislators directed the Department of Revenue to establish the amnesty period as part of the state budget bill adopted in 2025. That came as they scrambled in response to projections that tax collections would grow less than 1% each year of the state’s two-year budget cycle.
But state government’s financial picture has improved dramatically since then as tax revenue jumped 6.8% over the past year, which helped the state’s cash reserves grow by $1.5 billion to just shy of $4 billion.  
Money collected through the tax amnesty will be directed to the uses for each type of tax as called for under state law, according to the Department of Revenue.
“Many of the taxes such as individual income tax, corporate tax, and sales tax are deposited into the state’s General Fund to then be allocated to Indiana government activities,” the agency’s website said.
During the 2015 amnesty, out-of-state businesses paid about two-thirds — $125.6 million — of the delinquent collections, with 20% — $37.7 million — coming from Indiana individual taxpayers.
Going into this year’s amnesty, about 60% of the eligible past-due taxes are owed by businesses, according to the Department of Revenue. Roughly 60% of the delinquencies are from Indiana taxpayers and 40% are from elsewhere.
State working with collection company
The Department of Revenue isn’t alone in coordinating the amnesty period as contractor United Collection Bureau is handling much of the work contacting eligible taxpayers and taking phone calls about the program.
United Collection will be paid 5.5% of what it collects in amnesty payments — less than the 6.5% it receives from other state tax collections under a contract extension it signed with the state in December.
Wann, the Department of Revenue executive, said while amnesty inquiries had started off quickly, the success of this year’s program won’t be clear until the time period ends in September.
“In 2015 and in 2005, the majority of our volume (came) in in the last two weeks,” she said. “While we don’t want that to happen, that’s the way we’ve seen it happen in the past. So we are bracing ourselves for the last couple weeks.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Are we losing our freedom of speech?
description: Everywhere I look, the concept of free speech is getting a workout. A food truck, a cake, a flag — all have stirred up emotions recently here in Indiana. Of course, the First Amendment applies only to freedom of speech as it pertains to government action. That’s why you hear people say, “freedom of speech doesn’t […]
text:
A protester carries a sign about free speech in Oregon. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Everywhere I look, the concept of free speech is getting a workout. A food truck, a cake, a flag — all have stirred up emotions recently here in Indiana.
Of course, the First Amendment applies only to freedom of speech as it pertains to government action. That’s why you hear people say, “freedom of speech doesn’t mean freedom from consequences.”
But I’m tired of how society has become a game of gotcha. It’s practically a national pastime to drag people online and call for their firing over their opinion.
Even a food truck at the Statehouse market can’t have a little fun with a slogan without getting kicked out because the phrase offended someone’s fragile sensibilities.
The Smash Daddy’s Burgers, Fries, Etc. food truck had been showing up to the market for almost two years. On the side of the truck is the slogan, “you’ll love our meat in your mouth.”
Yes, it’s sexual innuendo. No different than “where’s the beef” was in the 1980s for Wendy’s. There’s a company that advertises fudge and candy in the most sophomoric way possible on billboards in Indiana but it hasn’t been stopped from operating.
But suddenly after someone complained — not in writing, by the way — the truck was told not to return by the Indiana State Personnel Department.
Talk about an overreaction. If you don’t want to eat there, then fine. But it was a place that always had a line and the complainers cost the truck’s owner thousands in revenue.
That’s where we are at as a society?
The food truck owner might have a legal case since the government was involved and the phrase doesn’t count as obscenity.
Calling for jobs
But that’s not the only free-speech issue popping up lately.
Let’s take about the cake. A comedian and guest lecturer at George Washington University in Washington, D.C., took a crass cake to U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham’s office offering “congratudolences” after his death. She also posted harsh criticism against Graham.
It was tacky and awful and, of course, I don’t approve. But now many people want her fired from her adjunct position at Indiana University teaching one law school course.
In a letter addressed to IU President Pamela Whitten and the dean of the university’s McKinney law school in Indianapolis, the IndyStar reported that Republican U.S. Reps. Marlin Stutzman and Mark Messmer said Elizabeth Booker Houston should be fired for comments they describe as “vile and cruel” and that violate the university’s handbook.
Heck, Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith went further and said IU should lose all its state funding.
This call is similar to what colleges and universities faced after Charlie Kirk was killed and some employees were outed for inappropriate comments. Ball State University did fire an employee over a social media post, but she sued and won a $225,000 settlement.
Some are angry that Ball State settled instead of buttressing the legal case for future firings.
And then we have Attorney General Todd Rokita, who continues to post photos and social media rants against teachers in Indiana and their classroom décor. One recently highlighted a Perry Meridian High School classroom that has signs supporting LGBTQ+ rights, Black Lives Matter and more.
Others pointed out the flags and decoration encouraged civility and love for one another.
Rokita provided no information in his tweet or on the Eyes on Education portal about the veracity of the photos. Perry Township Schools Superintendent Patrick Spray clarified to the Capital Chronicle that the photos are not recent. He said the teacher resigned last school year for reasons unrelated to the issue.
More importantly, he provided context about the photos, noting that the Black Lives Matter and Free Myanmar photos are of student art.
“That is a classroom that receives newcomers to the country, so primarily refugees … and they are allowed to represent their thoughts and feelings in the classroom,” he said. “Now, I will say that we have worked with our staff and talked about keeping political things out of the classroom, especially if they don’t adhere to the curriculum being taught. We’ve just told them it’s not worth the negative attention you may receive as an individual.”
Another day, another attack on freedom of speech. I miss the days when we worried more about our own lives than everyone else’s. I miss when we had tolerance for other viewpoints — even the distasteful ones.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: After losing SNAP benefits, some CT refugees are struggling to afford food
description: An estimated 1,745 refugees and asylum seekers are expected to lose SNAP in Connecticut, a DSS spokesperson said.
text:
Syrian natives Karam and Noor have spent long days this summer sitting in the respite of their small New Haven apartment, listening to the gentle buzz of the air conditioner and the hum of Karam’s dialysis machine.
Weakened by kidney failure, Karam is unable to work and is tethered 12 hours a day to the machine that cleans the toxins from his blood.
Noor, who does not speak English and has found it difficult to find work, has always taken pains to feed her husband and their children a healthy diet of fresh foods, often cooking dishes from their homeland. That’s gotten harder to do since the family lost its food stamps in December due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as H.R. 1, which ended access to the program for refugees and asylum-seekers.
But salty food is dangerous for Karam and the shelf-stable food carried by pantries they’ve come to rely on the last eight months is often high in sodium.
“There’s been a 180 degree change” in the conditions of their daily lives since the family stopped receiving help from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, Noor said through a translator. “Now we have to focus on the cost of everything and we can barely afford essentials.”
Karam and Noor are not the couples’ real names; they requested anonymity because they are in the process of applying for green cards and fear retribution in a time when the federal government has ramped up deportations of some groups, shut down some programs and ended funding for others that served immigrants.

From left to right, Maria Ramirez, Christion Gilbert, Elizabeth Johnston, and Ana Cardenas stand in the Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services in New Haven. All four work in the food pantry organizing distributions, managing the warehouse, and distributing goods to guests.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

In Connecticut, SNAP enrollment has decreased by about 35,000 since December, much of that tied to new federal work requirements, according to officials at the state Department of Social Services. An estimated 1,745 refugees and asylum seekers are expected to lose SNAP in Connecticut, a DSS spokesperson said.
Connecticut has partially filled the gap for people who have lost SNAP, providing millions in assistance to food pantries, grants to the Department of Agriculture, and $300 grocery cards for people who have recently lost SNAP. IRIS has also been able to provide a bridge of four months of supplemental assistance to families. 
The new federal policy affecting refugee food assistance is a stark reversal from the previous era of resettlements, in which such newcomers were helped with every step of the process — from searching for employment to securing housing and public benefits — by resettlement groups and federal funding. Today, groups like New Haven-based Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services, or IRIS, are focused on helping families secure the means of supporting themselves on an accelerated timeline, as supports like SNAP vanish and they must get the needed skills to quickly join the labor force.
“Everyone’s timeline for becoming self-sufficient and dependent on their own resources is largely dependent on the skills and resources they came to the country with,” said Daniel Pflueger, deputy director of stabilization services at IRIS. For people who arrive fluent in English, the route to finding stable employment is shorter, he said, while others may need to learn a new language or learn a trade. 
In addition to the rental assistance IRIS provided in the first year, families also have also historically been supported by both SNAP and Temporary Family Assistance, a program that provides cash to families under 55% of the poverty line for up to 36 months.
“Now without SNAP, that changes the whole framework where immediately there are hundreds or well over a thousand dollars in some cases that people don’t have,” Pflueger said.
Karam and Noor came to Connecticut two years ago with the help of the International Organization for Migration. They left Syria during the civil war and then lived in Jordan for a decade, before securing refugee status in the United States.

Kate Lee hands out corn to food pantry guests at IRIS in New Haven. Lee has volunteered with the organization for 20 years and lives in Guilford.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Though they are living in the U.S. legally, with humanitarian status, they also try to limit their time outside the apartment because they don’t want to risk coming into contact with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who have swept up many residents of their adopted city over the past year.
Noor said she learned in November 2025 that the family of eight would no longer receive more than $1,000 a month for groceries through SNAP. 
Though H.R. 1 ended the program for refugees beginning in December 2025, not all recipients lost the benefit at the same time, according to Pflueger.
“It’s only when a family would have, say, their next renewal, or there’s an updated family member or house address change, something that would require a DSS agent to to open up their case,” Pflueger said.
Much of the food Noor’s family eats comes from food pantries, like canned fruit, bags of beans and rice and limited fresh food, like cabbage, onions and potatoes.
A New Haven pantry run by IRIS sometimes offers Halal meats, but Noor said her family has mostly gone vegetarian since the cuts. They eat smaller meals earlier in the day with less variety and have replaced dinner with a late-day snack to get them through the night.
With limited financial resources, IRIS says they are focused on preparing families to survive on their own. 
“Is there an opportunity to get a second job? Is there a 17-year-old in the family who can work in the summer or part time in the school year? Is there anyone in the family who could really get to a better opportunity of getting employed if they got their English up to the next level?” Pflueger said are some of the questions they ask families.
Noor and Karam’s six children are in school, ranging from young adults studying in college to her youngest who is three. As the mother of teenagers, it can be especially challenging to stretch their food.
“When I cook a big meal, I expect leftovers the next day, but it’ll be completely gone from the fridge,” she said through a translator.

From Left to right, Barbara Shiller, Eleanor Weseloh and Elizabeth Johnston organize food on the choice table. The table is stocked with fresh produce and prepared foods from Trader Joes.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The family will also lose access to HUSKY, Connecticut’s Medicaid program, later this year. But Karam, who is currently on the state plan, should still be covered under a federal program for people with life-threatening conditions. Advocates say that for a family such as theirs, stress is coming from every angle. 
“Immigration enforcement is happening on a weekly basis, and when new policies come out, it is coupled with food insecurity for the population that we serve, it’s taking a toll on them,” said Mohammed Daad Serweri, associate director of resettlement services at IRIS. “It’s not only not having food — actual food on the table for the children to really have enough to eat— but it’s also the mental health and has really negatively impacted many of these parents.”
Families worry not only about how and where they will get enough food, but also whether it’s safe to visit a pantry because ICE could be present or how to schedule a job around pantry hours. “A lot of folks are making choices of what not to pay,” Pfleuger said. “So people are not paying their full rent, or people are skipping out on their utility bills so that they can buy food in the meantime.”
Many are hoping that they will be able to find a job to get back on track with those bills or that a green card application will go through, but currently “extraordinarily few” of those applications are being processed, according to Pflueger. A new policy allows immigration officers to hold the use of public assistance programs like SNAP and housing vouchers against green card applicants.
As they are confined to eating the foods they are given at pantries, families also lose access to the ingredients that help them summon the flavors of home. 
It’s now been eight months since Noor and Karam lost SNAP. They have received some assistance for their school-age children for the summer months through the SUN Bucks program — $120 per child — which has allowed Noor to buy healthy foods, and sometimes get her kids’ favorite snacks. 
Back in Syria, before he got sick, Karam was a farmer. Though there were other struggles, having enough to eat was never among them.
But difficult as the situation may be, the family is still glad to be here. 
“For my kids to be able to get an education at university level, I still see the benefits and I’m not really focusing on the drawbacks,” Noor said.
