name: Kansas Reflector
title: Mailers aim to sway us on Kansas Supreme Court amendment, but mostly they deserve the dust bin
description: I messaged my friends and family this week asking for political mailers that they received. The replies that I got were nearly identical:  I think I tossed them. I trash them as they come in. They went out with the recycling yesterday. Ha. I just trashed/destroyed them last night. Maybe “destroyed” is a bit harsh, […]
text:
Kansans have been swamped by mailers about the judicial selection amendment on the ballot Aug. 4. (Photo by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)I messaged my friends and family this week asking for political mailers that they received. The replies that I got were nearly identical: 
I think I tossed them.
I trash them as they come in.
They went out with the recycling yesterday.
Ha. I just trashed/destroyed them last night.
Maybe “destroyed” is a bit harsh, but it’s the same in our house. Most political mailers addressed to us don’t even make it in the house from the mailbox — they go straight into the garage recycling bin.
For that reason, it’s interesting to see how Kansas campaigns try to reach voters when we see each slick cardstock design as junk mail. Our culture’s attention span to media messages gets shorter each year, so the design, imagery and words on political mailers must cut right to the point.
Along with a mixed bag related to candidate elections, my neighbors and I mostly receive mailers related to the amendment that would establish direct elections of Kansas Supreme Court justices. The message here is even simpler than a candidate election, where voters need to remember a name.
Here, as the mailers make clear, it’s just “yes” (establish elections) or “no” (maintain the current process). 
What did I see? Blunt messaging and simple images, aimed at catching our reluctant gaze and quickly persuading us.
 
Vote yes
The mailers for “yes” come with conservative messaging from political action committees such as the Prairie Fire PAC, connected with Attorney General Kris Kobach, and Americans for Prosperity, founded by the Koch brothers of Wichita.

Two recent “yes” mailers borrow the look of official government mailings. One of them combines a warning symbol, the words “IMPORTANT NOTICE” and a yellow warning to “DO NOT DISCARD.” Using an aesthetic that looks like it came from the local government (which is to say it’s hammerhead ugly) is a clever tactical twist, making the mailer stand out from the polished noise of the PACs. 
The look also associates the message of “VOTE YES” with a mailing that could come from the election office. One mailer provides early voting locations as the county board of elections might do. 

Designers further connect the “yes” campaign with civic responsibility by emphasizing the image of “I Voted” stickers. One mailing shows folks with the stickers on their chests, pointing to them in case we missed it. The image of a circular button dominates another mailing. 
The words of the “yes” campaign go even further, branding the decision as the “RIGHT TO VOTE AMENDMENT,” suggesting that we “LET THE VOTERS DECIDE.” 
You might, like me, see hypocrisy in conservative voices celebrating the right to vote as they simultaneously work to suppress voting in many other ways. Nevertheless, it’s a patriotic, wholesome and effective association. Even if it doesn’t address the deeper issue actually on the ballot, how do you dispute the virtue of voting?
All of this seems legitimate if not clever political messaging on behalf of PACs pushing voters toward yes. 

However, a pair of Americans for Prosperity Kansas mailings dip into the political muck in encouraging “yes” votes. My neighbor received a mailing promising three “FACTS” about the amendment. Instead, the mailing delivers partisan rhetoric such as, “The Kansas Supreme Court has been too soft on crime!” and “The ones controlling the court are lying to you.” 
So much for facts.
The biggest fumble came from a mailing that boldly centers all-caps text on a yellow background: “YOU DESERVE THE RIGHT.” There’s more than one way to read that.

One option? “You deserve the power to use the ballot box to vote for the Supreme Court in Kansas” aligns with their campaign. However, I also read it as being about being stuck in Kansas with conservative politicians at the helm, as in “You deserve the disastrous politics of rightwing politicians, since you voted for them, you Kansas dummies.”
The second meaning seems like a tough appeal, especially to Johnson County voters who are gradually shifting away from the Republican Party.
Both of the Americans For Prosperity Kansas mailers use a blue-and-yellow color scheme, which conjures the color scheme of the state flag. Another association might be politically familiar if you were in Kansas during the 2022 vote related to abortion rights. In that election, PACs that wanted us to vote no (a progressive vote to protect abortion rights) used blue and yellow on their yard signs. 
Not to mention, during the last few months, signs dotting the yards and medians of Johnson County use the same color scheme — but those ask us to vote “no.”
Using the blue-and-yellow palette here for the “yes” campaign might be an effort to sway (if not confuse) moderate or progressive voters. Maybe it’s just the state flag. 
Finally, from all of the “yes” mailings, my nomination for the most effective distillation of why to vote yes: “Only Kansas has an oddball system where lawyers, not voters, choose the judges.” That single line does so much — targeting the novelty of the current system, playing on cultural distrust of lawyers and pointing to voters being robbed of their power. 
 
Vote no
Unsurprisingly, the mailers for vote “no” used quite different techniques. 
Of the six mailers that I collected, the most common approach was a two-step: an appeal to expertise while using Kobach as an adversary. Each of these mailers was sent by Kansas United for Impartial Courts, chaired by Micah Kubic, who also works as executive director of the ACLU of Kansas. 

Mailers presented a few different authorities, including former Kansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Lawton Nuss (“I’m voting NO because our Supreme Court is NOT FOR SALE.”) and OB/GYN physician Selina Sandoval — a mailing that connected a vote against the amendment with the protection of abortion rights. 
With these authority figures staring solemnly into the camera, the vote appears grave — especially when paired with a somber, black background for the text. 
From the same group, I received a similarly designed mailer with a woman from Lawrence quoted as saying, “We already decided this.” It’s a nod to the 2022 vote on the “Value Them Both” abortion amendment. 
More broadly, those words play on our collective fatigue with politics, politicians and their games. The mailer rolls its eyes that conservatives in Kansas can’t get the message. Those words can also be read as voicing frustration about President Donald Trump, whose election denialism in 2020, was the ultimate political example of “we already decided this.”
None of the vote “no” messaging portrays hope. Instead, the mailers are mired in disorganization, negativity and opposition. 
One folded mailer promises, “HERE’S THE TRUTH,” but then delivers a buckshot pattern of all-caps, bold-faced and underlined assertions that don’t cohere around a central political idea. The random visuals include a handshake, people voting and shoes striding across a textured floor. What are voters to summon from that? 
Just how little positivity is in the mailers for the vote “no” effort? Take this quiz for me. 
Taken from a no-frills, black-and-white mailer from the same PAC, one set of verbs below describes what will happen if you vote “yes.” The other describes the effects of voting “no.” See if you can tell which is which. 
List #1: replaces / enables / makes it easier / increases
List #2: retains / shields / continues / keeps
The first list is clearly more positive — yet, it describes the vote “yes” initiative. Those word choices portray action and progress, while the second list is verbal molasses, appealing to tradition, if not intransigence. It’s baffling that these are the words that the PAC used to frame the choices in their own mailer. 

Kansas United for Impartial Courts found a more effective message and design with a vertical mailer showing a full-bleed photo of Kobach’s face obscured by text reading: “SO NOW THEY’RE TRYING AGAIN.” Extra points to the graphic designer who found a way to allow one of Kobach’s eyes to peek creepily through the cluster of words.
It’s tempting to say that the PAC is painting Kobach as the bogeyman, but Kobach legitimately is the opposition here, since he leads a rival PAC supporting the amendment. He slides easily into the role of villain, encouraged by his deep unpopularity statewide. Voters who realistically could be persuaded to vote “no” likely don’t like Kobach, even before they open their mail.
The strongest expression of the vote “no” messaging? “This amendment is an attempt to take away our power and ban abortion.” It is more direct than some of the other confused language in vote “no” mailers.
We might believe that mailers aren’t significant, given our boredom, if not irritation, at receiving them. It’s also possible that with the election’s timing — a midterm, primary election — every voter swayed by the mailbox will matter. 
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana AG sues Merrillville, accusing town of blocking new ICE facility
description: Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita says Merrillville officials are "interfering" with land buys for a potential ICE facility in the town.
text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita backs an immigration bill on Thursday, Feb. 19, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita on Wednesday filed suit against a northwest Indiana town he says is interfering with federal immigration enforcement efforts to add a new detention facility there.
Merrillville, Rokita said in a news release, is “effectively aid(ing) and abet(ing)” criminals.
As President Donald Trump’s administration ramps up its mass deportation scheme, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been on the hunt for more immigrant detainee holding space.
ICE has been trying to buy property in Merrillville, Rokita confirmed.
He’s accusing town leaders of discouraging or even thwarting ICE real estate transactions with property owners, in violation of state laws requiring local government cooperation with ICE.
The Office of Attorney General didn’t immediately provide a copy of the complaint, and it was not available on the state’s MyCase platform.
The lawsuit comes about a month after Rokita’s office issued Merrillville a cease-and-desist letter.
The letter told leaders to rescind a non-binding resolution opposing the conversion of warehouses into detention space, stop interfering in resident-ICE land deals, and issue a public statement clarifying that the town won’t oppose transactions or retaliate against any land owners who sell to ICE.
“We requested that Merrillville comply with state law and they refused, choosing instead to play games, effectively aid and abet criminal illegal aliens, and making the illegals’ evasion of justice a higher priority than the safety of taxpayers throughout the region,” Rokita said. “That’s illegal under Indiana law.”
Immigration crackdown heads to Indiana governor after falling short last year

Merrillville didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Officials have previously said their resolution is an expression of opinion protected by the First Amendment — not an enforceable policy — and noted they’re “oath-bound” to follow all state and federal laws.
The lawsuit represents the first enforcement action taken under a controversial new immigration enforcement law, according to Rokita’s office. Senate Enrolled Act 76 was approved in March.
Some provisions didn’t take effect until this month, but others were effective immediately — including authorizing Rokita to sue units of local government for up to $10,000 per violation of an existing ban on limiting immigration enforcement activities..
Local governments must also comply with ICE detainer requests.
The law additionally prohibits businesses from knowingly or intentionally employing unauthorized workers. Violators face escalating punishments ranging from operating authorization suspensions at one site to permanent revocations at all locations.
Rokita is sending video remarks to be played at a Saturday mass deportation rally headlined by former U.S. Border Patrol head Greg Bovino.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Uninsured but undaunted, a Portland surgical patient searched the globe for a deal
description: Around the end of last year, Ronmel Rangel, 63, began to feel a familiar discomfort in his lower abdomen. Twenty-five years earlier, while living in his native Venezuela, he had undergone surgery to repair a hernia on the right side of his groin. Now, the same pain had returned — on the left. This time, […]
text:
Uninsured and in need of hernia surgery, Ronmel Rangel collected estimates from facilities near and far from his home in Portland,
Maine, including some outside the United States. “I wasn’t going to mortgage my life just to have surgery and spend the next 30
years paying off the debt,” he says. (Photo by: Brianna Soukup /KFF Health News) 
This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here under a Creative Commons License.

	Around the end of last year, Ronmel Rangel, 63, began to feel a familiar discomfort in his lower abdomen. Twenty-five years earlier, while living in his native Venezuela, he had undergone surgery to repair a hernia on the right side of his groin.
Now, the same pain had returned — on the left.
This time, Rangel was in the U.S. and lacked health insurance. In 2019, he moved to Portland, Maine, where one of his daughters lives.
As a green-card holder, he qualified to purchase health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But he quickly realized that the premiums for someone his age were beyond his budget. He decided to go without insurance, even though it had been a priority for him.
Instead, Rangel signed up for a plan at a concierge practice where patients pay as little as $70 a month for services, including unlimited office visits and minor procedures such as stitches and biopsies.
But when Rangel was diagnosed with a hernia, surgery became unavoidable. Ben Hagopian, his primary care physician, helped him compile a list of hospitals and surgical centers to consider. Rangel has a PhD in management, a field he pursued while serving in the navy in Venezuela. Armed with that knowledge and a naturally inquisitive mind, he began researching prices.
His efforts paid off when the bill came.
The medical service
Rangel had what is called an inguinal hernia, which occurs when the contents of the abdomen bulge through a weak spot in the lower abdominal wall. The condition is relatively common, particularly among older adults.
In most cases, surgery is required to fix the muscle wall and can be performed as an outpatient procedure. There are three main surgical approaches to repair an inguinal hernia: open, laparoscopic, and robot-assisted. Studies have shown that the three approaches have similarly low rates of hernia recurrence and are safe and effective.
Rangel underwent an open repair, an approach often preferred by physicians for recurrent hernias. He said his operation lasted less than two hours, and he walked out of the surgical center shortly afterward.
The bill
$2,900: The flat rate Rangel ultimately paid for his hernia repair at an outpatient surgery center in Maryland, including the surgeon’s fee and anesthesia. He said he also paid around $1,800 to travel to the surgery center from his home in Maine, including airfare, meals, and lodging for him and his wife.

The billing problem: No insurance — but time to shop
Because Rangel did not have insurance, he had no protections from high costs — except time and his ability to shop for an acceptable price for his procedure.
Rangel’s first stop was a nonprofit hospital close to home. He scheduled a consultation with a surgeon with MaineHealth, the state’s largest health system, and received an estimate showing it would cost approximately $23,000 to repair his hernia laparoscopically.
Laparoscopic procedures generally cost more because surgeons use more advanced tools. Still, the average laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair costs nearly twice as much at a hospital as it does at an ambulatory surgery center for a patient covered by Medicare, which pays $5,280 for the hospital-based option.
“I wasn’t going to mortgage my life just to have surgery and spend the next 30 years paying off the debt,” said Rangel, now 64.
So, he kept shopping. He considered a surgical center in Oklahoma that was far cheaper, but he ultimately ruled it out because it was so far away. He also explored traveling to Universidad de los Andes in Santiago, Chile, where another of his daughters lives. There, his hernia repair would have cost about $7,000, but once he added thousands of dollars in travel expenses, that option no longer made financial sense.
Gerard Anderson, a professor who analyzes healthcare spending at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said patients without health insurance are often the ones hit hardest by wide price variations.
A closer look at any hospital bill helps explain why. “Every hospital is different,” he said, “but generally about half of the total charge is the facility fee,” a charge added to hospital care to help cover overhead costs.
Anderson said hospitals often mark up prices far more than smaller facilities do.
Medical billing researchers say the price gap between hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers partially reflects the higher overhead costs of operating a hospital.
Hagopian, Rangel’s physician, acknowledged that hospitals have higher administrative expenses. “But that doesn’t explain the high costs.”
MaineHealth declined to comment to KFF Health News, directing questions about the hospital-based procedure’s cost to Jeffrey Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association.
Austin said that, unlike surgery centers, hospitals must absorb the costs of providing “money-losing” services, such as behavioral healthcare and care for Medicaid patients. He added that revenue generated by large hospitals in a health system supports other facilities, improving access to care.
Hospital prices, which can vary widely, are also driven by negotiations with insurers and market concentration. For uninsured patients, those list prices can become the starting point for negotiations — or the full amount owed.
Anderson noted that standardized payment rates exist for Medicare and Medicaid but not for most privately priced medical services. “In the private sector, providers can charge whatever they want.”

The resolution
Rangel has another daughter in Argentina, a son in Venezuela, and other family in Spain. But he decided to stop looking around the globe for a good price, because he finally found what he was looking for in Maryland.
In April, he traveled to the Affordable Hernia Surgery center in Rockville, where he said “an efficient, well-coordinated system” guided him through the entire process.
“I received professional and very human care,” Rangel said. He was fully recovered within two weeks, as his surgeon predicted, he said.
The surgery center charged Rangel a flat fee for his hernia repair. The added travel expenses for the two-day trip with his wife went toward airline tickets, transportation, meals, and one night in a hotel.
Rangel said he paid about $4,700 total.
Alan Kravitz, the surgeon who performed Rangel’s operation, said the price difference uninsured patients face compared with insured patients is far from fair. “In the predatory and strategic world of U.S. healthcare pricing, uninsured patients generally get charged more than providers would accept from Medicare or commercial insurance.”
Kravitz then pulled out an estimate another patient had received for an inguinal hernia repair from a different large health system. The price: $37,000.
The takeaway
Without insurance, many patients are on their own to negotiate.
“With the help of their primary physicians, patients can dig into prices and compare their options to avoid falling into medical debt,” Rangel said.
That approach, however, is most feasible for elective procedures with several surgical options offering comparable outcomes.
Patients facing medical emergencies do not have the luxury of comparing prices before seeking care, though many hospitals offer cash-pay discounts or charity care for those paying without insurance.
Billing analysts say patients who do have time to shop should look beyond cost alone. They recommend checking the quality of hospitals and surgical centers by reviewing publicly available ratings and patient reviews. Research has found that higher prices do not necessarily translate into a better quality of care, but it’s also important to select a reputable care provider.
Comparison shopping for medical care can be time-consuming. But for patients facing elective procedures, the effort can pay off — sometimes saving thousands of dollars.
“This was a learning experience for me,” Rangel said, “and I hope it will be for other people, too.”



Bill of the Month is a crowdsourced investigation by KFF Health News and The Washington Post’s Well+Being that dissects and explains medical bills. Since 2018, this series has helped many patients and readers get their medical bills reduced, and it has been cited in statehouses, at the U.S. Capitol, and at the White House. name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio cities brace for possible uptick of ICE activity after protected status ends for Haitians
description: Ohio cities with big Haitian populations are preparing for a possible uptick of United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after temporary protected status for Haitians ended this week.  Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said he recently heard of a new tactic ICE is using in Springfield.  “I received a call from a […]
text:
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield after temporary protected status for Haitians ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  Ohio cities with big Haitian populations are preparing for a possible uptick of United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after temporary protected status for Haitians ended this week. 
Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said he recently heard of a new tactic ICE is using in Springfield. 
“I received a call from a leader in our community who said that what’s happening is Haitians in Springfield are getting letters asking them to report to Homeland Security and ICE down in Cincinnati,” he said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“They’re asked to report in, and what I was told is that once they get there, they are asked to wear an ankle bracelet and report back in a month.”
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last month that President Donald Trump can end legal status for Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country.
About 330,000 Haitians are living in the United States with Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a program that allows people from specific countries in conflict or facing natural disasters the chance to live and work in the United States for a set period of time.
About 30,000 Haitians with temporary status live in central Ohio and 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.
“The federal officials are now telling us that they do not have any plans,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who was born in Springfield, told reporters on Wednesday. 
“They’ve received no instructions to have any kind of raids in Springfield. Now that can change, but they did tell us they’ve heard nothing.” 
Mike and his wife Fran DeWine help support the Becky DeWine School in Haiti, named after their late daughter, but the school had to close due to gang activity in 2024. 
“It’s a mistake to say that (Haitians) can no longer stay in this country,” DeWine said.
Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, speaks in support of Haitians living in Springfield during a press conference. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
“I think that the people who have come here to work, the Haitians who came to Springfield, were filling jobs that had not been filled before. They are part of the resurgence of Springfield.”
Springfield Mayor Rob Rue said he has not received information from ICE about enforcement operations. 
“I hope Congress will seize this opportunity to modernize our immigration system in a way that upholds the rule of law, strengthens our economy and reflects the values that have long made the United States strong,” he said in a statement. 
Maqueli Eldredge, a paralegal at Legal Immigration Services in Dublin, anticipates an uptick of ICE activity as a result of TPS ending. 
ICE detained more than 280 people in Columbus in December during Operation Buckeye. 
“I’m afraid it might turn into that, but I hope not,” Eldredge said.
“We might see some large numbers, but it wouldn’t be as public as it was in December.”
She said ICE has changed their tactics from detaining people in public spaces like courthouses and in the streets to instead knocking on people’s doors and detaining people where they live. 
Columbus Mayor Andrew Ginther called forcing Haitians back to Haiti “irresponsible and inhumane.”
“Our immigrant and refugee neighbors make positive contributions to our community through their unique perspectives, workplace contributions and participation in our economy,” he said in a statement. 
“We cannot prevent federal operations from happening in our city, and federal officers do not communicate their plans with us.”
Ruby is asking ICE not to come to Springfield.
“We will encourage people to protest peacefully,” he said. “There are many who are willing to place themselves between ICE and people who are targets for detainment and deportation.” 
Haitians were initially granted temporary protected status after Haiti’s earthquake in 2010 killed 222,570 people. The Biden administration extended Temporary Protected Status to Haitians in 2021 after the assassination of Haiti President Jovenel Moïse. 
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care,” according to the state department. A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped last month. 
“I’ve talked to families who are so afraid of going back to Haiti,” Ruby said. 
“Rape is endemic in Haiti right now, and if all of the Haitians who are in Springfield who have been on TPS were sent back to Haiti, some of the teenage girls who have sat in our city schools next to our own children are probably going to be subject to that.” 
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield after temporary protected status ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
Springfield experienced a shrinking population for decades as manufacturing jobs disappeared, but Haitian immigrants have grown Clark County’s workforce by more than 10,000 workers. 
The Clark County city became a flashpoint in the 2024 Election when Trump and JD Vance spread racist lies about Haitian immigrants there.
Rev. Michelle Boomgaard of Christ Episcopal Church talked about the growth Springfield had because of the Haitians. 
“We are seeing buildings long shuttered now open,” she said. “We are seeing new vibrancy in our communities.”
Deporting Haitians in Springfield would eliminate roughly $300 million in annual spending from Clark County, with an estimated economic loss projected to exceed $400 million.
Haitians also contribute millions of dollars in Columbus, said Yola Lamarre, an advocate with the Haitian Community Network.
“We’re going to see that impact because of this job loss,” she said. “We’re going to see the shortages in the healthcare industry and other industries that Haitians mostly populate.” 
Haitians in Ohio lost their work permits when TPS expired on Monday.
More than 1,000 children born in Springfield with American citizenship have Haitian parents. 
“I think that many of them are planning on taking their children with them, even if (the children) are U.S. citizens and have the protection,” Ruby said. 
Haitian parents are now faced with the choice of leaving their children or taking them back to Haiti “where they could be kidnapped, raped, or murdered,” Ruby said. 
“Imagine the dilemma that that is for mom and dad who love their kids, and that’s the situation that we have created for Haitian families right now, and it’s completely unnecessary.”
The Ohio Department of Children and Youth gave a grant to the Nehemiah Foundation and the Department of Jobs and Family Services to create a respite care network, said Tim Voltz of Champion City Church in Springfield. 
“There would be temporary places for those children to go, so they wouldn’t end up in a facility or detained somewhere,” he said. 
At least 18 families are part of the network, which can host children for up to 14 days at a time, Voltz said. 
“It is not a permanent solution,” he said. 
“It is only meant to provide a place for them while the state and the parents themselves and everyone tries to figure out how to reunite the parents of their children, or place them with kin. … The goal was to keep children from being shipped all over the state to foster care placements.” 
The emotional burden is overwhelming for Haitian families, said Jimmy Pierre of Gospel Grace Baptist Church in Springfield.
“Parents worry about what the future holds,” he said. 
“Some are having difficulty sleeping because they fear separation from their spouses or children. Many are dealing with anxiety, depression, and emotional exhaustion as they try to care for their families while living with uncertainty.”
Haitians can apply for asylum, but the Trump administration put an indefinite freeze on processing all asylum applications at the end of 2025.
About 4% of asylum cases are being approved, Ruby said. 
“Applying for asylum isn’t really a realistic option,” he said. 
At the federal level, the U.S. House voted in April to extend TPS for Haitians through 2029. The bill is now in the U.S. Senate, but the White House said President Donald Trump would veto the bill. 
U.S. Senators introduced an identical bill last month. 
“It’s time to put our ideology aside and focus on saving the lives of families,” Ruby said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Challenger to incumbent Ohio Supreme Court justice touts ‘originalism,’ strict immigration rulings
description: Former Judge Colleen O’Donnell, the Republican challenger hoping to unseat the Ohio Supreme Court’s only remaining Democratic justice, has been emphasizing her work as an immigration judge and her “originalism” stance in her campaign. Democratic Justice Jennifer Brunner won her seat in 2020. Ohio Republican lawmakers made the races for the state’s highest co[...]
text:
(Photo by Blair Miller/Daily Montanan)Former Judge Colleen O’Donnell, the Republican challenger hoping to unseat the Ohio Supreme Court’s only remaining Democratic justice, has been emphasizing her work as an immigration judge and her “originalism” stance in her campaign.
Democratic Justice Jennifer Brunner won her seat in 2020. Ohio Republican lawmakers made the races for the state’s highest court openly partisan starting in 2022 with the addition of party labels. Since then, Republicans have defeated two other incumbent Democrats to take 6-1 control over the court, with only Brunner remaining. Brunner has filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging the politicization of the court.
If elected, O’Donnell has pledged to maintain “judicial restraint” while interpreting the law based on what she interprets as the meaning the law writers intended at the time.
“I do not take the view that the Constitution, for example, is a living, breathing document, and so I honor both substantive and procedural judicial restraint,” O’Donnell said in a May interview.
The Capital Journal reached out to the O’Donnell campaign multiple times requesting a post-primary interview, but the campaign refused. A spokesperson for the O’Donnell campaign referred to comments made in a previous interview O’Donnell did with the Capital Journal prior to the May primary, but follow-up requests with specific questions did not receive a response.
Colleen O’Donnell, former Franklin County Court of Common Pleas judge and former federal immigration judge.
The former judge, and daughter of retired Ohio Supreme Court Justice Terrence O’Donnell, beat out a crowded field filled with appellate court judges. She took 32% of the vote, more than 280,000 votes in total, according to official results from the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office. The May primary election had a 22.68% voter turnout rate.
O’Donnell’s first job out of law school was serving with the Ohio Attorney General’s Office, before she clerked for a federal judge, spent time in private practice, and landed as a judge in Franklin County Common Pleas Court, where she appointed to serve after a retirement in May 2013. She served in the role until 2023, before being defeated in a re-election effort.
A new opportunity came about in the summer of that year, when she began presiding over asylum cases as a federal immigration judge, assigned to serve in Laredo, Texas.
“While I honored my oath and obligation to interpret the law with integrity and to approach every case with an open mind, I never granted asylum a single time,” O’Donnell told the Capital Journal in May.
In a post to her official campaign Facebook page, O’Donnell said she served as an immigration judge during what she called the “Biden border crisis,” in which she “enforced federal law precisely as written, finding zero cases to meet the necessarily high bar for asylum, and consistently ordering removals of illegal aliens.”
O’Donnell has said she has “always been interested and motivated by public service, particularly through the judiciary,” and she thinks “partisan politics really has no place in the courthouse.”
“Regardless of my personal, emotional feelings about what I think the law should say, or what might make it better, or what might make it worse, I’m quite comfortable with how to compartmentalize, how to honor the oath that any judge should take to simply interpret the law, rather than rewrite the law,” she said in a May interview.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Endorsements are a source of pride for O’Donnell, who told the Capital Journal before the primary that “endorsements can speak to the values of the candidate and of the endorsing agents.”
Recently on social media, she touted endorsements from Ohio’s Republican U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan, U.S. Rep. Dave Taylor, and U.S. Rep. Warren Davidson.

Absentee ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 2, received in a dropbox by Nov. 3, or received by the boards of elections by Nov. 7. Early voting occurs from Oct. 6 to Nov. 1.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A CT sheep farmer’s view from the solar field
description: A well-managed flock keeps vegetation under solar panels trimmed naturally, with minimal machinery, without pollution or the risk of damaged panels.
text:
Hillview Farm began in Ellington in 2014, built on a lifelong passion for animal agriculture. Sheep proved to be the most sustainable livestock we raised, but growing the operation meant finding affordable pasture, and that proved to be the central challenge.
We quickly outgrew the resources we had to make our farm profitable. Sheep, being a ruminant; thrive on pasture as they were born to graze all day and convert that grass into energy – not be fed grain and hay inside barns or on dry lots. Finding access to affordable pasture was cost prohibitive. Larger farms typically control the available farmland, and pastures we could access were often overgrown and in poor condition. Small farms simply cannot compete with larger entities.

Hillview Farm sheep grazing at a CT solar installation

Like many small farmers in this state, we spent nearly as much time worrying about margins as we did caring for our flock. Without access to pasture it made no sense to keep the flock, let alone expand. Even though demand for lamb and breeding stock continued, we couldn’t keep absorbing costs of production and expansion.
That started to change when we began working with solar developers to graze our sheep on land hosting photovoltaic arrays. Today, more than a decade into running Hillview Farm, our operation has grown dramatically, from starting out with just shy of a dozen sheep to the more than 130 in our flock today and plans to expand to over 300 head seasonally. This arrangement has proven valuable not just for us, but for Connecticut agriculture as a whole.
How solar grazing works, and why it works well 
The concept is straightforward. Ground-mounted solar panels require vegetation management beneath and between them. Uncontrolled grass and brush can shade panels, reduce efficiency, and increase maintenance costs. Traditionally, developers hired mowing crews, which is both expensive and pollution-generating. Flying rocks and debris can also crack panels, creating costly damage.
Sheep solve many of these issues. A well-managed flock keeps vegetation trimmed naturally, with minimal machinery, without pollution, and without the risk of damaged panels. The sheep graze, preferring the shaded panels which traditionally are the most difficult area to manage vegetation; the developer gets reliable, low-cost vegetation management; and we receive a per-acre fee for the service on top of what we earn from our animals, reinvested each year in equipment and improved management.
There are benefits for the sheep too. The shade provided by solar panels reduces heat stress on the flock during summer months, which supports better weight gain and animal welfare. Forage quality under the panels is often superior to open-field forage, with research showing significantly higher protein content in grass grown beneath arrays. Each site has a forage blend planted that is specifically selected for its nutritional value, added plant species that also support pollinators and improve soil structure. Our animals are thriving, and Hillview Farm is more financially stable than it has ever been.
The partnership with landowners matters
Some of the solar sites we work on are leased by developers from farm families who have worked the land for generations. These are landowners who embraced solar because they needed economic breathing room.  A 25- or 30-year solar lease provides reliable income during a period when commodity prices are volatile and input costs keep rising. But many of these families want to know that their land is still producing something and is still connected to agriculture.
Our presence on these properties gives them that. When a landowner sees our flock grazing where their grandparents once hayed, that means something. It is not a compromise. It is a continuation. We take seriously the responsibility of being good stewards on those sites, and the landowners we work with appreciate knowing that the land is not simply sitting under panels collecting dust.
The land comes back healthier 
People should understand what happens to farmland at the end of a solar project. Most arrays have a useful life of 25 to 30 years, after which the land is returned. The question is: returned to what condition?
Research conducted at commercial solar sites across the Northeast found that grazed solar sites showed significantly higher soil organic matter, soil protein, and active carbon than non-grazed sites. Sheep improve soil through natural fertilization and rotational grazing practices. When these projects conclude, land that has been carefully grazed throughout the solar lease should be well-positioned to support row crops, hay production, or other agricultural uses, potentially in better condition than when the panels went in. Connecticut-specific data remains limited, which is why the agrivoltaics study now mandated by state law matters so much.
House Bill 5340, passed by the legislature this spring, includes an agrivoltaics feasibility study to be completed by January 1, 2027. How many acres, how many farmers, what the economic impact looks like: none of that exists in organized form for Connecticut yet. The study aims to change that, and we are grateful that state leaders are investing the time to better understand this growing dimension of Connecticut agriculture.
Agriculture does not look the same as it did 50 years ago, and it should not have to. Embracing new models, including grazing sheep under solar panels, does not diminish farming, it sustains it. Our thriving flock, and the growth of Hillview Farm, are proof of that.
Natalie Cohen is the owner of Hillview Farm in Ellington.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Before you vote, learn Duverger’s Law
description: Democrats and Republicans both benefit from a structure that enables their duopoly by disadvantaging emerging competitors.
text:
Do you consider yourself an informed voter? If so, understanding Duverger’s Law can empower you to make strategic choices in upcoming elections, including the November midterms, regardless of your party affiliation.
In many undergraduate American Politics 101 courses, students learn that the United States has a “two-party system.” They study the histories of the Democratic and Republican parties, the shifting coalitions each has represented, their partisans’ general policy preferences, and the ideological differences between them. Yet considerably less attention is given to the electoral mechanics that preserve the dominance of these two large parties.
So-called “third parties,” of course, are not outlawed from participating in the democratic processes of our constitutional republic. They may nominate candidates, organize supporters, appear on ballots, and compete for public office. Why, then, have third parties so consistently remained minor parties?
The obdurate U.S. party “duopoly” does not endure because the electorate naturally sorts itself into two tidy political camps. On the contrary, the national motto, e pluribus unum (“out of many, one”), describes a nation forged in the crucible of profound social, cultural, and political diversity —not one whose individual citizens have ever fit squarely into two partisan categories. 
This diversity is currently reflected, at least partly, in Americans’ growing reluctance to identify with either major party. Gallup reported in January that a record-high 45% of American adults identified as political independents in 2025, including 56% of Gen Z (born between 1997 and 2007) and 54% of Millennials (born between 1981 and 1996). Although many of these self-identified independents still lean toward one of the two major parties, these figures hardly suggest widespread attachment to the existing partisan choices.
The continued dominance of only two nationally viable parties, then, cannot be explained solely by voter satisfaction, tradition, political culture, or media coverage. Instead, it is sustained and continually reinforced by the rules under which U.S. voters elect their public officials.
This is where Duverger’s Law, named for the French political scientist Maurice Duverger (1917–2014), offers valuable insight into one of the most durable patterns in electoral politics: single-member districts using plurality voting tend to produce competition between two major parties.
Let us begin unpacking this claim because, in its compressed form, it sounds much more complicated and perhaps less intuitive than it actually is.
Duverger developed his principle during the mid-20th century, most famously in his 1951 book Les Partis Politiques, published in English in 1954 as Political Parties. Under plurality voting in single-member districts (also called first-past-the-post or choose-one voting), the candidate who receives more votes than any other candidate wins, even without securing an absolute majority. In a four-candidate race, for instance, a candidate could win with only 35% of the vote if their opponents received 30%, 20%, and 15%, respectively.
At this point, the word “law” may still create some confusion. Duverger’s Law is not a legal rule enacted by a legislature or an electoral management body, nor is it an exceptionless iron command comparable to a mathematical certainty. Rather, it is a scientific law in the social-scientific sense: a concise statement describing a repeatedly observed relationship between particular conditions and a likely result.
Scientific laws identify regular patterns, but they do not necessarily imply that every individual case will unfold identically. Newton’s law of gravitation, for example, continues to describe the gravitational attraction between objects even when other forces, such as air resistance, affect their motion. Duverger’s Law likewise identifies a persistent tendency in certain electoral systems while allowing for exceptions arising from regional parties, unusual political divisions, electoral alliances, or other institutional arrangements.
Duverger’s central prediction thus remains remarkably useful for understanding U.S. electoral politics and the two-party system. Within this system, we have the following conditions: a) only one candidate can win a district, and b) victory requires only a plurality of votes (as described above, despite our majoritarian intuitions about electoral fairness, a candidate need not receive more than 50% of the vote to win). The result: political competition usually consolidates around two viable choices.
The logic hinges on two related forces.
The first is a mechanical effect. In “winner-take-all” elections, such as the presidential contests in nearly every state under the Electoral College, finishing second, even by a slim margin, yields no electoral votes from that state. Similarly, a political party could receive 40% of the vote in every single-member congressional district and still win no seats. Its support would be substantial but insufficient to secure office, as it never finished first.
Proportional representation, one of the most widely used electoral systems among democratic nations today, works differently. If a party receives 15% of the vote under a genuinely proportional system, it may receive approximately 15% of the seats, typically through multi-member districts. Winner-take-all elections in single-member districts provide no comparable reward or representation.
The second force is a psychological effect. Voters, candidates, donors, and political organizations anticipate the mechanical effect and adjust their behavior accordingly. For example, voters may strategically vote for a major-party candidate to avoid “wasting their vote,” and candidates may align with one of the two major parties to increase their chances of winning, thereby reinforcing the two-party system.
For this reason, promising candidates often join one of the two major parties rather than build a new one. Donors follow suit, hesitating to support campaigns regarded as incapable of winning from the get-go. Journalists concentrate on the two leading candidates. Voters may even abandon a preferred third candidate in favor of a less-preferred but more viable alternative.
The result becomes a self-reinforcing dialectic. Third parties struggle because voters doubt their viability, while voters doubt their viability because third parties struggle.
The 2000 presidential election provides the most famous example of Duverger’s Law at work in the United States. George W. Bush’s certified margin over Al Gore in Florida was just 537 votes (roughly 0.009%) of the nearly six million votes cast in the state. Because Bush finished first under Florida’s winner-take-all rules, he received all 25 of the state’s electoral votes.
Meanwhile, Green Party candidate Ralph Nader received 97,488 votes (1.64%) of the statewide total —far more than Bush’s margin of victory. If one assumes that most Green Party voters were ideologically to the left of the Democratic Party and hence preferred Gore to Bush, their votes for Nader may have helped elect the candidate they preferred least. In other words, voting for their first choice may have actually contributed to their least-preferred outcome. This is commonly known as the “spoiler effect,” in which support for a candidate with little to no chance of winning changes the outcome between the leading candidates.
Nevertheless, it would be inaccurate to claim that every Nader voter would otherwise have supported Gore. Some would have voted for Bush, chosen another candidate, or simply stayed home. The election also notoriously involved ballot-design problems, disputed recount procedures, voter-access controversies, and the Supreme Court’s consequential 5–4 decision in Bush v. Gore (2000).
Still, Florida demonstrates the strategic risk created by plurality voting. When only a few hundred votes separate two leading candidates, support for a third candidate can help determine which of the leading candidates wins —even when that third candidate has no realistic path to victory. Moreover, the ultimate victor may be further removed from third-party voters’ political preferences than the major-party candidate they chose not to support.
The 2016 election supplied another example. Donald Trump defeated Hillary Clinton in the swing state of Michigan by a margin of 10,704 votes (0.23%). Green Party candidate Jill Stein received 51,463 votes (1.07%) of the nearly 5 million votes cast in the state, while Libertarian Party candidate Gary Johnson received 172,136 votes (3.59%). The Michigan ballot also included candidates from the U.S. Taxpayers’ Party and Michigan’s Natural Law Party, who together received less than 0.40% of the statewide vote.
Those third-party voters by no means belonged to Clinton. Nor can analysts assign all the possibly right-leaning Libertarian votes to Trump. The figures instead reveal the razor’s edge upon which presidential elections may be decided.
Of course, the strategic problem can affect either major party.
In 2020, Joe Biden defeated Trump by 10,457 votes (0.3%) in Arizona, 11,779 votes (0.23%) in Georgia, and 20,682 votes (0.63%) in Wisconsin. Libertarian Party candidate Jo Jorgensen received more votes than Biden’s margin in each of those states.
Again, one cannot assume that every Libertarian voter would have chosen Trump in a two-candidate race. Yet a voter deciding among a favored third-party candidate, an acceptable major-party candidate, and an unacceptable major-party candidate should understand the possible consequences. The worst consequence is helping elect the candidate the voter opposes most.
Be that as it may, Duverger’s Law does not prove that third-party voting is foolish, immoral, or illegitimate. In a political system animated by deliberation, third-party campaigns can introduce neglected ideas, pressure major parties, provide political homes for dissatisfied citizens, and build organizations for future elections.
A protest vote can also serve a defensible purpose. Some voters use the ballot not merely to select an officeholder but to register opposition to the available choices. In a state or district where the outcome is virtually certain, the immediate risk of a “spoiler candidate” may be small. However, in a closely contested election, such a vote may be criticized as politically reckless or insufficiently attentive to its likely consequences. Indeed, some political scientists might call this sort of sincere voting behavior “naive” rather than “strategic.”
Therefore, voters should distinguish between two different uses of a ballot.
An expressive vote says, “This candidate most closely represents my beliefs.”
A strategic vote asks, “Which available choice gives me the best chance of producing an acceptable outcome or preventing an unacceptable one?”
Sometimes the same candidate satisfies both purposes. Sometimes the voter must choose between them.
Someone whose highest priority is building a third party may rationally vote for a candidate who is unlikely to win. Someone whose highest priority is defeating a particular major-party candidate, however, is better off voting for the most viable alternative.
This argument offers no defense of either major party. But it does explain why many voters feel as though they are stuck choosing between “the lesser of two evils.” Democrats and Republicans both benefit from a structure that enables their duopoly by disadvantaging emerging competitors. Yet both have also lost close elections in which minor-party candidates attracted potentially pivotal votes.
Now, Connecticut voters reading this in anticipation of August 11 should note that Duverger’s classic model does not apply as neatly to party primaries. Plurality primaries may encourage strategic voting: a voter may support a second-choice candidate if the preferred candidate appears unlikely to defeat a disliked rival. At the same time, crowded primaries may sustain several competing ideological or regional factions within the same party, making the outcome much harder to predict.
Americans who want more than two viable parties in general elections, however, need not wait for millions of partisan voters to become more adventurous. They can change the electoral rules that sustain the two-party structure.
Ranked-choice voting allows citizens to rank candidates in order of preference. A voter can support a third-party candidate first while identifying an acceptable major-party candidate as a backup. If the first-choice candidate is eliminated, the ballot transfers to the next-ranked candidate. This approach can reduce the spoiler problem, although it does not guarantee the development of a multiparty system.
Proportional representation offers a more direct route. Legislators may be elected from multi-member districts, with seats distributed according to each party’s share of the vote. A party winning 40% or 15% of the vote could then gain meaningful representation rather than repeatedly finishing second or third and receiving no representation at all.
Other reforms could include runoff elections, easier ballot access, more inclusive debates, fusion voting, and public financing to support competitive campaigns by political outsiders.
Connecticut already has experience with one alternative, namely “cross-endorsement” or “fusion voting.” Under this system, a minor party may endorse the same candidate as a major party while maintaining its own ballot line. For example, a voter can support the Working Families Party, the Independent Party, or another qualifying organization without splitting the total vote received by the endorsed candidate. The Connecticut State Elections Enforcement Commission (SEEC) also administers the Citizens’ Election Program, “allowing candidates to compete without reliance on special interest money.” That said, while such arrangements demonstrate that the current system is neither natural nor inevitable, they do little to create a genuinely competitive multiparty democracy in which third-party candidates have a realistic chance of winning office and their supporters have a meaningful chance of gaining representation.
In a word, electoral systems shape political behavior. Winner-take-all plurality elections reward large coalitions capable of finishing first and punish smaller organizations whose support is widely dispersed. Voters respond to those incentives whether they recognize Duverger’s Law or not.
Still, before entering the voting booth, voters should ask more than, “Which candidate do I like best?” They should also ask, “What am I trying to accomplish with this vote, and how do the rules translate my choice into political power?”
Duverger’s Law cannot answer that question for them. But it can help them understand the decision they are making.
Robert T.F. Downes is a PhD candidate in the Department of Political Science at the University of Connecticut, specializing in political theory and public law. He is also an Adjunct Professor at Rhode Island College.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Harford County residents fight back against battery storage proposal
description: Officials in Maryland’s Harford County say they’re concerned by a proposal to add a battery storage to a hillside along the “pristine” Deer Creek, a tributary to the Susquehanna River.
text:
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) speaks during a news conference Thursday encouraging the state to advance battery storage projects. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Harford County officials and residents say they’re concerned by a proposal to add a utility-scale battery storage facility to a hillside along the “pristine” Deer Creek, a tributary to the Susquehanna River.
Their testimony came Thursday as regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission reviewed four battery storage projects for eligibility for a new credit, created by state lawmakers in 2025. The other projects are planned on the site of a solar project near Westernport in Garrett County, at the Chalk Point power plant in Prince George’s County and at the former Dickerson coal-fired power station in Montgomery County.
But only the Harford project, a 500-megawatt proposal called the Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project, drew opposition Thursday, with critics citing concerns about fire risk and related environmental contamination.
“Environmentally, you would struggle to find a worse site for this project,” said Jennifer Wilson, a resident who said her children attend the nearby Norrisville Elementary School.
The mostly forested site already hosts Baltimore Gas & Electric’s Conastone Substation, located in the northwestern corner of Harford County. A representative from Tenaska, the company developing the project, said Thursday that the facility would be located at least 600 feet from the waterway, and that most of the 70 acres would remain forested.
Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly (R) also opposes the project, he said in an interview with Maryland Matters, particularly given that the beloved creek — a favorite kayaking spot for him and his family — is located downhill. He worried that firefighters would have trouble fighting any blazes at the site nestled behind the substation, and that any chemicals used for firefighting, or contained within the battery facility itself, would flow down into the river.
Harford County Executive Robert Cassilly (R). (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“If anything goes wrong with this thing, it goes right down into the Deer Creek,” Cassilly said in an interview. “This is a cherished waterway that feeds the water supply.”
In testimony to the commission, Matthew Kropp, director of Harford County’s planning and zoning department, expressed worries that “toxic heavy metals and chemicals” in the battery infrastructure could leach into the soil or water, and that local fire departments lacked “the training, knowledge and resources to deal with a potential emergency.” He worried that the proposal did not contain sufficient measures to contain a fire or other emergency.
A representative for Del. Lauren Arikan (R-Harford) also said at Thursday’s hearing that her office has gathered 1,300 signatures opposing the project near Deer Creek.
Lee Hine, who lives about a half mile from the proposed project, said he was surprised by its location, given the hilly terrain in a prized natural area.
“The watershed is a prime aspect of why we all moved to this area. It’s a natural preserve here,” Hine said. “I’m trying to understand why we’re not looking for ‘brown ground’ facility areas — or at least flatter areas. This is a mountain. We live on a mountain.”
Keith Latham, who leads battery storage development at Tenaska, said the company plans to use lithium-ion-phosphate batteries, a safer alternative to lithium-ion batteries, and house them in purpose-built enclosures complete with cooling systems.
“Additionally, code standards and best practices have also greatly reduced risk of issues in newer battery storage projects. As we move forward through the development process, we’ll also collaborate with local fire departments and the fire marshal. We’ll work with the first responders on an emergency response plan,” Latham said.
But residents also questioned the project’s cost-effectiveness. A study performed for the PSC found that the Oystercatcher project, the largest by megawatts, did not produce quite enough ratepayer benefit to equal the cost, using two different estimation models.
“I ask the commission to reject this project based on the fact that it doesn’t provide economic relief to BGE ratepayers, and it’s certainly going to put the ecosystem of Harford County at great risk,” Patti Hankins said at the meeting.
Even if one of the projects considered Thursday receives the credits, it still must receive construction approvals from the commission, according to a news release from the commission.
The PSC hearing came hours after a Baltimore news conference, during which environmental groups, unions and a few Democratic politicians extolled the benefits of battery storage technology, which can store extra power for four hours or more and release it to the grid later on. They argued, too, that some safety concerns may be overstated.
Adam Dubitsky, state director for the Maryland Land & Liberty coalition, speaks in support of battery energy storage projects during a news conference Thursday. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Adam Dubitsky, state director for the Maryland Land & Liberty coalition, a conservative nonprofit supporting renewable energy development, said much of the opposition is based on “outdated information about these systems.”
“They are safe when done right, and when firefighters know how to fight these fires — which is very possible — in the rare times when there is an incident,” Dubitsky said.
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) said any approved project must adhere to the National Fire Protection Association standards, which require separation between battery units to prevent fires from spreading between batteries.
“I understand that when new technology is coming to communities, people are asking questions — totally appropriate for folks to do that,” Charkoudian said during Thursday’s news conference. “It’s just really important that we don’t add to fear-mongering, and we make sure people have the accurate information about the things that keep batteries 100% safe.”
During Thursday’s PSC hearing, John Walser, a fire protection consultant at Fire & Risk Alliance, argued that fires at battery energy sites have become increasingly rare as safety standards have improved.
“This reduction is due to the lessons learned from early failures,” he said, including fires at other battery storage facilities.
At Thursday’s news conference, environmentalists largely focused on the overall benefits of battery storage. It’s particularly important now, they said, as residents face high power bills and the grid faces high demand from data centers and electrification, amid reductions in supply due to the retirement of some fossil fuel generators.
“For most of the history of the electrical grid, if someone flipped on a light switch, a power plant somewhere had to produce those electrons at virtually the same time. But battery storage is changing that,” said Rico Albacarys, political director for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 24. “It allows us to store electricity when it’s plentiful and the costs are less, and then deliver it back to the grid when demand is highest.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Maryland possesses very little utility-scale, battery storage connected to the transmission grid, Charkoudian said. That’s why the General Assembly stepped in last year with the Next Generation Energy Act, requiring the PSC to open a battery storage procurement for up to 1,600 megawatts. This year, the legislature extended the megawatt limit, as long as cost effectiveness requirements are met.
The facilities can also reduce emissions during high-demand situations, by avoiding the need for fossil fuel “peaker” plants to come online, said Rebecca Rehr of the Maryland League of Conservation Voters.
“Storage reduces reliance on the most expensive, most polluting, and harmful peaker plants that run only during the periods of highest demand,” Rehr said.
Still, the risks concern residents of Norrisville, the small town closest to the Oystercatcher project. Nancy Gladden, who said Thursday she moved to the “blink and you miss it” town in 1984, is concerned that battery projects are unproven, and their safety for the community “highly questionable.”
“We are surrounded by hills and beautiful rolling cornfields and meadows,” Gladden said. “It’s an idyllic place full of homes, happy kids, and wonderful outdoors for them to explore and grow up in. I’m commenting tonight because I’m concerned for the community — for my community.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore offers late admission, $800 credit for students disenrolled at Howard University
description: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Thursday the state would provide an $800 credit and expedited admission processing for any of the hundreds of incoming Howard University freshmen who were abruptly told last week that they no longer had a place at the school.
text:
The "M Circle" on the University of Maryland, College Park's campus. (Photo by Sam Gauntt/Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Thursday the state would provide an $800 credit and expedited admission processing for any of the hundreds of incoming Howard University freshmen who were abruptly told last week that they no longer had a place at the school.
The governor said in a statement that he directed the Maryland Higher Education Commission and the University System of Maryland to expedite the admission process for any of the affected students for the fall semester. The process will include identifying available programs, navigating financial aid and expediting late admissions available at the more than dozen colleges, universities and higher education centers in the state’s system.
First day of classes for schools in the state system start next month.
The offer is aimed at 502 incoming freshmen in Howard’s first-time-in-college program who were told last week that because they had not met payment or other financial reporting requirements for classes that start Aug. 17, they had been disenrolled.
“Students who did not meet the established payment, payment arrangement, or scholarship and other financial aid reporting deadlines have been notified that the University can no longer hold their place in the incoming class,” the school said in a statement July 23. “As Howard finalizes enrollment for the Fall 2026 semester … confirming enrollment is essential to planning academic programs, housing, financial aid, and student support services.”
State workers union sues Moore, university system for withheld raises

The notice left students, many of whom said they were waiting on scholarships or financial aid to clear, scrambling for options. As of Wednesday, more than 200 students had been reenrolled after they provided documentation, or the university reevaluated their paperwork, Howard President Wayne Frederick said to WTOP.
In the meantime, the University of the District of Columbia said Monday that it had extended its application deadline to Aug. 7.
On Tuesday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said the state would provide affected Howard students an $800 credit, and she directed the State University of New York (SUNY) and the City University of New York (CUNY) to expedite the late admissions review process for those students.
Moore on Thursday posted a message on social media telling the “hundreds of student disenrolled from Howard University just weeks before move-in, I want you to know this: Maryland, we’ve got your back.”
“These students worked hard, earned admission to college, and were preparing to begin the next chapter of their lives,” Moore said in the statement released by his office. “Maryland is moving with urgency to give them a clear path forward — with hands-on support, expedited admissions assistance, and financial relief – so they can stay on track toward earning their degree.”
Moore said the $800 credit was meant to offset a nonrefundable deposit the students made to Howard. If at least 250 students chose to accept the $800 credit, it would cost the state about $200,000.
A Moore spokesperson said in a text message Thursday information about the funding could come from the higher education commission Friday.
The affected students interested in applying to a college or university in Maryland can contact the Office of Student Financial Assistance (OFSA) at osfamail.mhec@maryland.gov.
“The University System of Maryland is committed to helping these displaced students,” University System of Maryland Chancellor Jay Perman said in a statement. “Our goal is to help these students continue with their education with as little interruption as possible.”
