name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Secretary of State agrees to turn over voter death error records following lawsuit
description: The New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office agreed earlier this month to release records related to state voters erroneously labeled as deceased, following a lawsuit from a national foundation that has filed similar lawsuits against states across the country.
text:
The New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office on July 13, 2026, settled a lawsuit with the Public Interest Legal Foundation to turn over records regarding voters erroneously being labeled dead in state voter rolls. (Photo by Leah Romero/Source NM)The New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office agreed earlier this month to release records related to state voters erroneously labeled as deceased, following a lawsuit from a national foundation that has filed similar lawsuits against states across the country. 
The Public Interest Legal Foundation filed a lawsuit in June after the Secretary of State did not produce records that would show how often and how quickly the state corrected its voter rolls upon learning it had erroneously deemed a voter as deceased. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Central to the lawsuit is the Electronic Registration Information Center, also known as ERIC, which New Mexico and 27 other states use to share information regarding voters who have moved or died. ERIC notifies New Mexico and other states when it learns, primarily through the federal Social Security Administration, that a voter has died. ERIC also notifies states if it later learns that state election systems wrongly marked voters as deceased.
A report last week from the national nonprofit think tank Brennan Center for Justice characterized the Public Interest Legal Foundation as a critic of ERIC and as “long a promoter of misleading claims about the breadth of errors on voting rolls.” 
The report notes that so-called “election integrity” organizations have targeted ERIC in legal challenges intended to destroy it and “replace it with something weaker.” 
But Logan Churchwell, the foundation’s research director, told Source NM in a recent interview that the lawsuits are simply trying to understand better how states deal with deceased residents on voter rolls. 
“It’s early days, but the goal is to understand not just how many people, but how long does it take to get corrected?” he said. “And if there is a significant gap between the correction and them being re-established, are they missing opportunities to vote?”
Churchwell declined to provide Source NM with the records his foundation successfully sued over, saying he was still analyzing them. 
Churchwell’s foundation also successfully sued Arizona and Oregon for its ERIC-related death records, according to a news release. 
The Secretary of State’s Office also did not provide Source NM the full list of records, but did provide an “example” of three voter records. 
The records show that three voters — two in Doña Ana County, one in Lea County — were erroneously declared dead between September 2020 and May 2021. The state restored all three to the voting rolls by early December of 2021.
Brennan Center report predicts mass voter challenges likely in midterm elections

In an interview this week with Source NM, New Mexico State Elections Director Mandy Vigil defended the state’s participation in ERIC, which has access to federal death records that the state does not, as well as the state’s efforts more broadly to maintain accurate voter rolls. 
She also said the risk is “extremely low” of anyone wrongly deemed deceased being prohibited from voting. 
If a voter wrongly listed as deceased tries to vote, Vigil said, they can file a provisional ballot. Doing so gives the state the opportunity to “research and get it right” while preserving a voter’s right to cast a ballot. 
“Based on the controls and the system that has been built over time, I just don’t think PILF is accurately reflecting the realities of how it works,” she said. “I think they’re attempting to create this idea that these corrections are unusual, widespread or significant in a way that people should be concerned. I don’t share that sentiment.”
Vigil cited an “administrative error” for the state’s failure to quickly provide the records the foundation requested. But she stressed that the state never refused to produce the records and produced them in full during the litigation. 
The records do not include Social Security numbers or other sensitive personal information like dates of birth. 
Churchwell’s foundation also successfully sued Arizona and Oregon for its ERIC-related death records, according to a news release. 
Federal judge dismisses USDOJ lawsuit seeking New Mexico voter rolls

The July 13 settlement agreement between the Secretary of State’s Office and the foundation requires the state to maintain each “deceased retraction” record it creates for at least two years. The state also agreed to release the records upon request as required under the federal National Voter Registration Act. 
The settlement agreement also required the state to pay the foundation roughly $2,800 in legal fees. 
Vigil said she hopes New Mexicans maintain their faith in the state’s election security despite efforts from the foundation to “sow doubt in the integrity of elections.”
“We’re highly ranked in the country for a good reason, and so [voters] should feel confident in their ability to participate,” Vigil said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: U.S. Rep. Scanlon makes unannounced visit to ICE’s Moshannon Valley Processing Center
description: Scanlon (D-5th District) told the Capital-Star she spent about four hours inside the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, a former federal prison with nearly 1,900 beds, near Philipsburg, Clearfield County.
text:
Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., on the steps of the U.S. House of Representatives on Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Nearly one year after she and other members of Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation were turned away, U.S. Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon said she was allowed Wednesday to inspect the largest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center on the east coast.
Scanlon (D-5th District) told the Capital-Star she spent about four hours inside the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, a former federal prison with nearly 1,900 beds, near Philipsburg, Clearfield County.
The center has been the subject of criticism by immigrant rights advocates and lawmakers who say detainees are subjected to inhumane conditions, lack adequate access to health care and face retaliation for complaints. It was also the site of two deaths last year.
Scanlon said she came away from the visit frustrated that she was not generally permitted to speak to detainees, although she was able to meet with a constituent. She said she’s also concerned that the central Pennsylvania facility appears to function largely using the labor of people involuntarily held there. Detainees can earn $1 a day for working, she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Why are we jailing, essentially, people who are not a danger to our communities, who are in many cases contributing members to our economy and our communities, folks who are employed and are paying taxes? Why are these folks being put in a prison setting?” Scanlon asked in an interview Thursday.
During her visit, officials told her the center housed 1,634 detainees, of whom 1,311 are “low security.” The detainees wear color-coded uniforms and lack liberty to move freely around the facility, she added. 
“This is not supposed to be punitive, but it’s pretty hard to say that this is anything but,” Scanlon said.
The Moshannon Valley center is operated on behalf of ICE by a private company under a contract with Clearfield County. That allows ICE to skirt a Biden-era ban on new federal contracts with private prison companies. The county pays for-profit prison operator The GEO Group to run the center.
ICE did not respond to an email seeking comment. 
The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Farmville Detention Center in Virginia, pictured in December 2019. (Photo: Screenshot of ICE courtesy video)
The GEO Group is an international provider of correctional services that runs about 100 facilities globally, with a capacity of more than 80,000 beds. According to the American Civil Liberties Union, more than a quarter of GEO Group’s capacity is used by ICE.
Under a 2019 federal law, members of Congress are authorized to inspect ICE facilities without prior notice. At the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the agency began turning away lawmakers at facilities across the country. Scanlon and U.S. Rep. Summer Lee (D-12th District) were prevented from inspecting the facility last August. 
Since then, a group of lawmakers sued ICE over the policy, asking the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to order the Trump administration to explain how it did not violate federal law. The court issued an order in December, affirming the authority of Congress members to conduct oversight of ICE facilities. 
Lee and U.S. Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-17th District) were first to visit Moshannon Valley in May. 
Scanlon said Thursday that she was permitted to enter the women’s pods in the center but not the men’s, which she was able to see through glass. Scanlon said she was able to speak to a person from her suburban and south Philadelphia district but declined to discuss details to protect the person from retaliation. Other inmates were not permitted to speak to her, she said.
“It makes it difficult to … follow up on issues about food and medical care if you can’t talk to people who are impacted,” Scanlon said.
It was clear, she said, that the detainees are responsible for cleaning toilets, showers and living spaces.
“There are two janitors for the entire facility of 1,600 people, and then they showed me that they have like just a row of like five spray bottles of cleaning spray in each pod, and oh, it’s there for the detainees to use, and they like doing it,” Scanlon said. “I guess the alternative is squalor.”
She said an administrator at the center conceded that they could not run the food service or laundry without using detainee labor.

ICE withdraws appeal of Pa. environmental directives tied to warehouse purchases


“So we have the situation where people are being jailed and then forced to work essentially for free to maintain basic sanitation, food, etc,” Scanlon said, adding “It’s inhumane. It’s traumatizing, and it’s particularly grotesque because this is then being done so private prison companies can make more profit.”
Under the contract, ICE pays Clearfield County more than $4 million a month plus additional considerations for transportation, on-call staff and $1 a day per detainee for the employee work program. 
Scanlon said the oversight by Congress is important because she believes “we’re not getting straight scoop” from the Trump administration.
“The administration said they were going after the worst of the worst, and the people they are scooping up, and we’re seeing this increasingly are people on the way to work, or to school, or their court appointments to pursue their legal path,” she said.
With appropriations of $145 billion in the last two years, Scanlon said ICE is spending “outrageous amounts” detaining people who are not a threat to public safety. 
“We would be much better off if we were actually spending money to create a functioning immigration system,” Scanlon said, adding, “We don’t have that now, and it’s a misdirection of money just to put out these quotas and scoop up people, many of whom have legal status.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho reports three heat-related deaths amid hot, smoky weather
description: Three Idahoans over the age of 55 died from heat-related complications in the past week, state health officials announced Thursday.  The cluster of deaths — the first heat-related deaths reported in Idaho this year —  came as temperatures in the state were often above 90 degrees. Wildfires have also pushed most Idaho counties into air […]
text:
The three Idahoans who had heat-related deaths all lived in different communities in southern Idaho, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare announced. (Photo by Getty Images)Three Idahoans over the age of 55 died from heat-related complications in the past week, state health officials announced Thursday. 
The cluster of deaths — the first heat-related deaths reported in Idaho this year —  came as temperatures in the state were often above 90 degrees. Wildfires have also pushed most Idaho counties into air quality advisories recently, with some reaching thresholds classified as unhealthy. 
The three Idahoans who had heat-related deaths all lived in different communities in southern Idaho, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare announced in a news release. Officials did not clarify which specific areas of the vast region that the people who died lived in.
As temperatures rise, state health officials urge people to be aware of heat-related illness symptoms and treatments. Last year, 180 people died of heat-related illness in the U.S., the National Weather Service reports. 
 The signs of heat-related illness

Signs of a heatstroke — the most serious heat-related illness and a medical emergency — include high body temperature, hot and skin, confusion or seizures, nausea, dizziness and fainting, the state health department says. 
People experiencing these symptoms who cannot get medical care should call 911 immediately and move to a cooler place and use wet cloths or ice to lower body temperature, including applying them to the head, neck, armpits and groin or giving them a cool bath or soaking their clothes with cool water. People having a heat stroke should not drink, as they may accidentally inhale the fluid rather than swallowing it. 
Heat exhaustion may occur before a heatstroke, with symptoms like tiredness, weakness, irritability, thirst, headache, nausea, muscle cramps and cold, clammy skin. People with heat exhaustion symptoms should move to a cooler place, loosen clothes, use cool clothes or a cold bath and sip cool water frequently. If they vomit or symptoms worsen or last longer than an hour, seek medical help.
 How to prevent heat-related illness

Staying cool and hydrated is key. Here’s how:

Wear lightweight, loose-fitting clothing.
Limit outdoor activity to the coolest hours — in the morning and evening.
Drink at least one cup of water for every 15-20 minutes of moderate activity lasting less than two hours. Drink before you are thirsty. 
Avoid alcohol and drinks with high caffeine or sugar.
Drink a low-sugar sports drink to replace salt and minerals, which you lose through sweating. If you are on a low-salt diet, have diabetes, high blood pressure or other chronic conditions, talk to your doctor first.
Check weather reports on local news, weather.gov or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s extreme heat tracker, HeatRisk.
Read more heat health advice from the CDC.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC joins multi-state effort to combat fraud of taxpayers’ money
description: Investigators in those states have found more than $350 million in potential fraud, leading to charges in 17 cases.
text:
Gov. Henry McMaster, with Assistant U.S. Attorney General Colin McDonald on the left and SC Attorney General Alan Wilson on the right, talks about fraud cases during a news conference at the National Advocacy Center in Columbia, S.C., on Thursday, July 30, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina is among seven Southern states that have agreed to share data and resources to crack down on fraud cases, officials from those states and the federal government said Thursday.
Since President Donald Trump announced the creation of a Department of Justice division dedicated to rooting out fraud, prosecutors have found more than $350 million in potential misspending across 17 cases, according to the federal agency.


States in the task force:

Alabama
Florida
Georgia
Louisiana
Mississippi
North Carolina
South Carolina

Source: Department of Justice


The target is misuse of taxpayer dollars across agencies and purposes, said the two dozen U.S. attorneys and attorneys general in Columbia on Thursday. They met in Columbia this week for a discussion on how to fight fraud.
Though most of the officeholders are Republican, the group is bipartisan: North Carolina’s attorney general, Jeff Jackson, is a Democrat.
Recent cases included charges of falsifying tax returns to receive tax credits, stealing identities to get rent subsidies, and misusing grocery and health care assistance.
The public programs are important for helping those who need them, including people who are poor and who have disabilities, said South Carolina U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling.
“That is your money that these people are stealing,” Stirling said.
The attorneys general and U.S. attorneys’ offices will pool information and resources to make it easier and faster for prosecutors to find fraud and file charges, said Colin McDonald, assistant attorney general of the National Fraud Enforcement Division, at the news conference.
The secretaries of state from Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina, as well as the treasurers from Florida, Mississippi and South Carolina signed agreements saying they would share data as needed, according to the Department of Justice.
Many agencies already share information. For instance, South Carolina and North Carolina joined forces last year to charge 11 people with defrauding government health insurance in schemes that amounted to more than $23 million.
But there’s no requirement for agencies to share what they know or specifications about what they should give each other, McDonald said. Instead, agencies rely on “hero agents and hero prosecutors” to make sure cases are based on all the information, he said.
“We now have that ability to quarterback the field of fraud, to have the full field in view, so that we can know where we need resources, where is the data missing, and how can we plug those gaps,” McDonald said.
The ultimate goal is to stop fraud entirely and restore faith in public programs, McDonald said. For a long time, prosecutors have gone after individual fraud cases, but partnering will allow them to look at the bigger picture, he said.
“Instead of little bites at the problem, we are endeavoring to solve the entire problem by putting an emphasis on it, by putting out money where our mouth is, by resourcing this fight and by developing these partnerships,” he said.
People can and often do commit fraud in multiple places, raising questions over whose jurisdiction a crime falls into and requiring records from more than one state or agency, said Meg Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia.
“The fraudsters are not going to stop in Savannah, Georgia,” Heap said. “They’re going to cross into South Carolina. They’re going to go down to Florida. They’re going to go to North Carolina.”
Fraudsters often work in teams to dupe investigators, said South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson.
“Why should we do anything differently when we combat these schemes and these scams?” Wilson said. “We need to be collaborating. We need to be communicating.”
Gov. Henry McMaster likened the partnership to President Ronald Reagan’s drug enforcement task forces of the 1980s, when U.S. attorneys, including McMaster, joined forces to track down drug smugglers. McMaster’s early ’80s crackdown on illegal smuggling of marijuana and hashish into the Lowcountry, called Operation Jackpot, resulted in more than 100 convictions. (A movie loosely based on the operation, produced and directed by one of the so-called gentlemen smugglers, was released last year.)
The new collaboration will give agencies “the power and sustainability to get this done,” McMaster said.
One of the 17 recent cases came from South Carolina. Misty Woody, an employee with ambulance service Vital Care was charged with forging a doctor’s signature on more than 100 forms for patients no longer under that doctor’s care, amounting to an estimated $1.8 million in false billing, according to the Department of Justice.
Woody pleaded not guilty, according to court records. Her attorney declined to comment.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lawsuit: Iowa worker stranded in Canada for a year due to visa-related delays
description: An Iowa man who alleges federal bureaucracy has left him stranded in Canada for a year, with no way to return to the United States, is now suing the federal government. Haider Raza, a citizen and national of Pakistan, is suing the U.S. Department of State in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of […]
text:
A Pakistani immigrant living in Iowa says in a federal lawsuit that delays in processing his visa-related application to remain in the United States have stranded him in Canada for a year. (Photo by Peter Dazeley/Getty Images)An Iowa man who alleges federal bureaucracy has left him stranded in Canada for a year, with no way to return to the United States, is now suing the federal government.
Haider Raza, a citizen and national of Pakistan, is suing the U.S. Department of State in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa for alleged delays in processing his visa-related application to remain in the United States.
Raza, 32, of Ames, works for Kingland Systems at the company’s headquarters in Clear Lake. In his lawsuit, he indicates he first arrived in America 11 years ago through a student visa, then attended Iowa State University where he received both a bachelor’s and master’s degree.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
After graduating, Raza was granted “H-1B status” — a temporary, employer-sponsored classification that allows foreign nationals to work in specialized fields within the United States — and, in October 2021, began working for Kingland Systems.
In 2024, Raza sought to extend his H-1B status for another three years. Visa requests by foreign nationals are adjudicated through the Department of State’s Bureau of Consular Affairs at U.S. embassies and consulates abroad. Because of that, the lawsuit alleges, Raza traveled to Canada last year and while there attended a visa-application interview at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto on Aug. 5, 2025.
At that time, the lawsuit claims, Raza was informed that his application would be placed in “administrative processing.” In the almost 12 months since then, the lawsuit alleges, the application has remained pending with no action taken.
The lack of action has left Raza “unable to return to the United States,” which has resulted in his being placed on unpaid leave from his job in Iowa.
“Despite numerous attempts to contact the consulate about the status of his visa,” the lawsuit alleges, Raza “continues to await the defendants’ action after almost a year of delay. … (He) left the United States to travel to Toronto, attend this routine interview, and receive a visa stamp with the expectation that he would soon return and resume his job and life.”
According to the lawsuit, Raza has inquired several times about the status of his application, and that he was initially told the process would take “several months” before being told the consulate was “unable to determine when this process may be concluded.”
Through Kingland Systems, the lawsuit alleges, Raza has enlisted the assistance of three members of Congress, all of whom have only been told the application remains in administrative processing.
Raza, the lawsuit states, “has no criminal history and no immigration violations whatsoever. He received a single traffic ticket in the United States, which … would not preclude the grant of a visa or cause the present delay. (He) cannot re-enter the United States absent a visa stamp and has been on unpaid leave from his U.S.-based job since October 15, 2025. He has encountered significant emotional and financial hardship as a result of the ongoing uncertainty relating to his work status … He remains in a state of limbo.”
The situation has made it difficult for Raza to fulfill his financial commitments in both Canada and the United States and also made it impossible for him to visit his Iowa-based physician and dentist, the lawsuit alleges.
The lawsuit seeks to have the court intervene and compel the U.S. Department of State to act on Raza’s application. The department has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.

title: NC Auditor’s office in public records fight over Dallas Woodhouse’s work
description: A left-leaning nonprofit says North Carolina Auditor Dave Boliek’s office is failing to comply with the state’s public records laws in the wake of the resignation of its controversial former employee.  After the nonprofit organization, American Oversight, filed public records requests with the state Auditor’s office for communications to and from then-electi[...]
text:
9th Congressional district candidate Mark Harris talks seriously with state Republican Party Executive Director Dallas Woodhouse in 2019 during a break after his son, John Harris, started to testify Wednesday at a hearing that will determine if his election is certified or not. (Photo: Melissa Boughton/NC Newsline)A left-leaning nonprofit says North Carolina Auditor Dave Boliek’s office is failing to comply with the state’s public records laws in the wake of the resignation of its controversial former employee. 
After the nonprofit organization, American Oversight, filed public records requests with the state Auditor’s office for communications to and from then-elections liaison Dallas Woodhouse, the group said it had not received Woodhouse texts that news reports had revealed. 
Wesleigh Stout, the Auditor’s office general counsel, said in a July 24 letter to American Oversight, reviewed by NC Newsline, that the office did not know about Woodhouse’s texts before they appeared in the news. 
The Auditor’s office took the proper steps to comply with American Oversight’s request for public records, Stout told the group’s senior counsel Elizabeth Haddix. That included the legal affairs division asking Woodhouse if he had any records on his personal devices that the office should hand over. 
Last year, state Auditor Dave Boliek appointed Woodhouse, a political operative and former state Republican Party executive director, to a newly-created job as his liaison to county elections boards.
Earlier this month, Woodhouse moved from that job to another in Boliek’s office amid a wave of controversy over his text messages to Republican county chairs about early voting sites and early voting dates. 
For example, Woodhouse texted the Jackson County elections board Chair Bill Thompson, “Don’t let them have a vote,” the morning before that county’s board was scheduled to decide on early voting locations, NC Local reported. The vote went ahead and the board approved in a 3-1 vote a location on Western Carolina University’s campus that Republican members said they received “pressure from Raleigh” to reject.
A GOP county elections board member said he was warned against voting for a campus polling site

Woodhouse resigned from Boliek’s staff about a week after he left the liaison position.  
Stout told Haddix that because Woodhouse no longer works for Boliek, the office no longer has access to public records that may be on his personal devices. 
“Since Mr. Woodhouse is no longer an agency employee, OSA no longer has access to his personal devices or accounts and no longer has any means of accessing any public records that may be stored on such devices or accounts,” Stout wrote. 
In a letter Thursday, Haddix told Stout his response contradicts state law. 
A North Carolina Court of Appeals ruling says that government records stored by a third party are subject to disclosure under the state Public Records Act. The public records law also requires “all individuals with custody of any public records to, at the end of such individual’s term of public office, deliver those records to the individual’s successor in office, or if no successor exists, to the Department of Natural and Cultural Resources,” Haddix wrote. 
The Auditor’s office knew at least since June 6, when news broke about Woodhouse’s texts, that he was frequently texting about official business, Haddix wrote. Yet, the records sent to American Oversight on July 15 did not include those texts or other staff records the organization requested. 
“In light of these circumstances, the timing of Woodhouse’s abrupt resignation, coupled with the unsupported contention that your office can no longer seek access to Mr. Woodhouse’s devices and personal accounts, suggests bad faith,” Haddix wrote.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia state agencies told to freeze spending and draft contingency plans
description: Gov. Brian Kemp’s office has instructed Georgia state agencies to keep spending level as they prepare budget proposals ahead of next year’s legislative session. Kemp is term-limited and signed his final budget earlier this year, cutting more than $300 million in new spending at the time to help pay for an income tax cut package […]
text:
Gov. Brian Kemp announces $300 million in budget cuts on May 12, 2026. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderGov. Brian Kemp’s office has instructed Georgia state agencies to keep spending level as they prepare budget proposals ahead of next year’s legislative session.
Kemp is term-limited and signed his final budget earlier this year, cutting more than $300 million in new spending at the time to help pay for an income tax cut package that lawmakers passed earlier this year. 
The next budget will be signed by Georgia’s new governor, who could be healthcare executive Rick Jackson, a Republican, or former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, but state agencies must submit their budget request by Sept. 1, giving Kemp some control over the process in his final months in office.
Office of Planning and Budget director Richard Dunn wrote in a memo sent to agency heads earlier this month that the budget for the next fiscal year has to maintain the current fiscal year’s level. Requests for funding increases must be approved by Dunn’s office and will be limited to an “urgent, unavoidable need that cannot be addressed through internal redirection without negatively affecting essential service delivery,” according to the memo. 
Dunn touted the Kemp administration’s accomplishments but hinted at the uncertain economic conditions that await. As state agencies prepare their new spending plans, Georgia is also still bracing for the financial impacts of the federal tax and spending bill that passed last year. 
“To sustain these achievements while implementing historic tax relief for our citizens, responsible fiscal management principles require that we continue to live within our means,” Dunn wrote in the memo.
The guidance instructed agencies to plan to redirect their current funds for non-mandatory spending and new projects and to draft contingencies plans that identify “potential efficiencies and savings.” 
“While current revenue projections are expected to be sufficient to meet the state’s mandatory growth obligations, these plans help ensure the state can respond effectively to changing economic conditions or new budget priorities that require the reallocation of existing resources,” Dunn wrote. 
The move drew criticism from the left-leaning Georgia Budget and Policy Institute. According to GBPI, inflation over the past eight years means the state is currently spending less per resident despite budget growth. Organization chief Staci Fox criticized Kemp’s administration for prioritizing tax cuts that will decrease funding to the state’s future budgets instead of spending on healthcare and education.
“While Gov. Kemp has already unilaterally issued budget cuts that will harm the most vulnerable Georgians, the budget instructions issued for the 2027 legislative session make clear that our state cannot afford to continue prioritizing corporations and the wealthy at the expense of everyone else,” Fox said in a statement.
The guidance comes after an income tax cut bill Kemp signed into law earlier this year. The tax cut lowered the rate from 5.19% to 4.99% and exempted some overtime and tips from being taxed and caused a $1.3 billion revenue shortfall for next year’s budget. 
That led to the governor cutting $300 million in new spending to address the deficit, which included $9.3 million for services for people with disabilities and $30.7 million for transportation funding for schools. He said then that not cutting some of those new services would have left the next governor with a “mess.”

name: VTDigger
title: Dispute over evidence preservation heats up in border agent’s killing
description:
Among the items at issue are cellphones — both personal and government-issued — used by authorities during a traffic stop that turned deadly and the investigation that led up to it.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Dispute over evidence preservation heats up in border agent’s killing.
text:
Police cruiser lights. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A legal battle is brewing over cellphones and other devices used by law enforcement around the time of a shootout in which a federal agent was killed in northern Vermont.
Teresa Youngblut, 22, of Seattle, faces several charges, including murder, in the death of Border Patrol Agent David Maland during a traffic stop in January 2025 that turned into gunfire on Interstate 91 in Coventry.
With the trial still to be set, the prosecution this week pushed back against a defense motion seeking to preserve certain electronic devices and the information stored on them.
Youngblut’s attorneys earlier this month requested a court order requiring the prosecution “to secure, extract, and preserve full forensic copies of all cell phones or other devices — work, personal, or otherwise — used by officers and agents involved in the surveillance, stop, arrest, and shooting and the leadup to and aftermath of those events.” 
The order was needed, the filing argued, to prevent the devices or data from being destroyed or deleted.
However, Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Lasher wrote in a filing Wednesday that the defense request was “impractical, invasive, and unsupported by law and the circumstances of the case.”
U.S. District Judge Christina Reiss this week set a hearing in September to air the dispute.
Prosecutors have filed notice with the court that they will seek the death penalty for Youngblut, if convicted. Vermont does not have a death penalty under state law. However, the case was brought under federal law where the death penalty is permitted. 
Youngblut was the driver pulled over in the January 2025 traffic stop, along with a passenger, whom authorities identified as Felix Bauckholt. Bauckholt also went by Ophelia Bauckholt. 
Bauckholt, a German national, was killed in the shootout. Youngblut was also shot. After receiving treatment at a hospital, Youngblut was taken into custody a few days later on federal charges.
Youngblut and Bauckholt had been linked by law enforcement to a group known as the Zizians whose members have been connected to six homicides across the country, including Maland’s death in Vermont.
The group is a breakaway faction of the so-called Rationalist movement in the San Francisco Bay Area. Zizian members reportedly subscribe to beliefs focused on veganism, gender identity and preventing harmful effects from artificial intelligence.
Lasher wrote in Wednesday’s filing that law enforcement agents who observed Youngblut before and during the vehicle stop used multiple electronic devices, including government-issued and personal cellphones.
Lasher raised privacy concerns regardless of ownership. Agents’ own devices would contain personal information unrelated to the law enforcement case, Lasher wrote. Additionally, government-issued devices would include data unrelated to this investigation and case, he added.
“Further,” the prosecutor wrote, “the number of devices included in the defendant’s request would be substantial and present issues with acquisition, storage, and review.”
Lasher wrote that a “case-specific approach” would be more appropriate. He added that he planned to provide more detail about what the government has done to address the issue “at or prior” to the September hearing. 
The prosecutor, in his four-page filing Wednesday, also briefly addressed an assertion in the defense motion that challenged the validity of the traffic stop.
Law enforcement documents, according to the defense motion, had claimed the stop was due to immigration concerns. But the defense team contended in its filing that by the time of the traffic stop, authorities had already determined that Bauckholt was in the U.S. on a valid visa. 
Lasher, in his filing, wrote that the government “does not concede” that the defense characterization is accurate. 
“The source the defendant cited for that premise indicated only” that a visa had been issued, not that it was still valid at the time of the vehicle stop, Lasher wrote.
Youngblut pleaded not guilty and is being held without bail awaiting trial.
Steven Barth, an attorney for Youngblut, declined to comment Thursday on the prosecution filing. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Vermont also declined to comment Thursday.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Planned Parenthood of Michigan to close three clinics after funding cuts
description: Planned Parenthood of Michigan announced on Thursday that, effective immediately, it would be permanently closing three locations in Lansing, Livonia and Warren in the face of funding changes and financial constraints after Republican federal legislation changed the eligibility of Medicaid coverage at Planned Parenthood.  A press release from the organizatio[...]
text:
Planned Parenthood, Detroit |Susan J. DemasPlanned Parenthood of Michigan announced on Thursday that, effective immediately, it would be permanently closing three locations in Lansing, Livonia and Warren in the face of funding changes and financial constraints after Republican federal legislation changed the eligibility of Medicaid coverage at Planned Parenthood. 
A press release from the organization said that it had faced a $4.2 million decline in patient care reimbursement and federal family planning funding from the prior fiscal year. 
“We have to reshape how we deliver care so Planned Parenthood of Michigan can continue serving patients for generations to come,” Paula Thornton Greear, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood of Michigan, said. “That means concentrating our resources at regional access points and procedural sites and continuing to expand virtual care across Michigan. These are painful decisions, but they are strategic decisions grounded in where we can preserve access for the greatest number of patients.”  
She added that the future of patient care cannot rely on federal funding that can be taken away based on the desires of the politicians in power at any given time. 
“Maintaining continuity of care for our patients is our highest priority,” said Dr. Kate Starr, Chief Medical Officer of Planned Parenthood of Michigan. “We are working directly with patients to make sure their treatment plans, prescriptions, and ongoing care continue. Whether patients see us in person at one of our health centers or through virtual care, our commitment to person-centered, evidence-based medicine remains absolute.”  
These closures were not unforeseen — in May, the organization said that they would be forced to close clinics if they did not receive additional one-time state funding. 
Planned Parenthood clinic in Marquette, MI on Dec. 9, 2021. The clinic closed in April 2025 due to funding cuts. | Allison R. Donahue
Though the ban on Medicaid coverage for non-abortion coverage at Planned Parenthood expired at the start of July, the group said in May that the federally-funded Title X program that had previously covered around a quarter of the group’s funding had already been used up for the fiscal year, which does not end until October.
Planned Parenthood of Michigan sent an open letter to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer requesting $5 million in state funding, writing, “Put simply: there is no one else who can act to save our health centers. It is down to you.” 
In response, however, Whitmer deferred to the state Legislature, with a spokesperson from her office saying at the time, “Under the Michigan Constitution, the legislature has the responsibility to allocate state funds. We would encourage any organization or individual to work with the legislature on their budget asks.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Thornton Greear criticized Whitmer’s inaction, saying that “Michigan patients are not a football to be tossed around from branch to branch of the government.”
Whitmer released a statement Thursday criticizing the closures as a result of “DC Republicans’ historic attacks on reproductive freedom, health care access, and Medicaid.”
“We’ve been clear about this since the passage of the ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ last year: these devastating cuts would force key health care providers like Planned Parenthood to close doors and shutter services, cutting Michiganders off from the critical health care they need,” Whitmer continued. “Planned Parenthood provides critical care, like cancer screenings, routine checkups, menopause treatment, and more, which are all at risk due to the DC Republicans’ cuts.”
Whitmer’s statement did not address Planned Parenthood’s earlier request for $5 million in state funding, and a spokesperson from her office did not respond to a request by Michigan Advance for comment on the impacts of her decision in May. 
At least one Democratic state legislator did criticize Whitmer for it on social media, however, including Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia), whose district includes the now-shuttered Livonia Planned Parenthood clinic.

*DC Republicans and MI’s Democratic governor who ignored Planned Parenthood’s pleas for help and legislators’ plans for how you could help fund them while trying to use them as leverage to appease Donald Trump.
Fixed that for you. Fight like hell though, right? https://t.co/3QcUjuWkPr
— Laurie Pohutsky (@lpohutsky19) July 30, 2026

Whitmer was not the only official to criticize the decision and to similarly blame Republican legislators for the funding crisis. 
“These closures make it harder for women to access routine and lifesaving reproductive care, and it is the direct consequence of every single Michigan Republican in Congress voting to pass Trump’s budget law that has ripped away healthcare and gutted Medicaid,” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said in a statement. “These closures lie directly at the feet of D.C. Republicans who have stood by Trump and his disastrous agenda.
Meanwhile, anti-abortion organizations celebrated the closures, with Right to Life of Michigan President Amber Roseboom saying that the closures are due to “mismanagement of their own national organization, not the government.”
“This is good news for Michiganders who care about quality care and accountability,” she said in a press release.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Rankin deputy who punched and broke inmate’s jaw gets a new role protecting schools
description: The Facebook page of the Rankin County Sheriff’s Office posted a photo Tuesday, July 28, 2026, showing that Jordan McQueary, fourth from left, received his Mississippi law enforcement training certification and announcing that he has been assigned as a school resource officer.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow examining immigration and criminal justice issues. She can be reached at mukta.joshi@nytimes.com.
A Rankin County jail guard who was caught on camera in 2022 punching an inmate and breaking his jaw will now police schoolchildren in the county. 
In a Facebook post Tuesday, the Rankin County Sheriff’s Department shared that Jordan McQueary, the former guard, had been assigned as a school resource officer, and congratulated him on completing his law enforcement training. 
In a video that surfaced in January, McQueary can be seen lunging and punching an inmate in the face, knocking him to the ground, after a verbal altercation. The inmate, Dustin Rives, suffered a fractured jaw and developed a deep infection during the following month, ultimately requiring surgery. 
In his incident report, McQueary quoted Rives as saying to a female guard, “Shut up, bitch, before I punch you in the face.” Rives said he did use that language, but said it was directed at the male trusty who accompanied the guards, not the female guard. 
“Before inmate Rives could do anything kind of harm to another officer, I struck him and placed him on the ground,” McQueary wrote. 
David Fathi, director of the National Prison Project at the American Civil Liberties Union who reviewed the incident for Mississippi Today, said punching a detainee could only be justified in self-defense, which was not the case according to McQueary’s own report.
Jason Dare, attorney for the sheriff’s department, said, “The single slap in response to Rives (1) calling a female jailer a “b****”, (2) threatened to punch her,  then (3) raising his right fist to follow through with his threats, appears permissible under Fourteenth Amendment standards.” 
About a minute and a half after McQueary punched Rives, McQueary can be seen escorting the inmate away with his hands behind his back, pants pulled down and genitals exposed. “I was begging them to pull up my pants,” Rives wrote in his 2022 complaint to the department. “They laughed and said they wouldn’t.”
Rives was one of at least nine jail inmates who filed complaints or federal lawsuits alleging that McQueary had assaulted them. As is true for other lawsuits against the department, most were filed by inmates themselves, without lawyers, and nearly all were dismissed. 
Dare said none of the pro se claims filed against McQueary resulted in a finding of impropriety against him.
A supervisor closed Rives’ complaint three days after he filed it, and Rives said he never heard from the department again. 
The supervisor wrote that the department had provided a “satisfactory response,” involving scheduling a medical appointment and informing Rives that he had a right to press charges against McQueary after he was released. The supervisor’s report did not indicate whether McQueary was questioned or disciplined about the incident. 
Mississippi Today and The New York Times had previously uncovered allegations of widespread violence in the jail and a culture of brutality condoned and encouraged by top officials.
In 2024, the sheriff’s department honored McQueary for his “outstanding” work in the jail. 
“School resource officers protect children from violence. So the question is — would parents, children, teachers, and/or faculty feel safe with Deputy McQueary protecting their school?“ Dare said. “Based on the totality of unmanipulated facts, Deputy McQueary appears capable of protecting a school and helping to maintain a safe, secure learning environment.”
McQueary did not respond to a request for comment.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma couple challenges casket law after state hands them $4,000 fine
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – A district judge on Thursday ruled an Oklahoma couple can challenge the constitutionality of a state law that only lets funeral directors sell caskets. The state had sought to dismiss the case, but Oklahoma County District Judge Don Andrews denied the motion. Candice Mentink and Todd Collard sued the Oklahoma Funeral Board […]
text:
Todd Collard and Candice Mentink, owners of Caskets of Honor, celebrate a legal victory Thursday inside the Oklahoma County Courthouse. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A district judge on Thursday ruled an Oklahoma couple can challenge the constitutionality of a state law that only lets funeral directors sell caskets.
The state had sought to dismiss the case, but Oklahoma County District Judge Don Andrews denied the motion.
Candice Mentink and Todd Collard sued the Oklahoma Funeral Board to overturn a state law, which they said prevents them from selling their specialty caskets in their shop in Calvin.
Their lawsuit alleges the state Funeral Board fined the Hughes County business owners $4,000 after they displayed their caskets for sale at the Tulsa Fair in 2021.
Their business, Caskets of Honor, sells caskets wrapped in personalized designs similar to businesses that use wrapping on vehicles.
The caskets are wrapped in religious imagery, hunting or fishing themes, sports colors, family pictures and commemorations of military service.
The married couple said they can ship the caskets to customers in almost every state except Oklahoma.
They’re challenging a state law that forbids them from selling directly to Oklahoma customers. Existing state law that limits that ability to funeral directors.
In order to become a funeral director in Oklahoma, people must complete a two-year program in mortuary science, spend a year as an apprentice under a funeral director and pass two exams on funeral services, the suit said. 
Directors must work in a licensed funeral establishment that offers the full range of facilities and equipment, the suit said.
The couple does not want to become funeral directors or offer funeral services, according to the lawsuit.
The state requirements have no substantial relationship to public health, safety or welfare and do not advance a legitimate government interest, the suit alleges, adding that the state doesn’t regulate caskets.
The law, named the Funeral Services Licensing Act, gives exclusive economic privileges to members of the funeral industry and imposes unreasonable burdens on the couple, according to their lawsuit filed in February.
“Caskets of Honor strives to keep its caskets affordable and avoid the substantial markups that funeral homes regularly place on caskets,” the suit said.
They are asking that the law not be enforced and be found unconstitutional after efforts to eliminate the requirement failed in the Oklahoma Legislature.
The state, represented by the Oklahoma Attorney General’s office, said the law was necessary to protect consumers and the intrastate funeral industry.
Funeral establishments must maintain an inventory of at least five caskets and ensure that bereaved consumers are presented with options without subjecting them to high-pressure sales environments that don’t offer reasonable alternatives, the state argued. 
Funeral establishments must also provide a printed price list for merchandise.
The law protects bereaved consumers making a time-of-need purchase, the state argued.
Advertising an illegal activity is not protected speech, the state argued.
Mentink and Collard said they were pleased the case could move forward.

name: WyoFile
title: Federal project aims to restore Greater Yellowstone’s whitebark pine forests
description:
Disease-resistant trees and climate-refugia mapping are driving ambitious plans to bring back iconic, threatened alpine tree.
The post Federal project aims to restore Greater Yellowstone’s whitebark pine forests appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Last fall, Grand Teton National Park employees loaded thousands of whitebark pine seedlings onto the backs of mules, then hiked them up Paintbrush Canyon. There, they dug small holes and planted the young trees in places where they had the best shot at reaching adulthood.
They were not ordinary whitebark pines, whose seeds already travel around Greater Yellowstone in the mouths of Clark’s nutcrackers. Instead, these trees had been carefully selected for their resistance to an introduced disease called white pine blister rust.
Planting these seedlings was part of a massive project beginning in 2013 to plant disease-resistant whitebark pines throughout the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. White pine blister rust along with mountain pine beetles have killed large swaths of whitebark forests in recent years, leading the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to designate the hardy tree as a federally threatened species in 2022.
To bring back the pine, the U.S. Forest Service, along with nonprofits and other federal agencies, have developed a pipeline to plant thousands of whitebark pines with innate resistance to blister rust in Greater Yellowstone each year. But while the effort to bring rust-resistance to the GYE is well underway, some people wonder if the planned reorganization of Forest Service could put the decades-long project in jeopardy.
“The decline [in whitebark pine] is solvable,” said Libby Pansing, a forest scientist at American Forests, a 151-year-old forest conservation organization. “We have the tools and the ability to solve this problem.”
Map of the ratio of whitebark pine trees within each study area as alive, dead, or infected with blister rust infection from surveys 2012-2015. (National Park Service)
Whitebark pines grow at high elevations throughout the western United States. Each fall, the trees produce a crop of fatty pine nuts that feed bears and birds alike. But throughout the Rocky Mountains, the trees have been dying off en masse, succumbing to white pine blister rust and mountain pine beetle outbreaks that many attribute to climate change. One study found that, as of 2016, the United States contained more dead whitebark pines than live ones.
Diana Tomback, a forest ecologist at the University of Colorado-Denver, has watched the tree’s decline with concern. In 2001, she helped start the Whitebark Pine Ecosystem Foundation, which has funded multiple research and restoration projects.
“The major threat to whitebark pine, if you read the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s species status assessment is white pine blister rust,” Tomback said of the disease that arrived in the U.S. accidentally on infected trees shipped from Europe. “It is a non-native disease that was introduced to the United States.”

A blister rust-resistant whitebark pine seedling grows in Idaho. (Coeur d’Alene Nursery/U.S. Forest Service)

The process for finding trees that are resistant to blister rust, Tomback says, is long. Foresters look for healthy whitebark pines growing areas where the disease is widespread, a sign that the tree might have specific genes that help it fight off a blister rust infection. They then put cages around the tree’s developing pinecones to keep hungry animals out.  As the cones ripen, the foresters return to collect the ripe cones and take them to a Forest Service nursery where workers extract the seeds and plant them in tiny pots.
As the seedlings grow, nursery workers deliberately infect the seedlings with blister rust and closely monitor them for any symptoms of the disease. At about 2 years old, if the trees have not shown signs of a blister rust infection, they are ready for planting.
Each year, the Forest Service nursery in Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, sends roughly 5,000 of these disease-resistant seedlings to Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks, according to Laura Jones, a plant ecologist for Grand Teton. Yet they form just a small fraction of the overall planting operation. 
The Coeur d’Alene Nursery shipped nearly 290,000 rust-resistant seedlings to national forests and national parks across Greater Yellowstone between 2021 and 2025, said Chandra Neils, the nursery’s superintendent.
“Our beneficial impact is not in replacing all that is lost, but in conserving the genetics that are needed to help the plants get through recovery and persist.”Laura Jones, plant ecologist, Grand Teton national park
But even hundreds of thousands of seedlings can only cover a small fraction of the whitebark pine’s range. “It’s too big to replant it all,” Jones said. “Our beneficial impact is not in replacing all that is lost, but in conserving the genetics that are needed to help the plants get through recovery and persist.”

Percentage of surveyed whitebark pine trees that are still alive, based on surveys conducted between 2007 and 2016. (U.S. Forest Service)

In Greater Yellowstone, blister rust is not the only threat facing whitebark pines. Mountain pine beetles have also killed large numbers of the tree. Unlike blister rust, however, whitebark pines have persisted through mountain pine beetle outbreaks for millenia. Research suggests, however, that the warming climate is increasing the frequency and severity of their assaults.
“We do have historical evidence that says that there have been very large [pine beetle] outbreaks before,” Pansing said. “But there is also some research that suggests that it is tied to climate change, and that we should expect to see more outbreaks because of increasing temperatures.”
A 2025 Forest Service study projected that climate change will shrink whitebark pine habitat 80 percent by 2050.
For his master’s thesis at Montana State University, data scientist Stephen Huysman identified high-elevation spots in Greater Yellowstone where water tends to collect. Not only do the precious rust-resistant seedlings have a higher chance of surviving in these sites, he said, but they are also more likely to continue supporting whitebark pines in a warmer, drier future. Huysman has been using his findings to help Grand Teton and Yellowstone decide where to plant their trees.
While whitebark pine restoration is well underway in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, its continuation is not guaranteed. In March, the Forest Service released details of its restructuring plan, which called for replacing its regional offices with state offices and closing many of its experimental forests. While there are no current plans to shutter the Coeur d’Alene Nursery, some details of the reorganization have not yet been released. The uncertainty has many scientists working with the species nervous.
“The Park Service and the BLM send all of their seeds that they collect from potentially resistant trees to Forest Service nurseries and to Forest Service screening centers,” Pansing said. “If that infrastructure falls, that entire part of our ability to restore whitebark pine fails.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Suspended Georgia lawmaker pleads guilty to pandemic unemployment fraud
description: A suspended state lawmaker pleaded guilty Thursday to unemployment fraud, the third in a series of Georgia Democrats to do so.  Former state Rep. Sharon Henderson, a Covington Democrat, was charged in December with fraudulently collecting thousands of dollars in pandemic-era unemployment benefits. Henderson will appear for a sentencing hearing on Nov. 3 befo[...]
text:
Sharon Henderson, who was suspended from her legislative duties earlier this year, has pleaded guilty to collecting nearly $18,000 in COVID-19 unemployment benefits. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderA suspended state lawmaker pleaded guilty Thursday to unemployment fraud, the third in a series of Georgia Democrats to do so. 
Former state Rep. Sharon Henderson, a Covington Democrat, was charged in December with fraudulently collecting thousands of dollars in pandemic-era unemployment benefits. Henderson will appear for a sentencing hearing on Nov. 3 before U.S. District Judge Michael Brown.
Previously, during an initial court appearance in December, Henderson pleaded not guilty. Gov. Brian Kemp suspended her from office in January. 
Henderson declined to comment on Thursday’s plea during a phone call with the Georgia Recorder. 
According to U.S. Attorney Theodore Hertzberg, Henderson falsely stated she was laid off as a Henry County substitute teacher in 2019 and collected $17,811 in unemployment benefits. Following her guilty plea, Hertzberg condemned the lawmaker for abusing the benefits program in a press release. 
“While running for and holding political office, Representative Henderson was fleecing taxpayers, lying to steal money from federal programs intended to help people who lost their jobs due to the pandemic,” Hertzberg wrote. “Her prosecution and conviction demonstrate that elected officials who enrich themselves through fraud will be held accountable for violating the public’s trust.”
According to Hertzberg, the state lawmaker applied for the emergency relief funds in June 2020 while running as a candidate for the Georgia House of Representatives. 
Hertzberg said court documents showed Henderson had not worked for Henry County since 2018, and had only been employed there for five days. On her unemployment benefits application, Henderson falsely claimed she had been employed with the school system until March 2020, and her employment ended because of COVID-19. Additionally, Hertzberg said Henderson continued to receive benefits after she was sworn in as state representative in 2021. 
Henderson represented District 113 for six years, having defeated incumbent Democrat Pam Dickerson in a 2020 primary and was reelected in 2022 and 2024. In April, Henderson unsuccessfully ran to unseat incumbent state Sen. Tonya Anderson of Lithonia in the Democratic primary. 
Two other former Georgia lawmakers, Rep. Karen Bennett of Stone Mountain and Rep. Dexter Sharper of Valdosta, both Democrats, pleaded guilty earlier this year to similar federal charges. Bennett was required to pay back $13,940 and a $1,000 fine but was not sentenced to any jail time by U.S. District Judge Eleanor Ross. 
“Pandemic relief programs were created to help Americans facing genuine hardship — not to enrich those willing to lie for personal gain,” Marlo Graham, special agent in charge of FBI Atlanta, wrote in the press release. “When an elected official abuses taxpayer-funded programs through fraud, it undermines public confidence in both government institutions and the integrity of public service. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to investigate and hold accountable anyone who exploits federal programs for personal benefit.”

title: State Farm auto policyholders in Louisiana can expect a dividend soon. Here’s how much.
description: We now know how much some State Farm auto insurance policy holders can expect to receive when the company sends out special dividends in the coming months. The Louisiana Department of Insurance said Thursday that State Farm’s preferred customers (not high-risk) with a private passenger auto policy in effect as of Dec. 31, 2025, can […]
text:
A Jaguar electric vehicle charges its battery at a rural EV charging station in Abita Springs, La., on June 1, 2024. (Photo credit: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)We now know how much some State Farm auto insurance policy holders can expect to receive when the company sends out special dividends in the coming months.
The Louisiana Department of Insurance said Thursday that State Farm’s preferred customers (not high-risk) with a private passenger auto policy in effect as of Dec. 31, 2025, can expect an average payment of $138 per vehicle. 
State Farm said it will reach out to its eligible customers through email by early September asking them to select a payment method. Customers without an email address on file will receive their checks in the mail.
State Farm customers who have questions about the payments should call 1-888-808-9532 or visit sfdividend.com. The company anticipates payments will be doled out in phases through the rest of the year.
State Farm, which covers about 30% of drivers in Louisiana, announced in February it would cut checks for customers after seeing a boost in business along with lower repair costs for claims filed in 2025. The dividends cover more than 49 million vehicles and total $5 billion, the largest amount in State Farm’s 103-year history. 
Payments to its Louisiana customers statewide are expected to total $136 million.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Stanly Community College trustee resigns after online post draws accusations of racism
description: A member of the Stanly County Community College Board of Trustees said Thursday he has resigned from the board after a controversial Facebook sparked public uproar and accusations of racism. Kelly Lowder wrote in a Facebook message to NC Newsline that he decided to resign because the media attention was a distraction to the college […]
text:
Stanly Community College in Albemarle, NC, (Photo: North Carolina Community College System)A member of the Stanly County Community College Board of Trustees said Thursday he has resigned from the board after a controversial Facebook sparked public uproar and accusations of racism.
Kelly Lowder wrote in a Facebook message to NC Newsline that he decided to resign because the media attention was a distraction to the college and its mission.
“My post had nothing to do with either education or the college and it appears the basement-dwellers from reddit found a way to be offended and wanted to attack me,” Lowder said. 
In the Facebook post that caused the controversy. Lowder, a trustee since 2016, complained about “double standards” for white people saying the “N-word,” as first reported by The Assembly.  
He went on to write that if “white people ‘lose’ in the US,” as he implies they have in other countries,  it will be “really, really, really bad” for everyone else in the world, and he concluded by writing, “maybe the world needs a good purge.”
In his post, Lowder referenced Shiloh Hendrix, a Minnesota woman who was found guilty of one charge of disorderly conduct after calling an 8-year-old autistic child a racial slur on a playground. 
“You can say the N-word 15 times in a 3 minute rap tune, but god forbid some ***hole gets on your nerves and your pasty self lets one drop. #Shiloh,” Lowder wrote.
The post also included a photo of Hendrix and Decarlos Brown Jr., a Black man whom a federal judge found incompetent to stand trial for stabbing a woman to death on the Charlotte light rail in 2025. The judge ordered Brown to spend up to four months in a prison medical facility to try to restore his competency. 
Court order forces NC Republican lawmakers to postpone hearing on high-profile Charlotte stabbing

The text attached to the photo in Lowder’s post read, “Shiloh Hendrix is on trial for saying a word before DeCarlos Brown is for murder. Insane.”
Lowder concluded the post by writing that the number of people who “can’t or won’t produce enough economic output to feed themselves has risen 5-fold in my lifetime,” and then suggests the world needs a “good purge.”
Lowder clarified in the comments under his Facebook post that he used “purge” to mean “starvation as a natural consequence of not having enough productive individuals to feed all the rest,” as reported by The Assembly. 
Lowder said in a statement to NC Newsline that he is proud to have charitably served on the board for 10 years, and that he was in charge of the Finance and Facilities committee when Stanly Community College built a new trades facility, which opened in 2025. 
Walter B. Davis was hired to build the new facility. The Charlotte-based company was founded as a “100% minority owned and operated General Contractor,” according to its website.
“Ultimately at my recommendation, we awarded that contract to Walter B. Davis. To suggest that I’m racist is preposterous,” Lowder wrote, adding, “I will find other ways to serve my community.”  
The post sparked outrage on multiple social media platforms including Reddit, where the post surfaced on the “r/NorthCarolina” board. One anonymous Reddit commentator wrote “SCCC is an excellent community college in an area of great need, and it sucks that this clown is sullying their good reputation.”
Stanly County Community College declined to comment on the controversy. In a statement, college spokeswoman Jennifer Aries clarified that the Board of Trustees is the college’s governing body and operates independently from the college’s administration.
“As a matter of Board governance, individual trustees speak and act only through official, collective action of the Board of Trustees.” Aries wrote. “Personal social media posts by individual trustees do not represent the official views, positions, or policies of Stanly Community College or its Board of Trustees.” 
The chairwoman of the Board of Trustees, Lisa Burris, did not respond to NC Newsline’s requests for comment. 
The North Carolina Community College System oversees community colleges throughout the state. Nathan Hardin, communications director for NCCCS, wrote in a statement to NC Newsline that local boards of trustees govern their colleges independently, and thus carry their own “responsibility and accountability.” 
“The North Carolina Community College System is committed to campuses where every student is welcomed and able to succeed,” Hardin told NC Newsline.“The System Office is in communication with Stanly Community College and trusts its board and leadership to act in the best interest of students, faculty, and staff.”
Six of the 12 trustees for each North Carolina community colleges are appointed by the General Assembly, and the other half by local county commissioners under state law. Lowder was appointed by state lawmakers to a four-year term ending in 2028. Neither state Rep. Cody Huneycutt, R-Stanly, or Sen. Carl Ford, R-Stanly, the county’s only two lawmakers, responded to requests for comment.
